title: In-house cell-to-module assembly beside the vehicle plant instead of buying finished modules
description: [800V BEV] Removes integrator margin/SG&A on non-cell value-add (~€2.5-3k per pack), and replaces bulky module/pack logistics with dense cell logistics; offset by own depreciation and overhead. Baseline: many premium OEMs buy finished modules or complete packs from the cell maker or a tier-1 integrator, often shipped long distance as UN3480 Class 9 dangerous goods in low-density module/pack dunnage, with the integrator margin and SG&A applied to all non-cell value-add (housings, busbars, CSC, assembly, EOL). Proposal: buy qualified cells (shipped dense, ~30% SOC, cell-level packaging) and run module assembly (stacking, compression, laser busbar welding, CSC fitting, module EOL) in a dedicated battery shop adjacent to the vehicle plant, feeding packs sequence-in-line. Engineering retains the module design, so design changes and cost-downs are not renegotiated with an integrator. Benchmark: Porsche builds the Cayenne Electric modules in-house at the Porsche Smart Battery Shop in Horná Streda, Slovakia (Porsche + Porsche Werkzeugbau), close to the Bratislava vehicle plant that started production after the November 2025 premiere; the Cayenne pack uses large pouch cells at 113 kWh gross. title: Dual-output 48V battery with internal 12V tap removes the 12V AGM battery
description: [MHEV] Deletes the 12 V AGM, its tray/hold-down/IBS and cable, and (where validated) the 12 V starter; adds a small buck stage and buffer inside the 48 V battery housing. Baseline: the MHEV carries two batteries - a 48 V lithium-ion pack (Defender: 14 × 8 Ah pouch cells, up to 200 Wh usable, under the floor) and a conventional 12 V lead-acid/AGM battery of 70-95 Ah, linked by a 48/12 V DC-DC converter that charges both. The AGM adds ~20-25 kg, a tray, hold-down, IBS sensor and its own cable set. Proposal: one 48 V battery with a second, low-voltage output. The pack keeps its 14-cell string; a bidirectional 600-800 W buck stage on the battery BMS board supplies a 12 V buffer rail (with 12 V supercapacitor or 4s LFP 5 Ah buffer, ~0.3 kg) for key-off loads and ASIL-relevant redundancy, while the main 2.5-3 kW DC-DC continues to supply 12 V loads during driving. Engine start uses the 48 V BiSG; the 12 V starter is deleted on markets where BiSG cold-start to -30 °C is validated. Quiescent loads (~30-40 mA at key-off) are fed from the 48 V string via the buck stage in low-power mode, with a 30-day park-time target.

title: Relocate MHEV 48V battery from underfloor into cabin dry zone above wading line
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Removes the underbody shield, the submersion-rated seal and membrane and the corrosion-protected bracket set; reduces wading/strike warranty exposure of the 48 V battery. Baseline: the Land Rover MHEV 48 V battery (14 × 8 Ah pouch, ~200 Wh) is packaged under the floor. On an off-road SUV with 900 mm wading (the figure quoted for the Range Rover Electric; an MHEV with the same brand requirement must match it), an underfloor battery is fully submerged and exposed to rock strikes, so it needs a sealed IP6K9K/IPX7-plus housing, a submersible pressure-equalisation membrane, a stone/strike shield and corrosion-protected brackets. Proposal: package the 48 V battery in the sealed cabin dry zone - the cavity under the second-row seat pan or behind the rear quarter trim (≥1,000 mm above ground) - in an IP54 housing with a single 8 mm vent tube led through a grommet to the body exterior so cell vent gas cannot enter the cabin. The underbody shield is deleted, the housing seal downgrades from submersion-rated to splash-rated and the 48 V cable to the BiSG is routed in the existing sill harness channel. 48 V (<60 V DC) is outside ECE R100 scope, but cabin installation still requires venting and crash-zone placement outside the rear crush space.

title: One cell-monitoring AFE chip and BMS software core across 48V and 800V packs
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] One software development, one ASIL safety case, one HIL and EOL toolchain amortised across 50,000 vehicles of both powertrains; AFE volume pooled for price. Baseline: the 48 V MHEV battery (Defender-type, 14 series cells) and the 800 V BEV pack are sourced from different suppliers with different analog front-end (AFE) ICs, MCUs, SOC/SOH algorithms, calibration tools and EOL test sets. Proposal: specify one automotive 14-18-channel ASIL-D-capable AFE family and one BMS software core (cell model, SOC/SOH estimator, balancing, diagnostics, AUTOSAR stack) for both. The 48 V battery uses one AFE (14 cells on one chip); the 800 V pack uses the same AFE in a daisy chain (e.g. ~12-14 chips for ~200 cells, more for a 925 V string). Chemistry-dependent parameters (OCV tables, ageing) sit in calibration, not code. Shared EOL test adapters and HIL rig. Benchmark: BMW Gen6 (iX3 Neue Klasse) shows module-free CTP with high series count; Land Rover MHEV shows a 14-cell 48 V string - both fit a single AFE family.

description: [800V BEV] The thermal headroom already paid for by the second plate is converted into smaller refrigerant hardware and lower charging energy instead of being left unused as a lower cell temperature. With one plate, cell-to-coolant thermal resistance at pack level is ~1.4-1.6 K/kW, so a 45 °C cell limit needs coolant near 20 °C minus the coolant temperature rise. title: Specify roughly 4C fast-charge cells rather than 6-10C megawatt-class cells
description: [800V BEV] Higher electrode loading spreads foil, separator, tabs and formation time over more Wh; avoids cooling and current-path hardware sized for megawatt charging. Baseline: the Chinese cost frontier is pushing charge rates to 6-10C - BYD Tang L launched on a 1000 V Super e-Platform with redesigned Blade LFP cells rated to 10C and 1,000 kW - and a luxury SUV programme can be tempted to match it. High-rate cells need thinner, lower-loading electrodes (e.g. ~2.8-3.2 mAh/cm² instead of ~3.8-4.2), more porous structures and higher-conductivity electrolytes; per kWh that means ~20-30% more current-collector foil and separator area, more formation time and a cooling and current path sized for 800-1,000 A. Proposal: specify the cell for ~4C peak (≈400 kW on ~105 kWh, 10-80% in ~18-20 min), the level BMW iX3 Neue Klasse (400 kW, 108.7 kWh usable, 4695 cells) and Lucid Gravity (400 kW, 123 kWh) offer, and take the higher electrode loading. Foil and separator are ~10-15% of cell cost, so higher loading saves ~3-5% of cell cost per kWh and raises energy density, while pack current stays within 500 A hardware at 900 V-class voltage.

title: Dealer-level repair of one faulty cell block instead of whole-pack warranty replacement
description: [800V BEV] Warranty cost per cell fault drops from a whole pack to one module plus labour; logistics of shipping whole packs as dangerous goods for repair is avoided. Baseline: in many premium BEVs a single faulty cell during warranty ends in replacement of the entire pack (€12,000-15,000) or a dangerous-goods return to a central repair centre, because the cell blocks are bonded into the tray, the joints between blocks are laser-welded and the lid is bonded. Proposal: on a pack that is already built from discrete blocks (the Porsche Cayenne Electric uses in-house developed modules), define a dealer repair process and design for it: each block held by four M8 bolts on a dry gap pad (no adhesive), joints between blocks bolted with torque-angle-monitored M6 screws under touch-safe covers, each block's monitoring board on a plug-in connector, and a bolted lid with a reusable seal on a carrier. An HV-certified dealer bay swaps the faulty block (€1,500-2,500 incl. labour), brings the replacement to within 20 mV of the pack with a balancing tool, reseals and runs a portable pressure-decay leak test. The removed block goes to remanufacture. Warranty, not piece cost, is the lever.

title: In-house battery shop also builds MHEV 48V batteries on shared weld and EOL cells
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Supplier margin and overhead on 48 V assembly value-add disappear; capex, maintenance and engineering staff are shared with the HV shop; inbound logistics moves to cells and housings. Baseline: the MHEV 48 V battery (Land Rover: 14 × 8 Ah lithium-ion cells, ~200 Wh usable) is bought complete from a tier-1, while HV modules for the BEV may be built in-house (Porsche builds the Cayenne Electric modules in its own Smart Battery Shop in Slovakia). The 48 V supplier carries its own stacking, laser-welding, EOL and overhead, plus margin. Proposal: when an in-house HV module shop exists, build the 48 V batteries on the same equipment classes: cell stacking robot with a 48 V gripper set, the same fibre-laser busbar welding cell (time-shared; one 48 V battery is ~28 welds vs ~400 per HV module set), and an EOL station variant (OCV, ACIR, isolation not needed at 48 V, CAN flash). Cells, housing and BMS board are purchased; the OEM owns the 48 V design. At ~50,000 MHEV batteries per year the incremental line is ~€3M (fixtures, gripper, EOL station) against a dedicated supplier line.

title: 14s LFP high-power prismatic cells replace NMC pouch cells in 48V battery
description: [MHEV] LFP high-power prismatic cells are cheaper per cell than NMC high-power pouch, and the rigid can removes the pouch support hardware and part of the cooling need. Baseline: the Land Rover MHEV 48 V battery uses 14 × 8 Ah lithium-ion pouch cells (NMC-type), ~400 Wh nominal with up to 200 Wh used; pouch cells need aluminium-laminate handling, compression frames, foam pads and tab welding. Proposal: keep 14 series cells but switch to LFP high-power prismatic cells of 10 Ah in aluminium cans. Voltage: 14 × 3.2 V = 44.8 V nominal; usable window 2.9-3.55 V/cell = 40.6-49.7 V, inside the ISO 21780/LV 148 unrestricted 36-52 V band, so the BiSG and DC-DC need no change and the BMS keeps 14 channels. Energy 14 × 10 Ah × 3.2 V = 448 Wh nominal. Cans are self-supporting so the compression frame and pouch foam are deleted; two 1 mm steel straps retain the stack. LFP gives higher thermal-runaway onset and long cycle life under the micro-cycling of start-stop/regen. Mass penalty ~1.0-1.5 kg. An LTO alternative (Toshiba SCiB, offered for 48 V mild hybrids) was considered and rejected on cost per Wh.

title: Pack lid with integral coolant channels doubles as the top cold plate
description: [800V BEV] Deletes the separate top cold plate (or the separate lid) together with its fasteners, brackets and one pair of hose connections; roll-bonding is cheaper than vacuum brazing per m². Baseline: the Porsche Cayenne Electric (113 kWh gross, large pouch cells) uses double-sided cooling - two cooling plates heat or cool the pack from above and below. Implemented conventionally, the top plate is a separate cooling plate with its own fixings, hoses and gap filler, sitting under a separate pack lid (stamped 6016-T4 aluminium or SMC). Proposal: make the lid itself the upper heat exchanger. The lid is produced as a two-skin AA3003/AA1050 panel (1.2 + 1.2 mm) with inflated channels 3-4 mm high; the inner skin contacts the module tops through a 1 mm gap filler, the outer skin is the sealing cover, and the coolant ports are brought out at the front lid edge to the same manifold as the bottom plate. The intumescent/mica layer under the lid is retained against top venting. One part replaces two, and top-side cooling becomes affordable for a 400 kW-class charge spec where one plate limits cell temperature rise.

title: Underbody strike logging from existing IMU drives condition-based pack inspection
description: [800V BEV] [Off-road] Turns blanket inspections and conservative replacements into data-driven decisions; evidence log reduces disputed claims; inspection labour is spent only after real events. Baseline: an off-road BEV SUV owner who grounds the pack on a rock has no record of impact energy; dealers inspect the pack underside at each service and after any reported strike, and goodwill/warranty decisions on dented trays and suspected internal damage are made conservatively (pack replacement at ~€12,000+). Proposal: fuse signals that are already on the vehicle - airbag/chassis IMU vertical acceleration, the four ride-height sensors, wheel speeds - with two €1.5 MEMS accelerometers placed on the BMS master board at the pack front and rear. A classifier estimates impact location and energy (J) from the pack-mounted accelerations and the height drop; events above threshold are logged with GPS/time, flagged to the driver, and trigger a pack isolation check (ISO 6469-3) and a dealer inspection. Below threshold, no inspection. The off-road requirement is real: G 580 needed a 57.6 kg underbody plate; Range Rover Electric wades 900 mm on rough ground.

title: Single-dock end-of-line pack tester with blind-mate HV, LV and coolant interfaces
description: [800V BEV] Removes 4 of 5 manual connection cycles and 3 stations of floor space and capex; shorter EOL lead time reduces WIP. Fewer stations also mean fewer floor-space square metres and maintenance contracts on test equipment. Baseline: pack end-of-line typically runs 5-6 stations - helium or pressure-decay enclosure leak test, coolant-circuit pressure decay, HV insulation/hipot, HVIL and LV functional test, BMS flash/calibration and final SOC set - with an operator mating 2-3 connectors and coolant couplings at each station (~1.5 min per mating, 9-10 min per pack). Proposal: design the pack with one EOL test face: the pack HV connector and DC charge port used as-is; LV, CAN and BMS debug via a 24-pin spring-probe field in a sealed lid pocket (covered by a snap cap after test); coolant inlet/outlet via the production dry-break couplings. A single docking fixture clamps the pack once and runs coolant decay, hipot, isolation, HVIL, flash and SOC set in sequence with automatic blind mating; only the enclosure leak test stays separate. Relevant where a pack or module line is built in-house next to the vehicle plant (as Porsche does for the Cayenne Electric).

title: Supplier cell data passport replaces 100% incoming cell OCV/IR re-test at pack plant
description: [800V BEV] Removes a redundant measurement station and its cycle time and quarantine inventory; binning by supplier data improves string matching at no cost. Cells are matched into strings from supplier capacity bins, improving pack balance at no added cost. Baseline: pack/module plants re-measure every incoming cell - open-circuit voltage, AC internal resistance at 1 kHz, dimensions/visual - before stacking, duplicating the cell maker's final grading, and then quarantine cells while k-value (self-discharge) is confirmed. For a ~105 kWh pack of large pouch or 4695 cylindrical cells that is several hundred to ~1,000 cell tests per pack. Proposal: buy cells with a digital data passport per cell (laser-marked ID linked to the supplier's formation data: capacity, ACIR, OCV at two dates and computed k-value, grading bin) transmitted by EDI before the cells arrive. The pack plant does a 2% statistical audit plus a fast OCV-only check in the stacking robot gripper (spring contacts, <0.3 s), and matches cells into modules/strings by supplier bin data. The full inline ACIR/dimension tester is removed. Relevant to in-house module builders such as the Porsche Smart Battery Shop (Cayenne Electric) and to high-cell-count packs like the BMW Gen6 4695 pack.

title: Insulation monitoring folded into the BMS master instead of a standalone IMD module
description: [800V BEV] Deletes an ECU (housing, MCU, power supply, connector, CAN node and harness) by reusing the BMS isolated ADC and processor. Reuses the existing HV dividers, so the added parts are two switches and two precision resistors. Baseline: many 800 V vehicles use a stand-alone insulation monitoring device (IMD) - a small ECU with its own housing, MCU, isolated supply, HV sense resistors and switches, LV connector and CAN node - wired to HV+ and HV- in the BDU, plus the BMS separately measuring pack and link voltages through its own high-ohmic dividers. Proposal: implement the switched-resistor (unbalanced bridge) isolation measurement on the BMS master board, which already has isolated HV measurement channels for HV+/HV- to chassis. Two solid-state photo-MOS switches insert known ~1-2 MΩ resistors alternately between each rail and chassis; the ADC measures the resulting rail-to-chassis voltage shifts and computes Riso+ and Riso- every ~2-5 s, with Y-capacitance compensation by waiting for the RC settle. Accuracy ±15% at 100 kΩ-10 MΩ meets ECE R100 thresholds (100 Ω/V DC, 500 Ω/V where required). At 900-1000 V platforms (NIO ES8 925 V max; BYD Tang L 1000 V) the dividers already exist for voltage measurement, so only the switches and resistors are added.

title: Airbag ECU fires the pack pyro-fuse directly, deleting the BMS crash-firing circuit
description: [800V BEV] Removes a duplicated firing circuit, energy reserve and crash-logic software from the BMS by reusing the ACU, which is already ASIL-D for firing pyrotechnics. Baseline: the pack pyro-fuse (or pyro-switch) is fired by a firing circuit on the BMS master: the airbag control unit (ACU) sends a crash signal over CAN and a hard-wired crash line, the BMS validates it and discharges an energy-reserve capacitor (~20-30 V, several hundred µF) into the igniter, with ASIL-D firing logic and its own diagnostics of the squib loop. Proposal: treat the pyro-fuse igniter like a seatbelt pretensioner. Connect it with a twisted, shielded squib loop to a spare deployment channel of the ACU (current ACUs carry 12-24 firing loops, often with spares), which already contains the energy reserve, squib-resistance diagnostics, crash algorithm and ASIL-D firing path. The BMS keeps only an input to know the fuse state (fuse open detected by link voltage). The igniter must meet the ACU firing envelope (e.g. 1.2 A for 2 ms all-fire). At 900-1000 V packs (NIO ES8, BYD Tang L) fast, certain crash isolation is especially valuable.

title: EN L5 envelope lets MHEV 48V and BEV 12V batteries share one bay
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] One battery bay, tray and clamp design across both powertrains: deletes the separate 48 V bracket set and its tooling, and one BIW variant of studs and holes. Baseline: on a shared platform the MHEV carries a bespoke-shaped 48 V lithium-ion battery (Land Rover: underfloor, 14 × 8 Ah cells) on dedicated brackets plus a 12 V lead-acid battery in its own bay, while the BEV carries a 12 V battery (lithium or AGM) in another bay - different body brackets, trays, clamps and harness drops per powertrain. Proposal: design the 48 V battery to the EN 50342-2 L5 footprint (353 × 175 mm, height ≤190 mm) with the standard bottom hold-down ledge, so it drops into the same body bay, tray and clamp as the BEV's 12 V L5 battery. A 14-cell 48 V string of high-power cells fits that envelope with housing and BMS. Body-in-white gets one battery bay with one set of weld studs; the powertrain-specific part is only the battery itself and its cable terminals (48 V terminal touch-protected and positioned differently from 12 V posts as poka-yoke).

title: BMS-signed battery health certificate replaces dealer full-cycle capacity test
description: [800V BEV] Removes most dealer capacity tests (bay time, cycler equipment) and the conservative pack replacements made when tests are inconclusive. The SOH record also supports used-vehicle residual values. Baseline: a customer range-loss complaint or a certified-used-car check triggers a dealer capacity test - a controlled full discharge and charge over 8-12 hours on a dealer cycler or driving procedure - or the pack is removed and sent to a repair centre; inconclusive results lead to goodwill pack replacements. With 100+ kWh packs (NIO ES8 102 kWh; Lucid Gravity 123 kWh) each wrong replacement costs €12,000+. Proposal: the BMS continuously estimates state of health from partial charge segments (coulomb counting between two rested OCV points ≥30% SOC apart, temperature-corrected), from DC-charge voltage curves (incremental capacity dQ/dV peak tracking) and from resistance growth, and stores a cryptographically signed SOH record with confidence interval. Dealers read the certificate in minutes; a full capacity test is needed only when confidence is low. Warranty rules (e.g. 70% SOH at 8 years) are decided on the certificate.

title: Pack shipped to vehicle line pre-filled with coolant, deleting battery-loop vacuum fill
description: [800V BEV] Shortens the vehicle-line vacuum fill/bleed cycle and removes air-related rework; pack plant already has coolant handling at EOL, so filling there is cheap. Baseline: the battery cooling circuit is filled at the vehicle line after marriage - vacuum evacuation of the whole battery/EDU loop (~10-12 l), fill, and air-bleed with the pump running - and the pack itself arrives dry, having been leak-tested with air at the pack plant. Air trapped in the cold-plate channels is the slowest part of bleeding and a source of warranty (gurgle noise, local hot cells). Proposal: fill the pack cold plates (~3-4 l) with the production coolant at pack EOL, under vacuum, right after the circuit pressure-decay test, and close them with dry-break couplings; the vehicle hoses carry the mating dry-break halves. At marriage the couplings connect with <2 ml spill and no air ingress; the vehicle fill station only fills and bleeds the remaining ~7-8 l of hoses, pump and chiller. Relevant to packs with two cooling plates (Porsche Cayenne Electric double-sided cooling), where the top plate is hardest to bleed.

title: Delete conformal coating on in-pack CMU boards using pollution-degree-2 creepage design
description: [800V BEV] Removes coating material, masking, spray, cure and AOI-UV inspection from 12-15 boards per pack; frees a bottleneck in PCBA lines. Coating-cure WIP also disappears. Baseline: cell monitoring unit (CMU) boards inside the pack are conformally coated (acrylic or silicone, selective spray ~50 µm, UV-fluorescence inspection, 30-60 min cure) on the assumption of condensation inside the pack; a ~200-cell 800-925 V pack carries 12-15 such boards. Proposal: treat the sealed pack interior as pollution degree 2 (non-conductive pollution, occasional temporary condensation) per IEC 60664-1 and design the CMU board for it: creepage on outer layers sized for the module/zone voltage (≤80 V between adjacent nets, so ≥1.0-1.2 mm is ample), HV-isolation barrier distances placed only at the daisy-chain isolation interface (slot-milled), solder-mask-defined pads, and no fine-pitch parts in drip zones. The pack keeps its pressure-equalisation valve and the BMS master (which sees full pack voltage) keeps coating. Coating, cure and inspection steps are deleted for the CMUs. Relevant to module-based packs with one CMU per module (Porsche Cayenne Electric uses in-house modules) and to high-series-count 900 V packs.

title: Conductive floor-sink cooling of 48V battery deletes fan and air duct
description: [MHEV] Deletes fan, its controller channel, duct, grille and filter, and the fan service item; reduces 12 V load and NVH. Removing the air path also removes the filter service item and the fan electrical load (~15-25 W when running), giving a small fuel saving. Baseline: some MHEV 48 V batteries use forced-air cooling - a 12 V brushless fan, intake grille and PP duct drawing cabin or underbody air through the cell stack - or a small liquid plate tied to the engine loop. Heat load is modest: at 20 kW BiSG peaks with ~25 mΩ string resistance the I²R is ~4.4 kW only for seconds, while the RMS over a WLTP-type cycle is ~60-120 W. Proposal: passive conduction cooling. Cells sit on a 1.5 mm, 3 W/m·K gap pad on an aluminium base plate (or the housing floor with insert plate) that bolts to the body floor pan, using the floor (a ~0.5 m² steel/aluminium sheet in airflow) as heatsink; thermal mass of the cells (~3 kg × 1.0 J/g·K) buffers transients. The BMS derates BiSG power above 50 °C cell temperature, which on a 2-hour hot-climate tow occurs only in the top percentile. Benchmark: Land Rover MHEV packages a ~200 Wh 48 V battery under the floor; Toshiba offers SCiB LTO cells specifically for 48 V mild hybrids, showing 48 V batteries are a power-sized, small-energy application.

title: Back-to-back MOSFET switch replaces electromechanical relay in 48V battery
description: [MHEV] Deletes the main relay, precharge relay and resistor; MOSFET switch price has fallen below a 400 A relay plus precharge circuit; no contact wear warranty. Baseline: 48 V MHEV batteries commonly disconnect with a 300-400 A electromechanical relay (or contactor) plus a precharge relay and resistor to charge the BiSG inverter DC-link before closing; 48 V DC arcs on opening under load, so relay contacts are large and wear. Proposal: a solid-state switch of 8-10 paralleled 80 V-class automotive N-channel MOSFETs (≈1 mΩ each) per direction in back-to-back configuration (≈0.25 mΩ total), driven by a charge-pump gate driver on the BMS board. Conduction loss at 150 A continuous ≈ 150² × 0.25 mΩ ≈ 5.6 W, spread on an IMS/thick-copper board coupled to the housing. The same MOSFETs perform precharge in linear/PWM mode, deleting the precharge relay and resistor, and open in microseconds on short-circuit (no arc), with di/dt-limited turn-off and a TVS clamp for the cable inductance. Fits the 14-cell 48 V string used in Land Rover MHEVs; 80 V devices cover the ISO 21780 maximum 60 V plus transients.

title: Match series cell count to 18-channel AFE pitch so no chip runs half-empty
description: [800V BEV] Fewer AFE ICs and daisy-chain links for the same cell count, purely by aligning electrical grouping to the chip channel pitch. Freed auxiliary inputs also absorb temperature sensors that previously needed a separate multiplexer. Baseline: pack series count is fixed by voltage and cell choice first, then AFEs are allocated per module; e.g. a 198s pack in 12 modules of 16.5 cells, or 14-channel AFEs on 16-cell modules, leaves chips partly used and forces one AFE per module even where channels are free (typical: 14-16 AFEs with 15-25% unused channels). Proposal: co-design series count, module/zone cell grouping and AFE channel count. With an 18-channel AFE and CTP sense zones of 18 cells, a 216s string (the 925 V-class configuration, as NIO ES8 runs) needs exactly 12 AFEs; a 198s string 11 AFEs. Each AFE removed deletes the chip, its isolated daisy-chain interface (transformer or capacitors), ~30 passives, connector pins and PCB area. Cell-temperature channels (GPIO/aux inputs) are reassigned to the freed slots. In a CTP pack (e.g. BMW Gen6 4695 cell-to-pack) grouping is free of module walls, which makes the alignment easy.

ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Fewer AFE ICs and daisy-chain links for the same cell count, purely by aligning electrical grouping to the chip channel pitch. Freed auxiliary inputs also absorb temperature sensors that previously needed a separate multiplexer.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Fewer CMU boards/AFE sites to place and test; CSC flex layout redrawn. No capex. CMU board count and test time fall in proportion to the AFEs removed (~2-3 fewer boards per pack). CSC flex layout is redrawn once at design stage; tooling unaffected.

title: Capacitor-coupled isolated daisy chain replaces pulse transformers between AFEs
description: [800V BEV] A pair of capacitors costs a fraction of a pair of pulse transformers; area and height on the CMU board also shrink. Magnetics are also single-source items with long lead times; MLCCs are multi-sourced commodities, lowering supply risk premium. Baseline: wired 800 V BMS daisy chains link each AFE to the next through an isolated differential interface using two pulse transformers per link (one at each side), plus common-mode chokes; for a 12-15 AFE chain that is 24-30 transformers at ~€0.6-1.0 each, plus board area. Proposal: within the pack, where adjacent AFEs differ by only one module/zone voltage (≤80 V) and share the same enclosure, use capacitive coupling - two 1 kV-class C0G/X7R capacitors (e.g. 2.2 nF) per line per link - supported by current AFE families. Keep transformer isolation only on the link from the pack chain to the BMS master (the reinforced isolation boundary to LV ground) and across any service-disconnect/pyro-switch split. Noise immunity is preserved by differential signalling and the AFE's built-in common-mode range; cable lengths inside a CTP pack are short (<0.5 m). Applies to wired high-series packs such as the 900-1000 V packs now launched (NIO ES8, BYD Tang L).

title: Contactor weld detection by voltage sensing deletes auxiliary mirror contacts
description: [800V BEV] Contactors without auxiliary contacts are cheaper and a standard variant; deletes auxiliary harness branches and BMS input channels. It also frees two BMS digital inputs per contactor and removes a failure mode (broken auxiliary wire) that otherwise generates false weld faults. Baseline: main positive/negative and DC-charge contactors in many packs are bought with auxiliary (mirror) contacts and their harness to the BMS to detect a welded main contact; this adds a contactor variant, ~€4-6 per contactor and a 2-wire branch each. Proposal: specify contactors without auxiliary contacts and detect welding from HV voltage measurements the BMS already makes. The BMU measures pack voltage (inside contactors), link voltage on the vehicle side of each pole (HV+ and HV-, referenced to chassis via the isolation-monitor divider), and DC-charge-port voltage. Sequencing: after commanded open, the link voltage must decay with the inverter DC-link discharge time constant; a welded pole is identified by opening one pole at a time and checking the vehicle-side voltage relative to chassis. The method covers each pole independently and is executed at every key-off. At 900-1000 V (NIO ES8, BYD Tang L) the existing high-voltage dividers already have the resolution required (±1 V).

title: Isolation-resistance trend after wading detects pack water ingress without humidity sensors
description: [800V BEV] [Off-road] Deletes 2-4 humidity sensors or detection strips, their harness and BMS channels by re-using a measurement that already exists for safety. Early detection also lets service dry and reseal a pack before corrosion forces replacement. Baseline: packs for off-road SUVs with 850-900 mm wading (G 580, Range Rover Electric) often add relative-humidity/dew-point sensors or conductive water-detection strips in the pack low points, wired to the BMS, to detect ingress after deep water. Proposal: delete these sensors and use the BMS isolation monitor (already mandatory) as the ingress detector. After the vehicle reports a wading event (wade-sense ultrasonic or ride-height + wheel-speed data), the BMS samples isolation resistance at 1 min intervals for 2 hours and compares with the stored dry baseline (typically several MΩ for an 800 V pack). Water bridging a busbar to the tray drops isolation in a characteristic step; condensation produces a slow drift that recovers with temperature. A ≥40% drop vs baseline or < 500 Ω/V triggers a service message before ECE R100 limits (100 Ω/V DC) are approached. Low-point drainage remains as designed.

title: Underbody pack plate fastened by 24 captive flanged bolts instead of 50 loose bolts
description: [800V BEV] [Off-road] Halves fastener count, removes separate washers and loose-part handling, and cuts fitting and service time. In service, shield removal after an off-road strike takes half the time, lowering repair labour. Baseline: the Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology attaches its 26 mm, 57.6 kg underbody battery plate with 50 bolts. Large off-road pack shields often use many loose M8/M10 bolts with separate washers, partly because the plate is flat and needs closely spaced attachment to stop drumming and edge peel under rock contact. Proposal: stiffen the shield with formed longitudinal beads (8-10 mm deep) and a turned-up perimeter flange so edge peel and panel modes are carried by the shield itself; attachment pitch can then rise from ~150 mm to ~300 mm, giving 24 attachment points. Use captive flanged M10 bolts (property class 10.9, zinc-flake coated for wading/salt) pre-assembled into the shield with retaining clips, run down by a multi-spindle nutrunner. First panel mode is kept above ~80 Hz to avoid road-induced drumming. Removal for pack service or after an off-road strike is quicker with half the bolts and none dropped in mud.

title: Overmoulded PA66-GF30 coolant spigots on cold plate replace brazed aluminium ports
description: [800V BEV] Eliminates machined spigots and their braze/weld joints; moulding is a single shot with the seal; furnace throughput rises with flat plates. Flat brazing loads also cut furnace energy per plate. Baseline: pack cold plates (bottom plate, and the top plate in double-sided designs such as the Porsche Cayenne Electric) carry machined AA6061 or AA3003 inlet/outlet spigots that are vacuum-brazed or TIG-welded to the plate, then fitted with SAE J2044 quick-connector beads and O-rings; each port is a separate machined part with a braze joint that must pass leak test. Proposal: punch/flare a plain hole in the plate and overmould a PA66-GF30 (hydrolysis-stabilised) spigot directly onto the flared collar with a laser-structured aluminium surface for mechanical/chemical interlock, plus a moulded-in fluoroelastomer (FKM) seal lip; the J2044 bead is moulded. The spigot is outside the brazed core, so the braze furnace load is a flat plate only (better fixture density). Two-plate packs need four ports, so the saving doubles where both sides are cooled.

title: Route DC fast charging through main contactors, deleting the separate charge contactor pair
description: [800V BEV] Removes two 500 A contactors, associated busbars and a fuse from the pack BDU; reduces BDU size. The BDU housing also shrinks by about one contactor footprint, and the HVIL and diagnostics lose two monitored devices; precharge reuse avoids a second precharge path for the charge port. Baseline: many 800 V packs carry a dedicated DC-charge contactor pair (DC+ and DC-, 400-500 A) in the battery disconnect unit so the charge inlet is isolated from the drive DC-link; with a boost-capable drive unit (Lucid Gravity boosts 400/500 V chargers through its rear motor) the charge path is already shared with the inverter. Proposal: connect the DC inlet to the vehicle-side DC-link bus through a pair of inlet-side contactors that are in any case required at the inlet for touch-safety (or a single inlet contactor pair in the front power distribution unit), and charge the pack through the existing main contactors (which are already rated for full charge current when peak charge current is held at ≤500 A, e.g. by a 900 V-class string). The BDU loses one contactor pair, its busbars, fuse branch and HVIL leg. Isolation of the inlet when not charging is kept by the inlet contactors; pack-side isolation by the mains. Welding diagnosis uses voltage sensing.

ideaData.title: Route DC fast charging through main contactors, deleting the separate charge contactor pair
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: many 800 V packs carry a dedicated DC-charge contactor pair (DC+ and DC-, 400-500 A) in the battery disconnect unit so the charge inlet is isolated from the drive DC-link; with a boost-capable drive unit (Lucid Gravity boosts 400/500 V chargers through its rear motor) the charge path is already shared with the inverter. Proposal: connect the DC inlet to the vehicle-side DC-link bus through a pair of inlet-side contactors that are in any case required at the inlet for touch-safety (or a single inlet contactor pair in the front power distribution unit), and charge the pack through the existing main contactors (which are already rated for full charge current when peak charge current is held at ≤500 A, e.g. by a 900 V-class string). The BDU loses one contactor pair, its busbars, fuse branch and HVIL leg. Isolation of the inlet when not charging is kept by the inlet contactors; pack-side isolation by the mains. Welding diagnosis uses voltage sensing.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Removes two 500 A contactors, associated busbars and a fuse from the pack BDU; reduces BDU size. The BDU housing also shrinks by about one contactor footprint, and the HVIL and diagnostics lose two monitored devices; precharge reuse avoids a second precharge path for the charge port.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Smaller BDU; fewer busbar laser-welds and bolted joints (~2 min at BDU assembly). No capex. Smaller BDU with fewer busbar laser-welds and bolted joints (~2 min less at BDU assembly); BDU EOL test sequence shortened by the charge-contactor checks. No capex.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count −6 to −8 in the BDU; simpler HVIL loop; one fewer contactor P/N. Part count −6 to −8 in the BDU; simpler HVIL loop; one fewer contactor part number and one fewer busbar variant; fewer high-current bolted joints to torque-audit.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium - one contactor pair deleted.
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: 2 × 500 A HV contactors €14-18 each = €28-36 + busbars €4-6 + fuse branch €4-6 + HVIL leg €1-2 = €37-50; minus higher main-contactor life spec €3-5 and validation €1-2 → €30-45. Net €30-€45 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €1.50M-€2.25M per year.

ideaData.riskNotes: Main contactors see more switching cycles (every charge) - check electrical life rating (switching under no load normally). Charging fault isolation path must be re-analysed (ISO 26262). Validate per IEC 61851-23, ISO 17409, ECE R100 rev.3, ISO 6469-3.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Lucid Gravity (2025, 926 V) — Charging path shared with the rear drive unit, which boosts 400/500 V chargers to the 926 V pack.. How this differs: Removes the pack-internal charge contactor pair once the charge path is shared with the drive DC-link.

title: Sprayed stone-chip coating limited to tray zones not covered by the underbody shield
description: [800V BEV] Coating material and spray time scale with area; covered zones gain no protection from a coating that the shield already provides. Lower coating mass also saves ~2 kg per pack. Baseline: the aluminium pack tray underside is fully sprayed with a 1.0-1.5 mm polyurethane or PVC-based stone-chip/underbody coating (~2.0-2.2 m², ~3.0-3.5 kg) to resist gravel and corrosion, even where a separate underbody shield later covers it - as on off-road BEVs where a full plate protects the pack (G 580: 26 mm plate attached by 50 bolts). Proposal: spray only the zones left exposed after the shield is fitted - the perimeter flange band (~120 mm), cross-member feet and the rear section outside the shield - with robot path masking (no tape), and leave the shielded area as bare or e-coated aluminium (AA6xxx with conversion coat). Coated area falls by ~60-70% on fully shielded versions and by ~30-40% on part-shielded versions. Coating thickness at the exposed edges is kept at 1.5 mm. The shield-to-tray gap is ventilated so the bare zone dries after wading.

title: Silicon IGBT inverter on secondary front axle, SiC reserved for primary rear
description: [800V BEV] Si IGBT die costs a fraction of SiC per ampere: a 1200 V/400 A-class IGBT six-pack is estimated at €130-€170 versus €300-€420 for an equivalent SiC module, so the front module delta is €150-€230. Shared housing, DC-link, control board and cold plate keep the variant cost low; a modest cold-plate/derating allowance is netted off. Baseline: many 800 V luxury SUVs specify 1200 V SiC MOSFET power modules on both axles, so the front inverter carries the same expensive SiC die area (typically 6 switch positions with several paralleled dies each) as the rear, even though in a rear-biased dual-motor calibration the front motor delivers only a minor share of WLTP cycle energy and spends most of the cycle at low torque or idle. SiC's advantage over Si is mainly lower switching and partial-load conduction loss; on an axle that contributes a small share of cycle energy, the cycle-efficiency gain from SiC is worth only a fraction of a percent of vehicle range. Proposal: specify a 1200 V trench field-stop Si IGBT six-pack (IGBT7-class, 400-450 A rated, with Si freewheel diodes) for the front inverter at 8-10 kHz switching, keep 1200 V SiC on the rear inverter. Both inverters share the housing casting, DC-link capacitor, control board (one gate-driver resistor/turn-off variant), connectors and cold plate interface; only the power module and gate-driver BOM variant differ. Benchmark

title: Flux-free freewheeling ASM front axle makes the disconnect unit unnecessary
description: [800V BEV] Removes 1.2-1.6 kg NdFeB (estimated €60-€80/kg incl. coating and magnetising → €84-€112) and the complete disconnect unit (€45-€70), partly offset by the ASM cage, extra copper/stack (€35-€55) and higher inverter current rating (€10-€15). Baseline: a typical premium dual-motor SUV puts a permanent-magnet synchronous machine (PMSM) with roughly 1.2-1.6 kg of sintered NdFeB on the secondary axle. Because rotor magnets induce back-EMF and stator iron loss whenever the wheels turn the rotor, the PMSM either costs range at cruise or must be paired with a mechatronic decoupler (actuator, clutch sleeve, fork, position sensor, control software). Proposal: choose the machine technology so that no decoupler is required: an asynchronous machine (ASM, magnet-free rotor with conductor bars) on the secondary axle. With zero stator current an ASM has essentially no air-gap flux, hence no magnet-induced iron loss and no back-EMF; the remaining parasitic loss is gear churning, bearing and seal friction, which this proposal accepts (estimated 150-300 W at 130 km/h with low-viscosity oil and reduced oil level). Torque is available within ~50-100 ms (flux build-up) without clutch synchronisation. The ASM needs a slightly longer active length, more stator copper and ~10% higher inverter current (lower power factor), which are netted off. Benchmarks: BMW iX3 Neue Klasse pairs a Gen6 EESM

Benchmarks: BMW iX3 Neue Klasse pairs a Gen6 EESM on the rear with a new ASM on the front axle - a magnet-free secondary axle; the Kia EV9 instead fits a Hyundai Transys Disconnector Actuator System to its PMSM secondary axle, credited with 6-8.3% electrical efficiency improvement, which shows the size of the magnet-drag penalty that the ASM avoids by physics rather than added hardware.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Rotor line drops magnet insertion, bonding and magnetising (and the magnet-handling safety cell) for the front motor; conductor bars can be bought-in. DAS sub-assembly and its EOL engagement test disappear from the EDU line; cage casting can be bought-in.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Deletes the actuator, dog clutch, shift fork, return spring, position sensor and connector (6-8 parts) plus one LV harness branch. No live-magnet handling, so rotor insertion into the stator no longer needs a guided magnetic-force fixture.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High - removes both rare-earth content and a mechatronic subsystem
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Low case: magnets €84 + DAS €45 - ASM extra €55 - inverter current €15 = €59; high case: €112 + €70 - €35 - €10 = €137 per vehicle; €59 × 50,000 = €2.95M; €137 × 50,000 = €6.85M.

ideaData.riskNotes: ASM rotor losses heat the rotor in sustained high-load (towing, off-road) - verify with continuous-power test and rotor temperature model. Validate efficiency in WLTP with torque-split calibration, NVH (slot harmonics), and functional safety of permanent connection (ISO 26262 for unintended torque). LV 124 and ISO 16750 for the inverter variant.

title: Twin-rear-motor double inverter sharing one DC-link, MCU and housing
description: [800V BEV] Removes one housing (€40-€55), 300-350 µF of film capacitance (€25-€35), one control board/MCU (€30-€45), one HV inlet + EMI filter (€20-€30), and one EOL test and assembly cycle (€8-€12); a larger cold plate adds €6-€10. Applied to twin-motor variants (assumed 20% take rate). Baseline: when a tri- or quad-motor variant puts two motors on one axle, suppliers often fit two complete single inverters: two housings, two DC-link capacitors (e.g. 2 × 500 µF film), two EMI filters, two HV input connectors, two control boards with separate MCUs, two LV connectors. Proposal: one double inverter in a single HPDC housing - two SiC six-pack power stages on one common cold plate, one DC-link capacitor, one EMI filter and HV inlet, and one dual-core lockstep MCU control board running both motor controllers. Interleaving the two PWM carriers by 90-180° makes the two inverters' DC-side ripple currents partially cancel, cutting capacitor RMS ripple current by an estimated 30-40%, so the shared DC-link can be sized at ~650-700 µF instead of 1,000 µF. One position-sensor interface per motor and two phase-busbar exits remain. Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology fits, per axle, two motors, two transmissions and a double inverter in a shared housing.

title: Low-range shift on rear EDU only; front EDU keeps a fixed shorter ratio
description: [800V BEV] [Off-road] Deletes the front planetary low-range set (€45-€60), its shift actuator and sensor (€25-€35) and extra housing machining (€8-€12), adding front-motor overload thermal mass/oil capacity (€8-€12). Applied to the off-road pack (assumed 30% take rate). Baseline: the electric off-road reference fits a shiftable two-speed transmission to every motor - a 2:1 low range usable up to 85 km/h - so each axle carries planetary sets, shift elements, actuators and position sensors. Proposal: in our luxury SUV keep the 2:1 sun-locked planetary low range only in the rear EDU, which carries the larger share of load in the cases that need low range (gradient climbing and 3,500 kg towing both shift weight rearward: at 30° climb with CG at 0.75 m and 3.0 m wheelbase, rear static share rises ~13 percentage points). The front EDU stays single-speed with a ratio about 10% numerically higher than the rear high gear and a 30-second overload current rating, so its wheel torque in crawl is traction-limited before it is motor-limited. Crawl control (2-8 km/h) is executed by both axles' inverters; only the rear changes ratio, so one shift actuator, one shift-position sensor and one planetary set are deleted. Benchmark: Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology - each motor has its own two-speed transmission, 2:1 low range up to 85 km/h, centrally shifted.

ideaData.title: Low-range shift on rear EDU only; front EDU keeps a fixed shorter ratio
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the electric off-road reference fits a shiftable two-speed transmission to every motor - a 2:1 low range usable up to 85 km/h - so each axle carries planetary sets, shift elements, actuators and position sensors. Proposal: in our luxury SUV keep the 2:1 sun-locked planetary low range only in the rear EDU, which carries the larger share of load in the cases that need low range (gradient climbing and 3,500 kg towing both shift weight rearward: at 30° climb with CG at 0.75 m and 3.0 m wheelbase, rear static share rises ~13 percentage points). The front EDU stays single-speed with a ratio about 10% numerically higher than the rear high gear and a 30-second overload current rating, so its wheel torque in crawl is traction-limited before it is motor-limited. Crawl control (2-8 km/h) is executed by both axles' inverters; only the rear changes ratio, so one shift actuator, one shift-position sensor and one planetary set are deleted. Benchmark: Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology - each motor has its own two-speed transmission, 2:1 low range up to 85 km/h, centrally shifted.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes the front planetary low-range set (€45-€60), its shift actuator and sensor (€25-€35) and extra housing machining (€8-€12), adding front-motor overload thermal mass/oil capacity (€8-€12). Applied to the off-road pack (assumed 30% take rate).
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Front EDU is the common single-speed unit used on the road variants: no front shift-calibration step at EOL, one fewer gear-set variant through hobbing/grinding. Rear unit keeps the two-speed line. Saves one actuator end-of-line function test.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Front EDU part count falls by ~25-35 parts (sun, planets, carrier, ring, shift sleeve, fork, actuator, sensor, bearings). Shift software handles one axle; service stocks one front EDU for all trims.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium - applies to off-road pack only
costSavingPotential.percentage: 8-12% of the front EDU cost on equipped vehicles

Mitigation: tighter front ratio or short-term inverter boost.

title: EDU gears hard-finished on shared MHEV transfer-case and axle gear cells
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Avoids one to two dedicated EDU grinding/hobbing cells (€3M-€5M capex amortised over 350,000 units in 7 years = €8-€14 per vehicle), and raises utilisation of shared cells to cut overhead per part (€4-€6 per vehicle), minus changeover and dual-purpose fixtures (€2-€3). Baseline: a platform building both MHEV and BEV usually puts EDU gears on a dedicated line - soft turning, hobbing, case-carburising, hard turning and generating grinding - sized for the BEV forecast. With an uncertain BEV/MHEV mix, a dedicated generating-grinding cell (estimated €2.5M-€3.5M each) may run at 45-60% utilisation. Proposal: constrain EDU gear design to the envelope of the MHEV transfer-case and rear-axle gears (normal module 1.5-2.5 mm, tip diameter ≤220 mm, shaft length ≤450 mm, same 20MnCr5 steel and low-pressure carburising + high-pressure gas quench recipe at 0.6-0.8 mm CHD) so both powertrains' gears run through the same hobbing, LPC furnace and generating-grinding cells with quick-change workholding. The line flexes with the actual mix rather than being duplicated. Benchmark: BMW is producing its Gen6 e-drive motors at Steyr - its historic engine plant - where it has started series production on a second e-drive motor line, illustrating reuse of an ICE powertrain plant for electric drive manufacturing.

title: Shaft grounding ring and one insulated bearing per motor manage 800 V shaft voltage
description: [800V BEV] A ceramic-ball bearing carries an estimated €20-€30 premium over steel; two per motor become one coated bearing (€8-€12 premium) plus one grounding ring (€6-€9). Applied to two EDUs per vehicle. Baseline: at 800 V with SiC switching at 20-50 V/ns, the inverter's common-mode voltage couples capacitively onto the rotor shaft and discharges through bearing oil films, causing EDM fluting. A conservative design specifies ceramic-ball bearings at both rotor positions of every motor and sometimes on the gearbox input shaft, paying the premium four to six times per vehicle. Proposal: a system-level architecture per EDU: (1) a conductive microfibre shaft-grounding ring on the rotor shaft at the gearbox end gives a low-impedance path to housing, keeping current out of the gearbox bearings; (2) one current-insulated bearing with an Al2O3 ceramic-coated outer ring at the non-drive end breaks the circulating high-frequency loop; (3) standard steel bearings elsewhere; (4) a low-impedance stator-to-housing bond and reduced-common-mode PWM at low speed lower the source voltage. Ceramic-ball bearings remain only where speed above ~18,000 rpm needs them for friction reasons. Benchmarks: Schaeffler's 800 V e-motor series uses ceramic balls to reduce friction and prevent current passage, and Schaeffler offers Insutect-coated current-insulated bearings; SKF supplies shaft grounding ring

title: Crawl-mode inverter strategy avoids sizing SiC die for off-road stall current
description: [800V BEV] [Off-road] Avoids a 15-25% die-area increase on the rear SiC module (estimated €45-€80 of die per off-road-capable inverter) at the cost of software, a coolant-priority calibration and junction observer validation (€5-€8 per vehicle amortised). Baseline: at near-zero speed (rock crawling, hill-start with 3,500 kg trailer) the motor's electrical frequency is only a few hertz, so one inverter phase leg carries close to peak current for a long fraction of each cycle instead of the sinusoidal average; junction temperature then follows the peak, not the RMS. Designers commonly upsize SiC die area by 15-25% to cover this stall/crawl case. Proposal: a combined crawl strategy so die area stays sized for road duty: (1) in crawl mode drop switching frequency from ~10 kHz to 4-5 kHz and use discontinuous PWM (DPWM) so each leg is clamped for 120° and switching loss falls ~35-50%; (2) raise coolant flow to the inverter by priority valve when vehicle speed <8 km/h and torque >60%; (3) use the low-range gear (where fitted) so motor speed and electrical frequency are doubled for the same wheel speed; (4) a junction-temperature observer limits torque only as a last step. Benchmark: Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology offers an off-road crawl function for 2-8 km/h together with a 2:1 low range - exactly the operating point that drives stall-current heating.

title: Rear EDU packaged motor-high above half-shaft line to gain clearance and delete guard

title: Inverter active-damping control lets EDU mounts use plain rubber, not hydraulic mounts
description: [800V BEV] Replaces 3-4 hydraulic EDU mounts (€22-€35 each) with rubber bushes (€8-€12 each): €14-€23 per mount position; two EDUs, about 3.5 mount positions each on average; software calibration amortised €2-€3 per vehicle. Baseline: luxury BEVs often isolate each EDU with three or four hydraulically damped or decoupler-type mounts (similar to engine hydro-mounts) to control low-frequency driveline shuffle (2-8 Hz) on tip-in/tip-out and regen transitions, while keeping high-frequency gear-whine isolation. Hydro mounts cost several times a rubber bush and add a fluid-leak failure mode. Proposal: move shuffle control into the inverter: a motor-speed-based active damping loop (observer on half-shaft twist, torque correction at 10 kHz control rate, bandwidth up to ~30 Hz) suppresses the first driveline torsional mode, and torque-rate shaping on regen transitions; the mounts are then specified as two-stage rubber bushes (NR/BR blend, with voids for low dynamic stiffness at gear-whine orders) tuned only for high-frequency isolation and travel limits. Benchmark: Lucid's drive unit integrates motor, gearbox and inverter in a 74 kg package - an integrated, low-mass unit where the inverter controls the whole driveline, which is the precondition for control-based shuffle damping; BMW's Gen6 likewise integrates the inverter into the motor housing.

title: Twin-motor axle shares one oil pump, filter and sump for both motors
description: [800V BEV] Deletes one electric oil pump (€25-€35), one filter (€4-€6), one oil-to-coolant exchanger (€15-€22) and one sensor (€3-€4); adds galleries/orifices and a larger pump (€6-€9). Applied to twin-motor variants (assumed 20% take rate). Baseline: when two motors and two reduction gearsets sit on one axle (tri- or quad-motor torque vectoring), a supplier-led design often duplicates each motor's oil system - two electric oil pumps, two filters, two oil-to-coolant heat exchangers, two temperature sensors and two sumps - because each motor-gearbox half was carried over from a single-motor EDU. Proposal: a common sump in the shared housing feeding one electric oil pump (BLDC, ~12-16 L/min), one suction/pressure filter and one oil-to-coolant plate exchanger, distributing to both motors' stator spray rings and rotor bores through cast galleries with calibrated orifices (e.g. Ø1.2-1.8 mm) for balanced flow. A dividing weir keeps oil levels equal in cornering. Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology places two motors, two transmissions and a double inverter in a shared housing per axle, which makes a shared lubrication and cooling circuit physically possible; Zeekr's 800 V drive systems use oil cooling with flat-wire motors, the cooling method this proposal shares.

title: Shift-by-wire park actuator shared between MHEV 8-speed and BEV EDU
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Doubles actuator volume (~50k/yr), cutting piece price 10-15% (€3-€5), removes one development/validation programme (€0.5M-€0.8M → €1.4-€2.3 per vehicle over 7 years), and simplifies software (€0.5-€1). Baseline: the MHEV 8-speed automatic uses an electrically actuated park lock (shift-by-wire) with its own actuator, and the BEV rear EDU uses a separate park-lock actuator from a different supplier - two BLDC actuators, two position sensors, two connectors and two software stacks for the same function: rotate a cam to engage a park pawl and hold 2.8 t on a 30% gradient. Proposal: specify one park-lock actuator (BLDC motor + worm/spur reduction + contactless angle sensor, IP6K9K, 12 V) with one mechanical interface - a splined output and three-bolt flange - used on both the 8-speed transmission and the EDU. Each gearbox adapts the cam/linkage; the actuator, its connector and its ASIL B software module are common. Benchmark: Hyundai Transys, a transmission supplier, also supplies the AWD Disconnector Actuator System on E-GMP EVs including the Kia EV9 - showing actuator technology shared between transmission and EV drive businesses.

title: Transfer-moulded single-switch SiC packages on a common pin-fin baseplate
description: [800V BEV] Transfer moulding is a high-throughput wafer-back-end process (estimated 15-25% cheaper per ampere than frame/gel modules), one package serves all variants (volume leverage), and copper clips replace wire bonds. Estimated €40-€70 saving per inverter, minus €8-€12 for the extra placement/sinter steps; two inverters per vehicle. Baseline: luxury-SUV inverters typically buy a frame-type six-pack SiC module: plastic frame, silicone-gel encapsulation, DBC substrates soldered to a baseplate, aluminium wire bonds, and a separate pin-fin or flat baseplate - with per-power-class module variants. Proposal: build the power stage from identical transfer-moulded single-switch (1-in-1 or half-bridge) SiC packages - die sintered to a copper lead-frame, copper clip top-side interconnect, epoxy mould compound - sintered or soldered onto one common pin-fin copper/aluminium baseplate. Power classes are set by populating more or fewer packages per phase (e.g. 3, 4 or 6 per switch position), so the package and the line are common across front, rear and performance inverters. Mould compound replaces gel, improving power cycling. Benchmark: Tesla's Model 3 inverter uses 24 single-switch (1-in-1) SiC power modules from STMicroelectronics assembled on a pin-fin heatsink, with copper clips and copper baseplates.

title: Two-phase current sensing with computed third phase in secondary inverter
description: [800V BEV] Deletes one current sensor (€6-€10), its core/housing feature and conditioning circuit (€1.5-€3), and an ADC/isolation channel (€0.5-€1); adds software validation cost amortised (€0.5-€1). Baseline: many traction inverters fit three closed-loop or open-loop Hall current sensors (one per phase) so that phase currents are measured directly and a phase-to-housing earth fault can be detected by the sum of the three currents. Proposal: on the secondary-axle inverter (lower power, lower ASIL torque-monitoring burden when the primary axle can provide safe torque), fit two phase current sensors and compute the third as ic = -(ia + ib) for a star-connected machine with isolated neutral. Earth-fault detection moves to the existing DC-link insulation monitor and a DC-bus current-balance plausibility check; sensor offset and gain drift are calibrated at standstill each key-on. This removes one sensor, its magnetic core/slot, signal conditioning and ADC channel. Benchmark: the Porsche Macan Electric already treats the front-axle inverter as a lower-specification secondary unit (silicon, max 350 A) versus SiC rear inverters up to 900 A, illustrating that the secondary inverter can carry a cost-optimised specification.

title: Cast-in sacrificial skid ribs on EDU sump replace separate EDU guard plate
description: [800V BEV] [Off-road] Deletes guard plate (€18-€28), 4-6 bolts and brackets (€4-€6) and assembly labour (€2-€3) per EDU; adds 0.4-0.6 kg aluminium and die modification (€2.5-€4). Applied to front and rear EDU on the off-road pack (assumed 30% take rate). Baseline: off-road luxury SUVs protect the low point of each EDU with a separate guard - typically a 3-4 mm aluminium or composite plate with 4-6 bolts and brackets to the subframe - because the HPDC gearbox sump is the lowest point and a rock strike can crack a 3-4 mm wall and dump oil. Proposal: thicken the sump floor locally to 6-7 mm and cast 4-6 longitudinal sacrificial skid ribs (8-10 mm tall, 6 mm wide, drafted 2°) into the EDU housing in AlSi10MnMg (T5/T6), so the housing itself slides over obstacles; ribs are designed to abrade, not crack, keeping the oil-wetted wall intact (minimum 5 mm under the ribs). The separate guard and brackets are deleted; underbody aero panel attaches to the ribs. Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology protects its battery with carbon-reinforced underbody panels and a protective plate rated for an impact of five times the vehicle weight - showing the importance and cost of underbody protection that this idea integrates into the EDU casting instead of adding a part.

The separate guard and brackets are deleted; underbody aero panel attaches to the ribs. Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology protects its battery with carbon-reinforced underbody panels and a protective plate rated for an impact of five times the vehicle weight - showing the importance and cost of underbody protection that this idea integrates into the EDU casting instead of adding a part.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes guard plate (€18-€28), 4-6 bolts and brackets (€4-€6) and assembly labour (€2-€3) per EDU; adds 0.4-0.6 kg aluminium and die modification (€2.5-€4). Applied to front and rear EDU on the off-road pack (assumed 30% take rate).
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: One-off die insert change on the housing tool (~€80k-€120k, included). Thicker local section requires vacuum assist / squeeze pin to avoid porosity. Guard installation station at vehicle assembly deleted (~60-90 s).
ideaData.dfmDfa: Removes 6-10 parts per EDU; no fastener torque checks; ribs double as handling features for EDU transport fixtures. Damaged ribs are cosmetic; inspection is visual at service.

title: Baffled EDU sump with pivoting pickup keeps lubrication on 45% off-road gradients
description: [800V BEV] [Off-road] Avoids a second scavenge pump and its controls (€20-€30) or alternatively the efficiency cost of a higher road fill; the baffle and pickup add €5-€8. Applied to the off-road pack, front and rear EDUs (assumed 30% take rate). Baseline: an EDU tuned for road use sets oil level low to cut churning loss; on a 45% (24°) climb or descent, or 35° side slope, oil migrates to one end and the pump pickup or the bearings at the high end starve. Typical fixes are a higher oil fill (more churning loss on road) or a second scavenge pump. Proposal: a moulded PA66-GF30 sump baffle insert creating a central reservoir with flap-valve doors that let oil in but slow its exit, plus a weighted pivoting pickup (or two pickups with a shuttle valve) so the pump draws from the low side at any attitude. Oil fill stays at the road-optimised level; at crawl speed the electric pump feeds the high-side bearings by jets. Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology provides an off-road crawl function between 2 and 8 km/h with low range engaged - the slow, steep operating mode where splash lubrication is weakest and forced feed matters most.

title: Single multi-output isolated supply feeds all six SiC gate drivers
description: [800V BEV] Replaces six isolated DC-DC channels (€2.5-€3.5 each = €15-€21) with one controller + one planar transformer + LDOs (€6-€8). Two inverters per vehicle. Baseline: many SiC inverters power each of the six gate drivers from its own isolated DC-DC module or transformer (six transformers, six controller ICs, six rectifiers), sized for +18/-4 V rails and SiC gate charge at 10-20 kHz (~1-2 W per channel). Proposal: one push-pull or flyback controller driving a single planar transformer with one primary and four isolated secondaries: three for the high-side drivers (each floating) and one shared for the three low-side drivers (common source reference on the negative DC rail). Secondary windings use reinforced insulation (≥8 mm creepage for 800 V systems per IEC 60664-1 pollution degree 2), and each rail is post-regulated by an LDO for ±2% accuracy. Benchmark: the Tesla Model 3 inverter's 24 single-switch SiC modules show that many paralleled devices can be driven from a compact integrated driver board; Xiaomi's YU7 runs all variants on an 800 V SiC platform where gate-driver cost is a meaningful share at high device counts.

title: Off-line linear-wound bobbins pushed onto detachable rotor pole bodies
description: [800V BEV] Off-line linear winding is faster and cheaper per coil than in-situ needle winding (estimated €8-€14 labour/machine-hour saving per rotor), higher fill cuts copper 5-10% (€2-€4), and a failed coil scraps only the coil (€1-€2 scrap saving); pole-tip machining adds €3-€5. Baseline: an EESM rotor field winding is commonly needle- or flyer-wound directly onto the salient poles of a one-piece rotor lamination stack: the winding nozzle must thread between poles, limiting copper fill to roughly 45-55%, cycle time is long (minutes per rotor), and a winding fault scraps the whole stack. Proposal: a rotor stack with detachable pole tips (dovetail or bolted pole shoes) so field coils are wound off-line on simple bobbins (linear winding, rectangular enamelled wire, fill 65-75%), then pushed over the pole bodies and locked by the pole shoes; coils connect by a laser-welded lead frame. Higher fill reduces field copper loss (I²R) by an estimated 15-25% at equal ampere-turns, or allows less copper. Benchmark: BMW's Gen6 eDrive uses an EESM with a fully redesigned rotor for the 800 V architecture, with Gen6 targeting 20% lower manufacturing cost than Gen5 - this proposal is one process route to that kind of rotor cost reduction.

title: One hairpin forming and laser-weld cell builds 48 V P2 and EDU stators

Baseline: on a platform with a 48 V MHEV and an 800 V BEV, the 48 V hybrid motor (P2 motor in the 8-speed bell-housing, high current/low voltage, few turns of large cross-section) is usually bought with a round-wire or bar winding from one supplier while the EDU hairpin stators come from a separate line - two winding technologies, two lines, two qualification streams. title: Layer-graded hairpin enamel: thick insulation only on line-end pins at 800 V
description: [800V BEV] Thick/extruded insulated rectangular wire is estimated €3-€6/kg more expensive than standard enamelled wire; limiting it to ~20% of 8-12 kg hairpin copper per motor saves 80% of the premium on the rest: (8-12 kg × 0.8 × €3-€6/kg) per motor, minus €1-€2 for a second wire payoff and SKU logistics. Baseline: 800 V hairpin stators fed by fast-switching SiC inverters see voltage overshoot at the motor terminals (reflected-wave, up to ~1.6-2× DC link, i.e. ~1,300-1,600 Vpk at 850 V) concentrated on the first turns of each phase, because the fast front distributes non-linearly along the winding. title: Moulded PPA-GF40 end-winding oil-spray ring replaces drilled aluminium spray tube
description: [800V BEV] Tube forming, hole drilling, deburring, brazing and bracket clipping (€6-€9 per ring) become one moulding shot (€2-€3 per ring). Two rings per motor, two motors per vehicle; mould cost (€60k-€90k per cavity set) amortised at €0.2-€0.3 per ring. Baseline: oil-cooled motors often distribute oil over the hairpin end-windings with a bent aluminium (EN AW-6060) or steel tube ring, brazed or welded to a feed fitting, with 12-24 drilled or laser-cut jet holes (Ø0.8-1.5 mm), deburred and cleaned to ISO 16232 cleanliness, then clipped to the housing with 3-4 brackets. Each motor needs two rings (both winding ends). Proposal: an injection-moulded polyphthalamide ring (PPA-GF40, heat-stabilised, continuous use 150 °C in ATF/e-fluid) with moulded-in jet orifices from core pins (±0.03 mm repeatability), integrated snap-in mounting feet and an O-ring spigot for the housing feed port. Moulded orifices are burr-free, so the deburr/clean step and its particle risk disappear; jet angles can be individually aimed (CFD-optimised) at no extra cost. Benchmark: Zeekr's 800 V drive systems adopt oil cooling with flat-wire motors, the cooling approach that requires such end-winding spray hardware.

title: Power-skived internal ring gear for planetary low range shared with MHEV transfer case
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cycle time cut from 3-6 min (shaping) to 1-1.5 min (skiving), combining turning and gearing in one clamping; broach tools eliminated; FNC instead of carburising and grinding on lower-loaded rings. Estimated €4-€7 per ring, one-two rings per vehicle across powertrains. Baseline: internal ring gears for planetary reductions (EDU two-speed/low range, MHEV transfer-case planetary) are commonly gear-shaped (cycle 3-6 min) or broached (dedicated broach per profile, €40k-€80k each, needs a long-stroke machine), then heat-treated; distortion often forces costly hard-finishing. Proposal: power skiving the internal teeth on a multi-function turning centre: the ring blank is turned, skived (cutter with axis crossing angle ~15-25°, continuous generating cut, cycle ~45-90 s for module 1.75-2.25, 80-100 teeth), then nitrocarburised (FNC, 570 °C) rather than carburised so distortion stays low enough to avoid hard finishing; or, for highly loaded EDU low-range rings, carburised and hard-skived. One skiving cell serves EDU and MHEV transfer-case ring gears. Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology fits a two-speed transmission with 2:1 low range to each motor, so planetary ring gears become a volume part in electric off-road drivetrains.

title: Wading-rated cassette seal with mud excluder on EDU output shafts
description: [800V BEV] [Off-road] Deletes the plunge-ground seal journal on the shaft (€1.5-€2.5 per shaft), the separate slinger/boot (€1-€1.5), and reduces wading-related leak warranty (€1-€2 per shaft over life); cassette costs €2-€3 more than a simple lip seal. Four output shafts per vehicle (two EDUs). Baseline: EDU output shafts typically use a single FKM radial lip seal plus a separate rubber dust boot or a pressed steel slinger on the CV joint, and on off-road variants a second outboard lip seal is added. During wading a hot EDU (90 °C oil) cools quickly and the air-gap pressure drops; a single lip combined with abrasive mud allows water and grit to pass, and lip wear on a hardened shaft groove leads to oil leaks - a common warranty item for off-road vehicles. Proposal: a unitised cassette seal - FKM main lip running on its own hardened steel sleeve (wear sleeve), with two axial NBR/HNBR excluder lips and a labyrinth formed between sleeve flange and case - pressed in one operation. The running surface is part of the seal, so the shaft no longer needs a ground, hardened seal journal (Ra 0.2-0.8 µm, plunge-ground, no lead). Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology claims 850 mm wading depth, 150 mm more than the AMG G 63 - the sealing requirement this cassette addresses for the drive units.

title: Delete NiCuNi plating on NdFeB magnets fully encapsulated in resin-filled rotor slots
description: [800V BEV] NiCuNi plating adds an estimated €3-€6 per kg of magnet; with 1.2-1.8 kg NdFeB per motor and one PM motor per vehicle the deletion saves €3.6-€10.8, minus €0.5-€1 for passivation and dry-storage logistics. Baseline: sintered NdFeB magnets for traction motors are usually electroplated with Ni-Cu-Ni (10-20 µm) or epoxy-coated to stop corrosion of the Nd-rich grain boundaries, then inserted into rotor pockets and fixed by adhesive or injection-moulded resin. Where the pockets are fully filled by injection-moulded epoxy/PPS resin that seals every magnet face, the plating duplicates the protection. Proposal: specify magnets with a thin phosphate passivation (or bare, with controlled storage under dry nitrogen up to insertion) and rely on full resin encapsulation (transfer-moulded epoxy, ≥0.2 mm on all faces) for lifetime corrosion protection. Benefit: removal of the plating cost and of the nickel layer's eddy-current contribution (minor). Xiaomi's YU7 V6s Plus motor uses segmented magnets to cut losses - segmentation increases magnet face area, making the per-face plating cost of each segment more significant, which this proposal removes.

ideaData.dfmDfa: No design change to the rotor; magnet handling unchanged. Fill verification becomes a critical characteristic; the moulding tool must fully cover magnet faces with defined resin gaps.

Keep plated magnets for oil-spray rotors without full encapsulation.

title: Self-bonding enamel wire for EESM field coils deletes trickle impregnation
description: [800V BEV] Removes resin (€1-€2 per rotor), impregnation and oven energy/labour (€3-€5), and resin-cleaning of tooling; bondable wire costs ~8-12% more than standard wire (€1-€1.5 on 2-3 kg Cu). Baseline: wound-rotor (EESM) field coils are typically wound with grade 2 enamelled copper and then trickle- or VPI-impregnated with epoxy/polyester resin to bond turns against centrifugal forces at 15,000-20,000 rpm and to conduct heat; impregnation needs preheating, resin dosing, gelling and a 1-3 h oven cure, plus resin waste and VOC handling. Proposal: wind the field coils with self-bonding (bondable) enamel wire - a thermoplastic/thermoset overcoat (e.g. polyamide or epoxy-based bond coat over a polyamide-imide base, thermal class 200 °C) - and bake-bond them by resistive current heating (passing DC through the coil to ~200 °C for 30-60 s) directly after winding. Turns bond into a rigid block without impregnation. Benchmark: BMW's Gen6 eDrive uses an EESM with a fully redesigned rotor for 800 V and targets 20% lower manufacturing cost than Gen5; a wound-field rotor is exactly where impregnation cycle time dominates.

title: Hairpin star point formed on the weld crown deletes separate neutral busbar
description: [800V BEV] Deletes neutral busbar and carrier (€2.5-€4), its separate weld/fixture step (€1-€1.5) and potting volume (€0.5-€1); adds special leg forming in the twist tool (€0.5). Two motors per vehicle. Baseline: many hairpin stators form the star (neutral) point with a separate stamped copper neutral busbar (Cu-ETP, 2-3 mm) carried in an insulating plastic carrier, laser- or TIG-welded to 3-6 hairpin leg ends (one per parallel path per phase) on top of the crown; the carrier is then overmoulded or potted. Proposal: design the end-pin set so the neutral connection is made by specially formed hairpin legs (longer leg tails bent radially in the twisting operation) that lie side-by-side and are laser-welded together in the same crown welding program that welds the regular pin pairs - a 'neutral pin' variant. The separate busbar, its carrier and the extra weld fixture disappear; only the three phase terminals leave the stator. Benchmark: Zeekr's 800 V drive systems use flat-wire (hairpin-type) oil-cooled motors, and BMW's Gen6 redesigned the stator for 800 V; crown-level interconnection is a common lever in such flat-wire stators.

title: Unipolar 0 V turn-off SiC gate drive deletes negative gate rail
description: [800V BEV] Removes per channel a negative-rail winding/rectifier/regulator and decoupling (€0.6-€1.0) - six channels per inverter, two inverters - minus a Miller-clamp-capable driver IC premium (€0.1-€0.2 per channel). Baseline: SiC MOSFET gate drivers typically use a bipolar supply (+18 V / -3 to -5 V) so the device stays reliably off when the opposite switch turns on at high dv/dt, because Miller current through Cgd can lift the gate above its threshold (~2-3 V at 175 °C for many SiC devices). The negative rail needs its own transformer winding, rectifier, regulator and decoupling per channel. Proposal: use a unipolar 0 V/+18 V drive with an integrated active Miller clamp (low-impedance clamp switch between gate and source when Vgs <2 V), a low-inductance Kelvin-source gate loop (<5 nH), and SiC devices with higher threshold voltage selected for this drive mode. The negative rail components disappear from all six channels. Benchmarks: Xiaomi's YU7 is one of many 800 V SiC platforms where per-channel driver cost multiplies with device count; Tesla's 24-switch SiC inverter illustrates how channel count drives gate-drive BOM.

title: Thicker 0.30 mm electrical steel for the low-duty front motor stack
description: [800V BEV] 0.30 mm grade is estimated €0.15-€0.25/kg cheaper than 0.25 mm, on 14-18 kg of front motor steel (€2.1-€4.5), and stacks 17% fewer laminations (stamping and stacking cost -€1-€2); range penalty is offset only if WLTP allows. Baseline: platforms often specify one premium thin-gauge non-oriented electrical steel (e.g. 0.25 mm, NO25 class, P1.0/400 ≈ 11-12 W/kg) for every motor so both motors share supply - although the front unit in a rear-biased dual-motor SUV spends little time at high power and high frequency. Proposal: specify 0.30 mm NO30 class (P1.0/400 ≈ 13-15 W/kg) electrical steel for the front motor stator and rotor stacks; iron loss at the front motor's typical operating points rises modestly, but because the front delivers a small share of cycle energy the vehicle-level range effect is expected to be about 0.1-0.2%. Thicker gauge also stamps faster with longer die life (fewer strokes per stack height: 17% fewer laminations) and has lower price per kg. Benchmark: the Porsche Macan Electric front motor is compact - 210 mm diameter and 100 mm active length for 175 kW peak - showing a secondary motor sized very differently from the rear; its lamination spec can likewise differ.

title: Moulded PPS-GF40 dovetail wedges replace shrunk retaining sleeve on wound rotor
description: [800V BEV] Replaces a stainless/carbon sleeve plus its shrink/wind process (€12-€25) or machined metal wedges (€10-€14) with moulded wedges (€2-€4 per rotor set); smaller air gap reduces field current requirement (excitation-supply savings not counted). Baseline: in a wound-field (EESM) rotor the field coils on salient poles are pushed outward by centrifugal force (a 1 kg coil set at 90 mm radius and 18,000 rpm sees ~320 kN total radial load), so designs use either a shrunk stainless/Inconel or carbon-fibre sleeve over the whole rotor, or machined aluminium/steel wedges between poles. A sleeve adds magnetic air gap (0.5-1.0 mm), raising field current and copper loss. Proposal: injection-moulded PPS-GF40 (or PEEK-GF30 for >18,000 rpm) wedges with a dovetail into pole-shoe slots, one per inter-pole gap (e.g. 6-8 per rotor), carrying coil centrifugal load in compression/shear to the pole shoes; wedges also form oil channels for coil cooling. No sleeve, so the mechanical air gap stays at the electromagnetic minimum. Benchmark: BMW's Gen6 eDrive uses an EESM with a fully redesigned rotor for 800 V; MAHLE's magnet-free MCT motor is an externally excited synchronous machine designed for high speeds - both depend on cost-effective field-coil retention.
