title: Fine-blanked park-lock pawl shared by MHEV 8-speed and BEV EDU
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Fine blanking at ~40-60 strokes/min replaces 6-9 machining operations (estimated €3.5-€6 piece-cost saving), doubles volume of one part (€0.3-€0.5 further), one PPAP instead of two. Applies to one pawl per vehicle (MHEV or BEV rear EDU). Baseline: park-lock pawls are often forged or cut from bar (e.g. 42CrMo4 or 16MnCr5), milled and ground on the engagement tooth and pivot bore, then case-hardened - around 6-9 machining operations - with separate designs for the automatic transmission and the EDU. Proposal: one pawl design used in both the MHEV 8-speed and the BEV rear EDU, fine-blanked from 8-10 mm 16MnCr5 (or C45 for induction hardening) strip: fine blanking produces fully sheared, flat, square edges (shear ratio >90%) and a ±0.02 mm pivot hole, so tooth and bore need no machining; then carbonitriding and tumble deburr. The two gearboxes use the same pawl with their own park gear and cam; the park gear tooth geometry is matched to the common pawl. Benchmark: the Kia EV9's DAS is supplied by Hyundai Transys, a transmission specialist, an example of transmission-derived mechatronic hardware reused in EV drives; BMW's Gen6 targets 20% lower manufacturing cost, the kind of target that forces such process changes.

ideaData.title: Common front cooling-module carrier shared by I6 MHEV and 800V BEV
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: a dual-powertrain luxury SUV typically carries two unrelated front-end cooling modules (CRFM). The I6 MHEV pack has an HT radiator (~620×480 mm core), an LT radiator for a water-cooled charge-air cooler, an R1234yf condenser and a 600-850 W fan in its own PP-GF30 shroud; the BEV pack has an LT radiator, a condenser or R744 gas cooler and a different fan/shroud, with separate carriers, brackets, rubber isolators and active-shutter interfaces — two tool sets and two line-side kits. Proposal: one injection-moulded PP-LGF30 carrier frame (single 2,300 t tool, 4 inserts) with identical body-mount points, a common 2-row slot geometry and one shutter/fan interface; the front slot takes either the MHEV condenser or the BEV condenser/gas cooler, the rear slot takes a 52 mm (MHEV HT) or 27 mm (BEV LT) radiator core built on the same header, tank and tube pitch so the brazing furnace fixture is shared. The MHEV I6 already has a low-temperature loop for an air-to-water intercooler (as BMW does on the B58), so the LT radiator core is the shared denominator. Heat rejection check: I6 at 3,500 kg tow, 12% grade, 40 °C needs ~95-110 kW HT + ~25 kW LT; BEV needs ~35-45 kW LT during 270 kW+ fast charge plus condenser duty — both fit a 0.32 m² frontal envelope with different core depth. Volvo states its SPA3 third-generation thermal/HVAC system costs about 20% less than the EX90 SPA2 set-up; this idea applies the same consolidation logic across powertrains rather than generations.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: One carrier tool and one fan/shroud tool instead of two (≈€1.6-2.0M tooling avoided, amortised); shared header/tank/tube pitch lets one brazing fixture family and one leak-test station serve both; volume of the common carrier doubles, cutting piece price ~8-12% on carrier, shroud and isolators.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: One CRFM sequencing line at the module supplier with variant-insert loading; brazing furnace fixtures shared (2 fixture families instead of 4); vehicle line uses one front-end marriage jig and one torque programme; variant chosen by broadcast code at kitting.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Carrier carries both radiator thicknesses with a stepped locator rib that rejects the wrong core (poka-yoke); 4 common body mounts; quick-connect coolant ports at identical positions so hose routing differs only behind the module; service replacement of any core without removing the carrier.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — commonisation across two module families of the same vehicle
costSavingPotential.percentage: 8-12% of the front cooling module cost
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Per vehicle: carrier/shroud piece-price volume effect €6-€9 + tooling amortisation avoided (€1.8M over 5 yrs ÷ 250k veh) €7-€7 + shared brazing/leak-test fixtures €2-€3 + added mass/spacers on BEV −€1…−€1 = €14-€18. × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €0.70M-€0.90M. Engineering estimate from piece-cost deltas; to be confirmed by should-cost engine and supplier RFQ.

ideaData.riskNotes: Package compromises: the BEV may carry a deeper slot than needed (mass +0.4-0.6 kg); MHEV tow case must still meet SAE J2807 towing grade test and 40 °C/12% grade cooling dyno; validate vibration to ISO 16750-3 and pedestrian-protection crush zone (Euro NCAP). Mitigation: shared carrier with replaceable slot spacers.

title: Market-variant 400V DC charge booster fitted only where 400V chargers dominate
description: [800V BEV] Booster BOM (€380-520) removed from the take rate that does not need it; at an assumed 45% fitment (NA + option buyers) the fleet average falls by €210-285 per vehicle minus the provision cost (€12-15). Booster also drops 6-9 kg and its coolant branch from non-fitted cars. Baseline: an 800 V luxury SUV that cannot reuse its drive inverter for boosting (e.g. an EESM or a front/rear motor whose neutral is not accessible) fits a dedicated 50-80 kW 400→800 V DC/DC boost converter (SiC MOSFET 1200 V, ~6-9 kg, liquid-cooled, ~€380-520) to every car, although in Europe, Korea and China most new high-power chargers are 800-1000 V capable. Proposal: package the booster as a bolt-in, plug-in module (two HV connectors, one coolant quick-connect, one CAN/LIN connector) on a pre-wired provision in the rear HV bay and fit it only by market/option code — standard in North America where 400-500 V chargers dominate, optional ("400 V DC fast-charge pack") elsewhere. Without booster, the car still DC-charges at any 800-1000 V charger and AC-charges at 11/22 kW. The provision costs a moulded blanking cover, a 2-way HV header and 0.4 m of HV cable already present in the junction box. Without booster, the car still DC-charges at any 800-1000 V charger and AC-charges at 11/22 kW. The provision costs a moulded blanking cover, a 2-way HV header and 0.4 m of HV cable already present in the junction box. Benchmark: Mercedes fits the GLC with EQ Technology 400 V DC converter on a country-specific basis, and launched the 800 V CLA in Germany, Austria and Switzerland without it, adding a factory converter from spring 2026 — the OEM proof that a market-variant booster is acceptable. Contrast: Porsche Macan splits its pack into two 400 V halves and Lucid Gravity boosts through its rear drive unit; those zero-hardware options are already in our library and are preferred where the motor topology allows.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Booster BOM (€380-520) removed from the take rate that does not need it; at an assumed 45% fitment (NA + option buyers) the fleet average falls by €210-285 per vehicle minus the provision cost (€12-15). Booster also drops 6-9 kg and its coolant branch from non-fitted cars.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Fitted in a post-trim station as a 4-minute plug-in operation (2 HV connectors + 1 coolant QC + 2 bolts); end-of-line HV isolation test covers both variants; one extra variant in the sequencing broadcast; booster supplier volume halves (piece price +6-8% assumed in the arithmetic).
ideaData.dfmDfa: Provision cover is keyed to the booster footprint; HVIL loop closes through a shorting plug when no booster is fitted so the same HV harness serves both; dealer retrofit is possible (customer upsell) because no harness change is needed.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — removes a €400+ module from ~55% of cars

costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Per vehicle: booster removed on 55% of fleet (0.55 × €400-520) €220-€286 + booster price uplift at lower volume on 45% (0.45 × €24-34) −€11…−€15 + provision cover/header on all cars −€12…−€15 = €197-€256. × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €9.85M-€12.80M. Engineering estimate from piece-cost deltas; to be confirmed by should-cost engine and supplier RFQ.

title: Pre-charged, leak-tested refrigerant module delivered sealed to the vehicle line
description: [800V BEV] Vehicle-line refrigerant station time cut from ~4 min to ~1.5 min; 6-8 fewer field joints (leak warranty); 250-350 g less refrigerant (R1234yf ~€80-120/kg); 6-8 fewer refrigerant lines and brackets; partly offset by self-sealing couplings. Baseline: the heat-pump refrigerant circuit of a luxury BEV is assembled in the vehicle plant: compressor, chiller, water-cooled condenser, accumulator, 3-5 EXVs/shut-off valves and 8-12 refrigerant lines are married across the front bay, then evacuated (~3-4 min), charged with 900-1,100 g R1234yf and helium/tracer leak-checked on the line; each threaded/pad joint is a leak path and a repair loop. Proposal: put everything except the cabin evaporator and front condenser/gas cooler into a compact refrigerant module (compressor on isolators, chiller, LCC, accumulator, EXVs on one brazed AlMn1 manifold block), built, evacuated, helium-tested and pre-charged at the supplier with sealed self-closing valves on the 2-4 remaining interface ports. title: Single 48V main coolant pump with rotary split-cooling valve for the I6
description: [MHEV] Deletes one 12 V auxiliary pump (€35-45) and its bracket/hoses (€8-12), the wax thermostat housing (€14-18) and a separate block shut-off valve (€12-16); main pump moves to 48 V (thinner feed); rotary valve adds €22-28. Baseline: a 3.0 L I6 MHEV in this class typically carries a belt- or electrically-driven main water pump plus one or two 12 V auxiliary pumps (turbo after-run, heater circuit, intercooler LT loop), a wax or map-controlled thermostat and separate block shut-off hardware for split cooling — the Range Rover 3.0 L MHEV parts catalogue lists both main and auxiliary water pumps. Proposal: one 48 V, 800-1,000 W wet-rotor main pump (variable speed 0-6,000 rpm, 0-300 L/min) drives the HT circuit, and a single two-disc rotary valve (stepper, LIN) meters head, block, radiator, heater and turbo branches — performing split cooling (head-first, block-closed warm-up), thermostat function and heater priority. The auxiliary heater pump is deleted because the 48 V main pump runs at low speed with engine off (stop-start and after-run); turbo after-run uses the same pump. Only the LT (charge-air) loop keeps its own small pump. Benchmark: BMW B58 replaces the wax thermostat with an electrically operated heat-management module whose rotary valve opens the coolant ducts variably, and runs split cooling (head and turbo always fed, block flow reduced or shut off during warm-up);

Proposal: a predictive thermal manager that uses trailer detection (tow-ball sensor / trailer module), trailer mass estimation from longitudinal dynamics, navigation gradient preview and ambient to pre-cool coolant and ATF (or the BEV pack and EDUs) 5-10 K below normal set-point before a climb, using the thermal mass of the coolant (~12-14 L), ATF/oil (~9 L) and engine/EDU metal as a buffer. Energy basis: ~25 kg of coolant+oil at ~3.5 kJ/kg·K pre-cooled by 8 K stores ~0.7 MJ, and ~120 kg of engine/transmission metal at ~0.5 kJ/kg·K × 8 K adds ~0.5 MJ; 1.2 MJ covers a 15-20 kW heat-rejection deficit for ~60-80 s, i.e. the steepest segments of most real climbs, with a controlled power derate as the backstop. This lets the fan step down one size (1,000 → 850 W) and the HT core lose one tube row (52 → 42 mm) while still passing the SAE J2807 Davis Dam test. The BMW B58 already runs map-based electrical heat management (rotary valve controlled from coolant and head material temperature), so the actuators exist.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: No new hardware or stations; smaller core shortens braze cycle marginally; one fewer fan variant if the 850 W fan is commonised with non-tow trims (tow pack becomes software + tow bar only).
ideaData.dfmDfa: Tow pack reduces to tow bar, trailer module and calibration — no cooling hardware variant, which simplifies order-to-build and removes one front-module part number; dealer can enable towing calibration on retrofit tow bars; service unchanged.

title: Front EDU hosts PDU for e-compressor and HV heater, deleting front junction box
description: [800V BEV] Front HV junction box (housing, busbars, fuses) deleted (€35-45), ~5 m shielded HV cable shortened to ~1.8 m (€22-30), two connector pairs and brackets deleted (€14-18); added fuses/headers on inverter (€14-18). Baseline: in a dual-motor 800 V luxury SUV the e-compressor and HV coolant heater in the front bay are fed from a separate front HV junction box (or from the pack via two dedicated 4-6 mm² shielded HV cables, each ~3.5 m), with their own fuses, connectors and brackets — the front EDU inverter already has a 50-70 mm² DC link from the pack only centimetres away. Proposal: fold a small PDU into the front EDU inverter housing: two fused HV taps (30 A each, 1000 V DC fuses or e-fuse) on the inverter DC busbar with two 2-pole HV headers on the inverter cover, feeding the e-compressor (~0.8 m) and HV heater (~1.0 m). The separate front JB and ~5 m of shielded HV cable are deleted; the inverter DC-link capacitor also serves as the input capacitance for the short feeds. Benchmark: Huawei DriveONE X-in-1 integrates the motor control unit, motor, reducer, OBC, DC-DC, PDU and BCU in one powertrain unit, used on the AITO M9 full-800 V dual-SiC platform. This idea takes only the PDU element into the front EDU — a smaller step than full X-in-1 consolidation already in our library.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: a premium 800 V SUV fits an 11 kW OBC (PFC + isolated DC/DC with its own transformer) and a separate 2.5-3 kW 800→12 V LDC (phase-shifted full bridge with its own transformer, output choke and control board), even if co-housed. Proposal: a three-port (triple-active-bridge) transformer on one ferrite core (Mn-Zn, e.g. N97-class) links the grid-side PFC bus, the 800 V battery bridge and a 12 V synchronous-rectifier bridge. In charging, power flows grid→battery with the 12 V port supplied from the same core; in driving, the battery bridge drives the 12 V port directly (the PFC side idles). Shared: one magnetic core set, one controller (dual-core MCU), one cold plate, one EMI filter on the HV side. The OBC battery-side bridge doubles as the LDC primary (1200 V SiC MOSFETs, 40 mΩ). title: 22 kW AC option built from two paralleled 11 kW OBC power stages
description: [800V BEV] Avoids buying a 22 kW OBC on 11 kW cars (assume 70% take 11 kW: saves €150-190 each, averaged €105-133), single board design at higher volume (−5-7%); added parallel-capable controller and connector on all (−€8-10) and a slightly larger housing (−€5-7). Baseline: luxury SUVs offering 11 kW standard and 22 kW optional AC charging usually buy two distinct OBC designs (different magnetics, semiconductor sizes, housing and cold plate) or fit a 22 kW unit to every car for simplicity, paying for 11 kW of unused capacity on most cars. Proposal: one 11 kW three-phase power-stage board (PFC + LLC/DAB, 1200 V SiC) designed for parallel operation with current-sharing control; the 22 kW option fits a second identical board in the same housing (pre-provisioned second cavity on the shared cold plate, one extra 16-pin board connector), the 11 kW car has a blanking cover. Housing, AC filter, inlet harness and controller are common; the controller is sized for master/slave operation. Benchmark: Polestar 4 offers 22 kW AC charging alongside 200 kW DC, while Kia EV9 uses 11 kW AC — the market splits between 11 and 22 kW. The idea lets one OBC family serve both with board count as the only variant.

ideaData.title: 22 kW AC option built from two paralleled 11 kW OBC power stages
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: luxury SUVs offering 11 kW standard and 22 kW optional AC charging usually buy two distinct OBC designs (different magnetics, semiconductor sizes, housing and cold plate) or fit a 22 kW unit to every car for simplicity, paying for 11 kW of unused capacity on most cars. Proposal: one 11 kW three-phase power-stage board (PFC + LLC/DAB, 1200 V SiC) designed for parallel operation with current-sharing control; the 22 kW option fits a second identical board in the same housing (pre-provisioned second cavity on the shared cold plate, one extra 16-pin board connector), the 11 kW car has a blanking cover. Housing, AC filter, inlet harness and controller are common; the controller is sized for master/slave operation. Benchmark: Polestar 4 offers 22 kW AC charging alongside 200 kW DC, while Kia EV9 uses 11 kW AC — the market splits between 11 and 22 kW. The idea lets one OBC family serve both with board count as the only variant.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Avoids buying a 22 kW OBC on 11 kW cars (assume 70% take 11 kW: saves €150-190 each, averaged €105-133), single board design at higher volume (−5-7%); added parallel-capable controller and connector on all (−€8-10) and a slightly larger housing (−€5-7).
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: One SMT/power-board line, one housing tool; 22 kW variant adds a 3-minute board insertion and torque at the OBC supplier; EOL tester runs 11 kW or 22 kW profile by variant code.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Second board cavity keyed; blanking cover avoids coolant bypass (cold plate channel continuous); boards interchange for service; harness from AC inlet already rated 32 A × 3 phases on all cars.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — avoids over-specifying 22 kW and halves design count
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Per vehicle: 22 kW OBC avoided on 70% of cars (0.7 × €150-190) €105-€133 + single-board volume effect €8-€11 + parallel-capable controller/connector −€8…−€10 + larger housing −€5…−€7 = €100-€127. × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €5.00M-€6.35M. Engineering estimate from piece-cost deltas; to be confirmed by should-cost engine and supplier RFQ.

ideaData.riskNotes: Current-sharing instability between boards, larger housing than an 11 kW-only design (mass +0.6 kg on 11 kW cars). Validate IEC 61851-1/-21-1, EN 61000-3-12 harmonics at 22 kW, CISPR 25, thermal at 22 kW in 45 °C ambient.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Polestar 4 (2024) / Kia EV9 (2023, E-GMP) — Polestar 4 offers 22 kW AC charging; EV9 offers 11 kW AC. How this differs: Delivers both ratings from one board design fitted once or twice in a common housing

title: DC-side V2H through the charge inlet keeps the OBC unidirectional
description: [800V BEV] Bidirectional PFC uplift avoided (€45-65), grid-code certification and market variants avoided (€8-12 amortised), smaller AC filter (€6-9); ISO 15118-20 software and DC reverse-flow validation (−€6-8 amortised). Baseline: luxury 800 V SUVs increasingly fit a bidirectional AC OBC for V2L/V2H (Hyundai ICCU, Lucid Wunderbox), which needs a bidirectional PFC (totem-pole SiC instead of boost diodes), grid-forming firmware, anti-islanding/grid-code certification per market and extra filter capacity — roughly +€60-90 over a unidirectional 11 kW OBC. Proposal: keep the OBC unidirectional and provide V2H via DC through the CCS2/NACS DC pins to a bidirectional DC wallbox (ISO 15118-20 BPT), where the inverter and grid-code certification live in the home unit; provide V2L (3.6 kW) with a compact 230 V portable inverter accessory plugged into the DC inlet, sold as an accessory. The vehicle adds only ISO 15118-20 bidirectional power transfer software and DC contactor/precharge logic for reverse flow. Benchmark: BMW Gen6 Energy Master manages all bidirectional energy functions in the pack; E-GMP achieves 3.68 kW V2L through its bidirectional ICCU; GMC Hummer EV exports up to 6 kW to charge other EVs. The difference: no grid-tied inverter hardware or per-country certification is carried on every car.

title: Twin-core jointly shielded 800V cable replaces two single-core shielded leads
description: [800V BEV] One shield and jacket instead of two (−30-35% shield copper per metre), two shield ferrules fewer per feed, one clip track instead of two; across 4 auxiliary feeds totalling ~8 m: material €14-18, termination €8-11, clips €3-4; twin-core connector inserts cost slightly more (−€4-5). Baseline: HV feeds to the e-compressor, HV heater, OBC and DC-DC are typically two single-core 4-10 mm² cables, each with its own braided copper shield, outer jacket and shield-termination ferrule at each connector — four shield terminations per feed and two cable runs to clip. Proposal: for auxiliary feeds up to 40 A (e-compressor ~10-15 A, heater ~5-10 A, OBC ~15-30 A at 800 V), use a twin-core cable: two XLPE-insulated 4-6 mm² conductors laid up together under one common shield and one jacket (outer Ø ~13 mm vs 2 × 10 mm). Because HV+ and HV− currents are equal and opposite in the same shield, the loop area and radiated field fall and shielding effectiveness improves for the same shield coverage; shield terminations halve (one per end). SEI documents that HV cable shields can be braided, lateral-wound or metallic-foil structures selected per required noise level, and at 800 V current halves versus 400 V so conductor size can drop after thermal and voltage-drop checks. Twin-core suits the short, low-current auxiliary runs; the main pack-to-EDU feeds stay single-core.

title: Regional charge-inlet carrier accepts CCS2 or NACS inlet modules
description: [800V BEV] One flap/carrier tool and one aperture instead of two (tooling ~€0.4-0.6M avoided), one DC harness from inlet to BDU (avoids a variant harness with 50-95 mm² conductors), higher-volume flap actuator; adds a small bezel and pigtail connector. Baseline: a global luxury SUV sold in Europe (CCS2) and North America (NACS/SAE J3400) typically has two charge-port assemblies with different flap housings, body-side apertures, inlet harnesses (DC cables 50-95 mm², temperature sensors, lock actuator) and sometimes different side-panel stampings or aperture trims. Proposal: one charge-port carrier (PA6-GF30 moulding with the flap, flap actuator, LED, drain and seal) with a standard 4-bolt inlet interface and a common DC/AC harness pigtail connector behind it; the market inlet module (CCS2 or NACS) bolts into the carrier from outside with its own short pigtail. Body aperture, flap, actuator and the main DC harness to the BDU are identical; only the inlet module and a trim bezel vary. The NACS inlet is physically smaller so a CCS2-sized carrier accepts it with a bezel adaptor. Benchmark: Lucid Gravity ships with a NACS charge port and 900 V-class architecture, while European 800 V SUVs use CCS2 — the same model sold in both regions needs both.

title: Bidirectional EXVs replace EXV plus shut-off valve pairs in heat-pump circuit
description: [800V BEV] 4 solenoid valves (€9-12 each) and 2 check valves (€3-4) deleted = €42-56; one extra EXV (€18-22) and higher spec EXVs (+€2-3 each × 5); fewer LIN/PWM drivers and harness branches (€4-6). Baseline: a heat-pump refrigerant circuit in a luxury BEV commonly uses 3-4 electronic expansion valves plus 3-5 solenoid shut-off valves and 1-2 check valves to switch between cooling, heating, dehumidification and chiller modes — each solenoid adds a coil, connector, harness branch and two brazed or pad joints. Proposal: specify stepper-driven EXVs with full-close tightness (≤ 5 g/h leak) and full-open bore (≥ 6 mm, near-zero ΔP) that are rated for flow in both directions; each EXV then serves as both an expansion device and a shut-off, so mode switching is done by the EXVs alone. A typical R1234yf heat pump drops from 4 EXV + 4 SOV + 2 check valves to 5 bidirectional EXVs; for R744 the same approach applies with 150 bar-rated valves. Benchmark: VW uses an R744 heat pump with a 5.5 kW compressor harvesting drivetrain and ambient heat, and has publicly worked to cut the cost of that system; Valeo catalogues heat-pump heat exchangers for both R1234yf and R744, showing tier-1 standardisation of the circuit around which valve count can be optimised.

title: Coaxial internal heat exchanger built into the R744 suction line
description: [800V BEV] Stand-alone IHX block deleted (€18-24), four joints and one bracket (€6-8), the separate suction line merged into the coaxial line (€8-11); coaxial line costs more than a plain suction line (−€10-13). Baseline: an R744 (CO2) transcritical heat pump needs an internal heat exchanger (IHX) between gas-cooler outlet and compressor suction to reach acceptable cooling COP at high ambient; many systems fit it as a separate plate or tube-in-tube block with four brazed/pad connections and its own bracket, plus separate high-pressure (≤ 140 bar) and suction lines. Proposal: make the suction line itself the IHX — a 1.2-1.5 m coaxial line where the high-pressure gas-cooler outlet flows in an inner multi-channel extrusion (EN AW-6063/3003, 6-8 channels, burst > 3× 140 bar) inside the outer suction tube (Ø 16-18 mm). Effectiveness of 0.4-0.5 is reached over that length, enough for a 5-8% COP gain at 35 °C. Two connections and one bracket replace six joints and two brackets; the line follows the existing routing from front module to compressor. Benchmark: VW ID heat pumps use R744 with a 5.5 kW CO2 compressor (Hanon) and VW has worked to raise efficiency and lower cost of the system; Valeo offers heat exchangers for R744 heat pumps. Coaxial IHX lines are an established MAC technology; the idea is to adopt it as the default for our R744 circuit rather than a stand-alone IHX.

ideaData.title: Coaxial internal heat exchanger built into the R744 suction line
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: an R744 (CO2) transcritical heat pump needs an internal heat exchanger (IHX) between gas-cooler outlet and compressor suction to reach acceptable cooling COP at high ambient; many systems fit it as a separate plate or tube-in-tube block with four brazed/pad connections and its own bracket, plus separate high-pressure (≤ 140 bar) and suction lines. Proposal: make the suction line itself the IHX — a 1.2-1.5 m coaxial line where the high-pressure gas-cooler outlet flows in an inner multi-channel extrusion (EN AW-6063/3003, 6-8 channels, burst > 3× 140 bar) inside the outer suction tube (Ø 16-18 mm). Effectiveness of 0.4-0.5 is reached over that length, enough for a 5-8% COP gain at 35 °C. Two connections and one bracket replace six joints and two brackets; the line follows the existing routing from front module to compressor. Benchmark: VW ID heat pumps use R744 with a 5.5 kW CO2 compressor (Hanon) and VW has worked to raise efficiency and lower cost of the system; Valeo offers heat exchangers for R744 heat pumps. Coaxial IHX lines are an established MAC technology; the idea is to adopt it as the default for our R744 circuit rather than a stand-alone IHX.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Stand-alone IHX block deleted (€18-24), four joints and one bracket (€6-8), the separate suction line merged into the coaxial line (€8-11); coaxial line costs more than a plain suction line (−€10-13).
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Line supplier adds coaxial extrusion and end-forming (one brazed end block per side, induction brazing ~40 s); vehicle line installs one line instead of an IHX plus two lines (~45 s saved); 4 fewer leak points to helium-test.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Two end blocks with keyed pad fittings that cannot be swapped high/low side; one bracket instead of three; no separate IHX package volume in the front bay; four fewer joints to torque; service replaces the line as one item.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low-Medium — one component and four joints deleted
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Per vehicle: IHX block deleted €18-€24 + joints/bracket €6-€8 + separate suction line merged €8-€11 + coaxial line premium −€10…−€13 = €22-€30. × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €1.10M-€1.50M. Engineering estimate from piece-cost deltas; to be confirmed by should-cost engine and supplier RFQ.

ideaData.riskNotes: R744 pressure (gas cooler ≤ 140 bar, standstill up to ~120 bar at 50 °C) — burst/fatigue of the inner extrusion; suction superheat too high at low load (compressor discharge temperature limit). Validate SAE J2843 R744 components, burst ≥ 3× MOP, pressure cycling 250k cycles, helium leak test, climatic COP at 35/45 °C.

title: Water-cooled charge-air cooler in the I6 intake plenum replaces front intercooler
description: [MHEV] Deletes the front air-to-air intercooler (€45-60), ~1.5 m hard duct/hoses and 6 clamps (€22-30), and two brackets (€4-6); adds WCAC core in plenum (€38-48), LT pump and lines (€14-18) — net positive when the LT radiator is the platform-common core. Baseline: some I6 luxury SUVs still use a front-mounted air-to-air intercooler with ~1.6-2.2 m of 60-70 mm charge-air ducting (PA6-GF hard ducts + silicone/AEM hoses, 6-8 clamps) between turbo, front module and throttle; boost pressure response suffers from the ~6-8 L charge-air volume. Proposal: an indirect water-cooled charge-air cooler (WCAC, brazed EN AW-3003 bar-plate core, ~18-22 kW) integrated into the PA6-GF35 intake plenum, fed by the low-temperature loop and its LT radiator in the front module. Charge-air path shrinks to ~0.6 m, volume to ~2.5 L (better transient response, allowing the 48 V MHEV torque fill to work with a smaller turbo margin). Benchmark: BMW B58 I6 uses an air-to-water intercooler integrated with the intake. The LT loop is also the loop that the shared front-module idea (MHEV/BEV commonisation) builds on, so the LT radiator is shared with BEV production.

title: Coolant-to-ATF plate exchanger on LT loop deletes the tow-pack air oil cooler
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Air-oil cooler deleted (€28-36), ~2 m of ATF lines and fittings (€14-20), ATF bypass thermostat (€8-10); larger plate HX (−€10-14) and LT branch hoses/valve (−€12-15). Baseline: a 3,500 kg-towing MHEV SUV usually fits an ATF warmer/cooler on the engine HT loop plus, for tow-pack or hot-market cars, an additional air-to-oil cooler in the front module with ~2 m of steel/rubber ATF lines and a thermostatic bypass — Range Rover owners still report gearbox overheating when towing and fit additional coolers. Proposal: move the transmission heat exchanger to a larger 12-14 plate stacked-plate coolant-to-ATF exchanger (EN AW-3003/4343, CAB-brazed, ~8-10 kW at ΔT 40 K) mounted on the transmission, plumbed into the low-temperature loop (which is held at 45-55 °C by the LT radiator and pump), with a coolant-side 3-way proportional valve from the HT loop for cold-start warm-up. Because LT coolant is 40-50 K colder than the HT loop, the same plate area rejects ~2× more heat, so the separate air-oil cooler, its long ATF lines and bypass thermostat are deleted for all markets, making towing capability a non-hardware variant. Rated at ATF ≤ 110 °C on SAE J2807 Davis Dam at 3,500 kg.

title: Input-series 650V GaN half-bridges replace 1200V SiC in the 800V LDC
description: [800V BEV] 4 × 1200 V SiC (€22-30) → 4 × 650 V GaN (€10-14) plus 2 extra for stacking (€5-7); smaller magnetics (€6-9) and cold plate (€3-4); added balancing control (−€3-4). Baseline: a 2.5-3 kW 800→12 V LDC in an 800 V SUV typically uses a phase-shifted full bridge of 1200 V SiC MOSFETs (4 × 40-80 mΩ) at 100-200 kHz, a wound transformer and a 12 V synchronous rectifier, because the 800 V bus (up to ~920 V) exceeds 650 V devices. Proposal: an input-series, output-parallel (ISOP) topology — two 400 V half-bridge LLC stages stacked in series on the 800 V input (capacitor-split mid-point with active voltage balancing), each using 650 V GaN HEMTs (e.g. 50 mΩ, ~€2.5-3.5 each) at 500 kHz-1 MHz, outputs paralleled at 12 V. Higher frequency shrinks the two planar transformers to ~40% of the single 150 kHz transformer volume, and GaN switching loss lets the cold plate shrink. Benchmark: Hyundai/Kia ICCU integrates a liquid-cooled LDC that steps HV down to 12 V; Xiaomi YU7 and Li i8 show 800 V SiC is the default for traction — the LDC is a low-power stage where SiC is not required.

title: Charge-communication controller folded into the OBC, deleting a standalone module
description: [800V BEV] EVCC housing, connector and PCB substrate deleted (€14-18), bracket and LV harness (€6-8), duplicate MCU/power supply (€8-10); added modem/drivers on OBC board (−€7-9). Baseline: many premium BEVs carry a stand-alone charging control module (EVCC: PLC modem for ISO 15118/DIN 70121, control-pilot/proximity circuitry, inlet lock and flap driver, inlet temperature sensing) in its own housing with a 20-40 pin connector, LV supply, CAN and a harness to the charge inlet. Proposal: put the EVCC function on the OBC controller board (the OBC already sits close to the inlet and has an automotive MCU with spare cores and HSM): add a HomePlug Green PHY modem IC, CP/PP front end, two H-bridge drivers for lock and flap and NTC inputs. The inlet harness lands on the OBC; the stand-alone module, its housing, bracket and ~2 m of LV harness are deleted. Benchmark: BMW Gen6 Energy Master handles communication with the charging system centrally, and Hyundai ICCU merges OBC and LDC — both consolidate charge-related electronics into fewer boxes; this idea consolidates the EVCC into the OBC as the smallest step.

title: Foil-plus-drain shield replaces braided copper shield on short 800V feeds
description: [800V BEV] Braid copper (≈ 40-55 g/m on 6 mm² cable) replaced by foil + drain (≈ 8-12 g/m); braiding is a slow process (~10-20 m/min) versus foil wrapping inline with extrusion (~60-100 m/min); termination simplified. Baseline: 800 V shielded cables in luxury BEVs generally use a tinned-copper braid with 85-90% optical coverage (0.15-0.20 mm strands) over the insulation — braid accounts for 25-35% of cable material cost on 4-16 mm² sizes and requires a crimped shield-ring termination. Proposal: for short (< 1.5 m), low-current auxiliary feeds with modest EMC exposure (HV heater, PTC, e-compressor feed inside the EDU/front bay), use an aluminium-PET foil wrap with 100% coverage plus a tinned-copper drain wire (or a sparse 40-60% spiral) instead of the full braid; terminate via the drain wire in an IDC-style shield contact. Transfer impedance at 1-30 MHz must stay below ~10-20 mΩ/m; foil gives 100% coverage at HF while the drain carries LF shield current. SEI documents that HV cable shields can be braided, lateral winding or metallic foil tape and are selected according to the required noise-shielding level — this idea makes that selection per feed rather than defaulting to braid everywhere.

Transfer impedance at 1-30 MHz must stay below ~10-20 mΩ/m; foil gives 100% coverage at HF while the drain carries LF shield current. SEI documents that HV cable shields can be braided, lateral winding or metallic foil tape and are selected according to the required noise-shielding level — this idea makes that selection per feed rather than defaulting to braid everywhere.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Braid copper (≈ 40-55 g/m on 6 mm² cable) replaced by foil + drain (≈ 8-12 g/m); braiding is a slow process (~10-20 m/min) versus foil wrapping inline with extrusion (~60-100 m/min); termination simplified.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Cable supplier removes the braiding step for these part numbers (braiders are the bottleneck); harness supplier uses drain-wire termination (crimp) instead of braid fold-back + ring (~15 s saved per end).
ideaData.dfmDfa: Lighter and more flexible cable eases routing in the crowded front bay; drain wire termination is visually checkable; colour band identifies foil-shield variants to avoid use on long runs.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low — limited to short auxiliary feeds
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Per vehicle: braid Cu material (~4 m) €5-€7 + braiding process €2-€3 + termination labour €2-€3 + foil + drain material −€2…−€2 = €7-€11. × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €0.35M-€0.55M. Engineering estimate from piece-cost deltas; to be confirmed by should-cost engine and supplier RFQ.

ideaData.riskNotes: Foil cracking under repeated flexing (EDU-mounted feeds) and lower LF shielding; risk to CISPR 25 radiated emissions class 5. Validate per feed: transfer impedance IEC 62153-4-3, CISPR 25 ALSE, flex test ISO 19642-2, thermal ageing 3,000 h at 150 °C (class D).

title: Al-XLPE 70 mm² conductor for the pack-to-rear EDU DC run
description: [800V BEV] Copper conductor (~445 g/m at ~€9/kg ≈ €4.0/m) replaced by Al (~190 g/m at ~€3/kg ≈ €0.6/m); over ~4 m total: ~€13-15 conductor saving; larger shield/insulation and Cu-Al lugs add €4-6. Baseline: the main DC cables from the pack junction to the rear EDU inverter in an 800 V SUV are typically 2 × 50 mm² copper, shielded, ~1.5-2.5 m each (rear EDU current ≈ 400-450 A peak, ~150-200 A continuous). Proposal: specify 2 × 70 mm² aluminium (EC-grade Al 1370, class 5/6 stranding) with XLPE insulation and braid shield, terminated by friction-welded or ultrasonic-welded Cu-Al transition lugs at both ends. Resistance: Al 70 mm² ≈ 0.443 mΩ/m vs Cu 50 mm² ≈ 0.386 mΩ/m (+15%) — acceptable because at 800 V the continuous current is half the 400 V equivalent; thermal check: I²R at 200 A = 17.7 W/m in a Ø 15 mm cable stays within 150 °C insulation class with 40 °C ambient. Mass: Cu 50 mm² ≈ 445 g/m conductor vs Al 70 mm² ≈ 190 g/m (−57%). Sources: Sumitomo Wiring Systems states aluminium wires significantly reduce harness weight; shielded XLPE aluminium HV cables are catalogue items; 800 V halves current and allows conductor optimisation after thermal and voltage-drop checks. Library already covers aluminium busbars and AC charge cables — this idea targets the main shielded DC run with an upsized Al section.

title: Thick-film heating element replaces PTC ceramic stones in HV coolant heater
description: [800V BEV] Ceramic stones, clips, insulating films and multi-stage switches (€38-48) replaced by printed element on substrate (€22-28) and one PWM switch; smaller housing (€5-7); fewer assembly steps. Baseline: many 800 V HV coolant heaters use stacks of barium-titanate PTC ceramic stones clamped between aluminium fins with spring clips and insulating films, 6-8 kW, 2-3 power stages, ~2.5-3 kg; PTC stones at 800 V need high-voltage grades and thick insulation, and the self-limiting characteristic makes power control coarse. Proposal: a thick-film element — dielectric glass-ceramic layer screen-printed on a stainless (EN 1.4509 ferritic, 1.5 mm) or aluminium substrate, with printed Ag-Pd resistive tracks fired at ~850 °C — bonded to a die-cast coolant channel; controlled by one 1200 V SiC MOSFET with PWM for stepless power. Power density 15-25 W/cm² vs ~8-10 W/cm² for PTC stacks; mass ~1.2-1.6 kg. Benchmark: Porsche Macan Electric heats its battery as required through a high-voltage heater integrated into thermal management, alongside a standard heat pump; Li Auto shows pack heating at 1.2 °C/min at −10 °C is a fast-charge enabler. Thick-film enables fast, stepless response to those heating requests at lower part count.

title: Ferrite rotor magnets replace bonded NdFeB in 48V coolant pumps
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] NdFeB (bonded ~€60-90/kg) replaced by ferrite (~€2-4/kg); ~15-25 g NdFeB per pump × 5 pumps averaged across powertrains; slightly more copper/steel for longer stack. Baseline: 100-400 W wet-rotor electric coolant pumps commonly use injection-moulded or compression-bonded NdFeB ring magnets (Br ~0.6-0.7 T) in the rotor to keep the canned motor small; a platform with 3-4 pumps on the BEV and 2 on the MHEV carries ~40-90 g of NdFeB in pumps. Proposal: switch to sintered strontium ferrite segments (e.g. Y35-class, Br ~0.42-0.44 T, Hcj ≥ 240 kA/m) or a bonded-ferrite ring (cheaper, Br ~0.28 T for small pumps) in a spoke/flux-concentrating rotor; the 48 V supply (see the shared 48 V actuator idea) lowers current, so the slightly larger stack (+15-20% axial length) is within the canned envelope. Pump hydraulic efficiency unchanged; motor efficiency falls ~2-3 points at nominal point, i.e. ~3-5 W on a 200 W pump — negligible versus vehicle load. Benchmark: Ingenium I6 MHEV runs electrically controlled water pumps and the platform commonisation idea moves all pumps to 48 V; Xiaomi YU7 illustrates the Chinese focus on cost-down in 800 V power hardware. No OEM pump-magnet data is claimed.

title: PPS-GF40 rotary split-cooling valve body replaces die-cast thermostat housing
description: [MHEV] HPDC Al housing + 4 machining ops + press-in spigots (€16-21) replaced by PPS-GF40 net-shape moulding (€9-12); no separate thermostat insert in housing (function in rotary disc). Baseline: I6 engine thermostat/coolant outlet housings are often HPDC aluminium (EN AC-46000) with machined O-ring grooves, sensor bosses and press-in spigots (~0.6-0.9 kg), with the wax thermostat as a separate insert. Proposal: for the rotary heat-management valve (see the 48 V pump assembly idea), mould the valve body in PPS-GF40 (continuous use 200 °C, glycol-resistant, low creep) with moulded-in spigots, sensor pocket and stepper flange; the two rotary discs in PPS-GF40 or PA6T-GF; Al4 seal faces by moulded FKM/EPDM. Net-shape moulding removes machining (≈ 4 operations) and press-fitting of spigots; mass ~0.35-0.45 kg. Benchmark: BMW B58 uses an electrically operated heat-management module with a rotary valve in place of a wax thermostat, and uses split cooling of head and block — this part idea specifies the material route for that valve body on our I6.

title: Down-gauged long-life alloy radiator tubes on the shared LT/HT cores
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Aluminium content per core −12-15% (two cores, ~2.2-2.8 kg Al total at ~€4.5/kg clad strip) ≈ €1.5-2.0; long-life alloy premium on strip (~+3-4%); thinner fin increases fins per kg. Baseline: brazed aluminium radiator cores in luxury SUVs often use 0.25-0.27 mm EN AW-3003 tubes clad with 4343 and a Zn-diffused outer for corrosion, and 0.08 mm fins, sized conservatively for 15-year salt exposure and 2.0-2.5 bar pressure cycling. Proposal: move to a post-braze high-strength "long-life" 3xxx core alloy (Mn + Cu + Mg-limited, post-braze Rp0.2 ≥ 60-70 MPa vs ~40-45 MPa for 3003) with a sacrificial Zn-containing inner/outer liner, allowing tube gauge 0.20-0.22 mm and fin 0.065-0.07 mm. Burst margin is kept because the higher post-braze yield compensates the ~18% thinner wall; corrosion life is held by the sacrificial liner (SWAAT/OY test). Core mass drops ~12-15%. This applies to the common carrier’s LT core shared by MHEV and BEV and the MHEV HT core. Benchmark: Volvo SPA3 shows a ~20% cost reduction in a new-generation thermal/HVAC system; Valeo catalogues heat exchanger families for heat pumps — tier-1 alloys are the lever, not a new technology.

ideaData.title: Down-gauged long-life alloy radiator tubes on the shared LT/HT cores
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: brazed aluminium radiator cores in luxury SUVs often use 0.25-0.27 mm EN AW-3003 tubes clad with 4343 and a Zn-diffused outer for corrosion, and 0.08 mm fins, sized conservatively for 15-year salt exposure and 2.0-2.5 bar pressure cycling. Proposal: move to a post-braze high-strength "long-life" 3xxx core alloy (Mn + Cu + Mg-limited, post-braze Rp0.2 ≥ 60-70 MPa vs ~40-45 MPa for 3003) with a sacrificial Zn-containing inner/outer liner, allowing tube gauge 0.20-0.22 mm and fin 0.065-0.07 mm. Burst margin is kept because the higher post-braze yield compensates the ~18% thinner wall; corrosion life is held by the sacrificial liner (SWAAT/OY test). Core mass drops ~12-15%. This applies to the common carrier’s LT core shared by MHEV and BEV and the MHEV HT core. Benchmark: Volvo SPA3 shows a ~20% cost reduction in a new-generation thermal/HVAC system; Valeo catalogues heat exchanger families for heat pumps — tier-1 alloys are the lever, not a new technology.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Aluminium content per core −12-15% (two cores, ~2.2-2.8 kg Al total at ~€4.5/kg clad strip) ≈ €1.5-2.0; long-life alloy premium on strip (~+3-4%); thinner fin increases fins per kg.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Same CAB brazing furnace and cycle; tube mill set-up for 0.20-0.22 mm (tighter weld/fold control); fin mill tooling adjusted for 0.065 mm strip; scrap rate monitored closely during the ramp-up.
ideaData.dfmDfa: No change to interfaces, tanks or core dimensions — a drop-in change for the module and vehicle lines; lighter cores ease handling at the module line; same service part interchangeability across years.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low — material trim on two cores
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Per vehicle: aluminium mass −12-15% €2-€3 + fin material €1-€1 + long-life alloy premium −€1…−€1 = €2-€3. × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €0.10M-€0.15M. Engineering estimate from piece-cost deltas; to be confirmed by should-cost engine and supplier RFQ.

ideaData.riskNotes: External corrosion (salt, mud — relevant to off-road use) and erosion by coolant at high flow; pressure-cycling fatigue. Validate SWAAT ASTM G85-A3, OY water corrosion, pressure cycling 0-2.5 bar 200k cycles, thermal shock, stone impact.

title: Debris screen moulded into the lower grille protects off-road cooling cores
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] [Off-road] Separate stone-guard mesh and clips/brackets deleted (€9-14), grille tool gains lattice inserts (amortised €1); field warranty for fin damage/blocked condenser reduced (€2-3). Baseline: off-road-capable luxury SUVs protect the front cooling pack from stones, mud and vegetation with a separate stainless or aluminium mesh stone guard (or aftermarket guard) clipped behind the bumper grille, plus a separate active-shutter frame; mud packing in the condenser/gas-cooler and LT core is a known cause of high-temperature derates during low-speed crawling and towing in summer. Proposal: integrate a fine debris screen (4-6 mm aperture lattice, 1.2 mm ribs, ~70% open area) directly into the lower grille moulding (PP-TD20 or PA6-GF15 two-shot with the visible grille), positioned 40-60 mm ahead of the core with a drain gap so mud falls rather than packing on fins; the screen is user-cleanable from the front with a hose. The separate mesh, clips and brackets are deleted. Air-side pressure drop added ~10-15 Pa at 3 m/s, offset in fan sizing. For BEV, it protects the gas cooler/condenser which carries the fast-charge heat load. Benchmark: Range Rover owners retrofitting additional transmission coolers for towing illustrate that front-end heat rejection margin matters in real use; protecting core cleanliness preserves that margin cheaply.

title: Multi-port extruded tubes replace folded clad tubes in R744 gas cooler
description: [800V BEV] Extruded MPE at ~€6-7/kg vs formed/clad high-pressure tubes at ~€9-11/kg; ~1.0-1.3 kg tube mass per gas cooler; fewer braze failures (scrap −1-2 pts) because no internal fold joints. Baseline: high-pressure heat exchangers for R744 (gas cooler working ≤ 140 bar, burst ≥ 3× MOP) need small hydraulic diameters; some designs use folded, internally finned clad-sheet tubes or thick-walled round tubes, which are expensive to form and braze tightly at that pressure. Proposal: use multi-port extruded (MPE) microchannel tubes in EN AW-3102 or 1xxx-based extrusion alloy (e.g. 16-20 ports, Dh ~0.6-0.8 mm, wall 0.25-0.30 mm) with zinc arc-spray for external corrosion protection and non-clad tubes brazed to clad fins/headers. MPE tubes take the pressure via small port spans, give higher refrigerant-side heat transfer, and are extruded continuously at low cost per kg; headers become round extruded tubes. Benchmark: Valeo catalogues heat exchangers for both R1234yf and R744 heat pumps, and VW runs more than one million EVs with R744 heat pumps, which drives tier-1 MPE capacity; VW has worked to reduce the cost of the CO2 system. This part idea specifies MPE as the tube route for our R744 gas cooler.

title: Sealed wading-rated BLDC fan motor deletes fan-inhibit relay and splash shield
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] [Off-road] Fan-inhibit relay/driver output and wiring (€4-6), splash shield and fasteners (€5-7) deleted; brushless motor warranty claims after wading reduced (€3-5); BLDC premium over brushed largely already paid in 48 V fan (net −€2-3). Baseline: off-road luxury SUVs with deep wading capability protect the cooling fan with wading-mode logic (fan inhibit to avoid blade/water strike and brushed-motor ingress), a dedicated relay or driver output, and a separate splash shield/deflector below the fan shroud; brushed fan motors and their speed controllers are vulnerable to water ingress and are a warranty item after wading. Proposal: specify a brushless (BLDC) 48 V fan motor with integrated controller potted to IP6K9K/IPX7, sealed bearings and a breather with hydrophobic membrane, and fan blades in PA66-GF30 tolerant of water impact at reduced speed; the controller runs a wading speed-limit (e.g. ≤ 400 rpm) via LIN instead of a hard inhibit relay; the separate splash shield is deleted because the shroud lower edge carries a moulded deflector lip. The 48 V supply comes from the platform-common 48 V actuator idea (Cybertruck shows a 48 V architecture powering everything except drive motors).

title: Low-pressure coolant hoses moved from EPDM to extruded PA12 tubes with spin-welded ports
description: [800V BEV] EPDM hose (~€3-5/m) + clamps (€0.3-0.6 each) replaced by PA12 tube (~€1.5-2.5/m) + welded ports; ~5 m converted; clamp count −14-18; quick connectors partly offset. Baseline: the BEV low-temperature coolant circuits (pack, EDUs, OBC/LDC, chiller; 25-60 °C, ≤ 2.5 bar) are commonly plumbed with peroxide-cured EPDM hoses (Ø 16-25 mm, ~6-9 m total) with textile reinforcement, spring or worm clamps and moulded elbows. Proposal: replace the rigid-routed sections (~60-70% of length) with extruded PA12 (or PA612) single-wall or corrugated tubes, thermoformed to shape, with spin-welded or laser-welded PA connectors and SAE J2044 quick connectors; keep short EPDM/TPV sections only where isolation is needed (EDU to body). Because the LT loop never exceeds ~70 °C (no 120-130 °C ICE coolant), PA12 is fully adequate; the BEV is a better fit for plastic lines than the MHEV HT loop. Mass falls ~35-45% versus EPDM hose. Benchmark: Tesla Model Y routes battery, drive-unit and cabin coolant through the Supermanifold/Octovalve with short connections; Volvo SPA3 cut thermal-system cost ~20% — plastic LT lines are a standard lever in that class of redesign.

ideaData.title: Engine-agnostic 48V P2 motor in 8HP bell-housing replaces petrol and diesel BiSG variants
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: a P0 belt-integrated starter-generator (BiSG) on the front-end accessory drive, as on the Ingenium P400/D300 and Audi Q8 BAS. Because the petrol and diesel I6 have different FEAD layouts, the BiSG needs two bracket castings, two pulley/tensioner sets, two belt lengths and, in many BiSG applications, a retained 12 V pinion starter for cold cranking — roughly 14-16 unique parts per engine type. Proposal: move the 48 V machine into the transmission bell-housing as a P2 module, exactly the ZF gen-4 8HP MHEV option where the 48 V e-motor sits between the torque converter and the front torsional damper (BMW B58TU2 X5/X7 LCI uses this, branded 8HP60XMH). The motor sees transmission input speed, so one stator/rotor (≈ 20-25 kW peak at 48 V, ~200 Nm) serves both fuels; the engine side keeps a simple mechanical or electric-ancillary FEAD with no high-torque tensioner. Physics: a P0 BiSG must transmit up to ~60 Nm crank torque through a poly-V belt at a 2.5-3:1 pulley ratio, which drives a two-arm decoupling tensioner and an 8-rib belt; a P2 motor is gear-free and torque-unlimited by belt slip, so it also recuperates more (no belt slip, and the engine can be decoupled by the lock-up clutch).

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Engine dress line loses the BiSG fit-and-tension station (~45 s) and belt-tracking check; transmission plant receives a pre-assembled motor module from the gearbox supplier. ideaData.dfmDfa: Removes ~12 fasteners and two HV-style 48 V phase-cable runs across the engine front; the 48 V connector moves to a fixed transmission flange position, keyed and coded so it cannot be swapped with the 12 V harness. title: Delete 48V electric supercharger by using P2 motor torque-fill for launch transients
description: [MHEV] Removes the eSC unit (motor, inverter, compressor wheel, housing), the bypass valve and duct, a 48 V cable branch and a CAN node; the torque-fill function is software on hardware already paid for (P2/ISG motor and 48 V battery). Baseline: the 3.0 l I6 carries a twin-scroll turbo plus a 48 V electric supercharger (eSC) in series in the intake, as on the Ingenium P400 (eSC spools to 65,000 rpm in 0.5 s, torque rise up to 300 Nm/s) and the Mercedes M256 (BorgWarner eBooster, up to 70,000 rpm). The eSC brings a ~5-7 kW high-speed motor, its own 48 V inverter, a bypass valve, extra ducting and a 48 V harness branch. Proposal: delete the eSC and fill the first 0.5-1.0 s of turbo lag with crank-level torque from the 48 V P2/ISG motor, which in BMW B58TU2 form lifts system torque from 520 to 540 Nm. Physics: at 1,200-1,500 rpm a 20 kW machine delivers ~130-160 Nm at the crank — the same order as the torque gap the eSC closes before turbine enthalpy builds; at the wheel through 1st gear (≈ 5:1) and 3.2:1 final drive that is >2,000 Nm, matching the perceived step. The battery cost of torque-fill is small: 20 kW × 1 s = 20 kJ ≈ 0.006 kWh per event.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Foundry: one rotacast cell family with shared dies (~€2.5-3M tooling avoided). Machining: one FMS cell family with program-selected features; changeover by part-ID read (DMC) rather than fixture swap. Leak-test recipes 2 → 1 hardware with two programs.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Shared liners, main-bearing caps, bolts, oil-pump mounting and timing-cover interface; DMC code on each casting drives machining program so wrong-program machining is prevented; common assembly pallets for both fuels.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — tooling and volume leverage

Net €28-€43 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €1.4M-€2.15M.

title: Petrol I6 Euro 7: 48V heated catalyst trades PGM loading and secondary air
description: [MHEV] PGM (Pd/Rh) is the most expensive line of the aftertreatment; cutting 20-30% of ~4 g saves more than the EHC disc costs, and deleting the secondary-air pump/valve/hoses and retard-heating fuel penalty adds further. Baseline: to hold Euro 7 limits for 10 years/200,000 km (main lifetime 8 years/160,000 km) a large petrol I6 typically adds catalyst heating by ignition retard, a raised PGM loading on the close-coupled brick (often 3-5 g PGM on a 1.5-2.0 l brick) and, on some engines, a secondary-air pump with valve and pipework. Proposal: a 48 V electrically heated disc (2-4 kW) ahead of a thin-wall close-coupled TWC, energised for 15-30 s pre-start and post-start from the 48 V battery; PGM loading reduced 20-30% and secondary air deleted. Vitesco’s EMICAT — first high-volume EHC, SOP 2022 on 48 V diesel MHEVs — cut WLTP NOx 40% and CO2 3% with 4 kW. Physics: heating 0.3 kg of substrate by 250 K needs ~0.3 × 0.9 kJ/kgK × 250 ≈ 68 kJ (≈ 17 s at 4 kW), well within a 0.2-0.5 kWh 48 V pack (energy used ≈ 0.02 kWh), and the light-off moves from ~20-30 s of engine operation to start-of-drive.

title: Diesel I6: close-coupled SCRF plus 48V EHC deletes underfloor second SCR brick
description: [MHEV] Deletes the underfloor SCR substrate (~2 l Cu-zeolite), its can, second doser, mixer and one NOx sensor; the EHC disc and 48 V control cost less than half of that hardware. Baseline: a Euro 6d / Euro 7-ready 3.0 l diesel commonly runs DOC + SCR-coated DPF (SCRF) close-coupled, followed by an underfloor SCR + ammonia-slip catalyst (ASC) with a second AdBlue doser — a "twin-dosing" layout that adds a 2-3 l ceramic brick, a can, a doser, a mixer, NOx and temperature sensors and roughly 4-5 kg. Range Rover L460 D300/D350 MHEVs list SCRF aftertreatment. Proposal: keep a single close-coupled DOC + SCRF with one doser, and add a 48 V electrically heated catalyst ahead of the DOC so the SCRF reaches 200 °C dosing temperature in urban driving; shrink the underfloor element to a small ASC-only brick. Vitesco data with a 4 kW EHC on a 48 V diesel MHEV: SCR efficiency 97% and NOx −62% in the slow Traffic-for-London cycle. Physics: the underfloor SCR exists mainly because the close-coupled SCRF cools below dosing temperature at low load; heating at 48 V restores that, so the second SCR is redundant.

title: Disconnecting front driveline: transfer-case clutch plus front-diff decoupler for MHEV AWD
description: [MHEV] Savings are primarily CO2-compliance value (fleet credit) and smaller front axle oil volume/cooling; the front diff can use a lighter carrier because peak torques are unchanged but continuous thermal load drops, enabling a smaller oil fill and deleting the front-axle oil cooler on hot-market variants. Baseline: luxury MHEV SUVs with a single-speed on-demand transfer case keep the front propshaft, front differential and half-shafts rotating at all times; the multi-plate transfer clutch is only partly open, so bearing, seal and oil-churning losses of the front axle (typically 1-2% of tractive energy at cruise) are always paid. Proposal: adopt Audi quattro ultra logic on a longitudinal rear-biased layout — the transfer-case clutch fully opens and a 12 V electromechanical dog clutch on the front differential output disconnects one half-shaft, so propshaft, pinion and ring gear stop. Audi measured ~0.3 l/100 km saving in real traffic and the system was ~4 kg lighter than its predecessor. Predictive reconnection uses steering angle, lateral acceleration, torque request and Terrain Response mode, with permanent connection in all off-road modes. Physics: removing ~120-180 W of drag at 100 km/h on a 2.4 t SUV is roughly 0.15-0.25 l/100 km — of the same order as the CO2 credit priced by OEMs.

title: Single-speed transfer case standard with bolt-on low-range reduction module on common housing
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Vehicles without the off-road pack (assumed 55-65% of MHEV volume) no longer carry the planetary set, shift fork and range motor; the off-road variant uses the same main housing, so no second housing die/machining line is needed. Baseline: a luxury off-road SUV either fits a two-speed transfer case to all vehicles (carrying a planetary reduction set, range-shift fork and motor on buyers who never use low range) or develops two different transfer cases with separate housings. The Range Rover Sport L461 makes the two-speed transfer case optional and the Land Rover parts catalogue lists a 1-speed L461 variant; Ineos Grenadier and Land Cruiser 250 fit two-speed units with a ~2.5:1 low ratio. Proposal: one transfer-case main housing (AlSi9Cu3 HPDC) with an input-side mounting face that accepts either a 1:1 input spigot cover or a bolt-on planetary low-range module (2.5-2.7:1, 4-pinion, helical) with its own electric range-shift actuator. The clutch pack, chain drive, output shafts and control unit are common. Physics: the low-range module adds ~60 mm of length; the propshaft is supplied in two lengths (one extra part), while the housing machining remains one fixture family.

title: Three I6 hardware builds instead of six: ratings set by 48V boost
description: [MHEV] Halves Euro 7 type-approval/durability families (each costs several €M), cuts part numbers for turbos, injectors, pistons and intercoolers, increases volume per part, and reduces service stock. Baseline: luxury SUV I6 families typically offer 5-7 power ratings (e.g. petrol P360/P400/P440 and diesel D250/D300/D350 in Ingenium terms), with differences in turbocharger trim, intercooler, injector flow, pistons and calibration — each a separate Euro 7 type-approval family requiring its own durability demonstration over 200,000 km. Mercedes publicly targeted a ~50% reduction of engine variants going into Euro 7; ACEA’s study put Euro 7 direct costs near €2,000 per ICE car. Proposal: freeze three hardware builds (one petrol, two diesel at most) and derive the rating steps from calibration and the 48 V ISG/P2 boost (e.g. +12-20 kW and +200 Nm as on BMW xDrive30d B57 MHEV), using the Ingenium-style modular 500 cc cylinder commonality. Physics: rated power differs by turbo map and fuel mass; within the same turbo, the peak-power limit is mostly thermal (exhaust temperature ~950-980 °C) — so lower ratings are de-rates of the top hardware, and torque differentiation at low speed comes from the electric machine.

title: 8HP MHEV launch element: torque converter replaced by wet start clutch with motor launch
description: [MHEV] A wet start clutch module is lighter and has fewer precision-brazed hydrodynamic parts than a converter; the motor already present provides the torque multiplication function. Fuel/CO2 benefit from no converter slip adds compliance value. Baseline: in the ZF gen-4 8HP MHEV configuration the 48 V motor is added between the torque converter and the front torsional damper, so the vehicle carries both a hydrodynamic converter (impeller, turbine, stator with one-way clutch, lock-up clutch, ~12-14 kg with fluid) and an e-motor. ZF states the gen-4 is modular with different starting elements; its PHEV versions replace the converter with a wet clutch. Proposal: on the MHEV, replace the converter with a wet multi-plate launch clutch (6-8 sintered-paper friction faces, ~250 mm OD) plus a dual-stage spring damper, using the 48 V motor to hold idle-speed creep and fill launch torque so the clutch slips for <1 s. Physics: the converter’s torque multiplication (~1.8-2.0 at stall) is what allows gentle launches; a 20-25 kW motor supplying ~150-200 Nm at 0 rpm input gives equal launch torque at the gearbox input without slip losses, and removes converter slip losses (~1-2% fuel in urban).

title: 8HP hydraulic supply: single power-split pump in place of twin-pump layout
description: [MHEV] Deletes the self-contained auxiliary unit (housing, BLDC drive, controller, check valve, suction line); fewer hydraulic leak paths; reduced parasitic drag because the mechanical path no longer needs margin for engine-off duty. Baseline: earlier hybridised 8HP transmissions used a twin-pump layout — a vane-cell unit driven from the input and a second, self-contained auxiliary unit with its own BLDC drive to keep shift elements pressurised while the combustion engine is stopped (stop-start, sailing, electric creep) — each with housing, seals, check valves, and the auxiliary unit with its own controller. ZF’s gen-4 8HP replaced these with one power-split pump: a planetary stage lets the input shaft drive it while the engine runs and a small motor drive it when the engine is off. Proposal: specify the gen-4 single power-split unit on our MHEV 8HP rather than a carry-over twin-pump hydraulic layout, and size its motor at ~250-350 W on the 12 V side. Physics: with a 48 V MHEV the engine stops often (coasting shut-off, stop-start), so the hydraulic supply must cover ~1-2 l/min valve-body leakage plus shift-element fill at 5-10 bar; the planetary power split lets a small motor cover that standby duty while the mechanical path supplies full flow at speed, so no element is sized twice.

title: 48V/12V DC-DC: four-phase 100V GaN converter replaces five-phase silicon MOSFET design
description: [MHEV] One fewer phase (switches, driver, inductor, current sense), smaller magnetics and capacitors, smaller heat sink and housing; the efficiency gain also cuts 12 V-side generation losses that cost CO2. Baseline: a 3-3.5 kW bidirectional 48/12 V converter built with 80-100 V silicon MOSFETs at ~100 kHz needs five interleaved buck phases (≈600 W/phase), five coupled inductors and a liquid- or large air-cooled aluminium heat sink. Proposal: four interleaved phases with 100 V enhancement-mode GaN HEMTs at 250 kHz. Published converter work shows GaN at 250 kHz reaching 97% efficiency and 800 W/phase, allowing a 3.5 kW converter in four phases instead of five, 1.5 percentage points higher efficiency, and >35% smaller and lighter. Physics: switching loss scales with Qg·Vds·f and GaN has ~5-10x lower Qg and zero Qrr, so frequency can rise 2.5x at the same loss; inductance per phase scales ~1/f, so each inductor drops from ~2.2 µH to ~0.9 µH and its core volume by roughly half. The 1.5-point efficiency gain at 3 kW is ~45 W less heat, enabling the converter to share the 48 V battery cold plate.

title: Direct-injection-only petrol I6: delete port-injection rail using 48V-assisted cold start

ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count −12 to −15 (6 injectors, 6 seals/clips, rail, sensor, harness branch); fuel line to the engine becomes one LP feed to the HP pump; fewer fuel connections reduce leak and fire risk in the hot V.

title: Miller two-step intake cam with wide-authority VVT replaces electrohydraulic variable lift
description: [MHEV] Deletes the high-pressure oil chamber module, six solenoid valves, its accumulator and complex machined carrier; a sliding cam uses standard roller-finger followers and two actuators. Baseline: Ingenium-type I6 engines use an electrohydraulic fully variable valve lift (oil-chamber lost-motion system with a high-pressure pump element on the camshaft and six solenoid valves) to throttle-less control the intake charge, plus cam phasers. Proposal: replace it with a two-step sliding intake cam (two lift profiles: a short-duration Miller early-intake-closing profile for part load and a full profile for rated power), switched by two 12 V electromagnetic actuators per bank, plus a wide-authority (≥70° crank) mid-lock intake phaser. BMW’s B58TU2 uses the Miller cycle with shortened intake opening and redesigned ports and chambers. The 48 V torque-fill compensates for the reduced low-speed volumetric efficiency of Miller timing. Physics: early IVC lowers effective compression (~9.5-10 vs geometric ~11-12), cutting pumping work and knock; a 2-step plus phaser covers ~85-90% of the BSFC benefit of fully variable lift in WLTP because most operating points cluster in a narrow load band.

title: Mono-scroll wastegated turbine housing replacing twin-scroll once 48V torque-fill is present
description: [MHEV] One sand core instead of two, no divider wall machining, fewer casting defects (divider-wall cracking is a known scrap/warranty driver), simpler manifold flange; casting weight −0.4 to −0.6 kg of high-temperature alloy. Baseline: the I6 uses a twin-scroll turbo (Ingenium inline-six, Mercedes M256), splitting cylinders 1-3 and 4-6 into two divided volutes so pulse energy spools the turbine at low speed. The divided turbine housing needs a two-core sand-casting (separate scroll cores, a divider wall that cracks under thermal cycling) in high-silicon or Ni-resist cast material, and the exhaust manifold must keep the two pulse groups separate to the flange. Proposal: with 48 V crank torque-fill covering the first ~1 s of transient (P2/ISG ~150-200 Nm at low rpm), switch to a mono-scroll turbine housing with an electric wastegate and a merged 6-into-1 manifold. Physics: twin-scroll pulse separation mainly raises turbine efficiency below ~2,000 rpm; above that, a mono-scroll is equal or better (no divider wall heat loss and lower back-pressure, ~2-4% better BSFC at rated). The low-speed torque deficit (~8-12% at 1,250 rpm) is within the authority of the electric machine.

title: 48V P2 motor sized for road duty; long crawls use engine plus low range
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Shorter stator stack (~20-25% less copper and electrical steel), smaller inverter MOSFET array and no dedicated spray-cooling circuit; the motor is cooled by the transmission oil already present. Baseline: if the 48 V P2/ISG is expected to deliver its peak assist continuously in off-road crawl (2-5 km/h, 3,500 kg trailer, 40 °C ambient), its continuous rating must approach peak — a longer stator stack, oil spray cooling with a dedicated circuit, a higher-current inverter and thermal sensors on each phase. GWM’s Hi4-T off-road hybrid (Tank 500) explicitly lets the electric machine be engaged or disengaged so it is protected from overheating in prolonged challenging situations, leaving the combustion engine to propel the vehicle. Proposal: size the 48 V machine for on-road duty (e.g. 20 kW peak for 10 s, ~8-10 kW continuous) and, in Terrain Response crawl modes with low range engaged, run it only for stop-start, creep smoothing and brief assist, with a temperature-based torque derate; the 2.5:1 low range (as on Ineos Grenadier/Land Cruiser 250) multiplies engine torque so no electric assist is needed for sustained crawl. title: Non-pressurised MHEV fuel reservoir: six-layer HDPE/EVOH blow moulding instead of welded steel
description: [MHEV] Removes deep-draw dies, seam welding, coating/painting and leak repair; integrates mounting bosses, rollover-valve and pump-module carriers in the mould; weight saving adds CO2 value. Baseline: some luxury SUV platforms carry a welded steel saddle tank (e.g. 1.0-1.2 mm DC04 + Zn-Ni or terne-coated, ~80-90 l, straddling the propshaft/transfer case), often because a PHEV sibling needs a sealed, pressure-rated tank: PHEVs may not purge the canister for many drive cycles so the vessel must stay sealed under pressure. A 48 V MHEV runs its engine regularly and purges normally, so the pressure requirement disappears. Proposal: a co-extrusion blow-moulded six-layer HDPE / regrind / adhesive / EVOH / adhesive / HDPE reservoir (~5-6 mm wall, EVOH ~3% of wall) with twin-sheet or in-mould kiss-offs for saddle stiffness. Plain HDPE permeates 25-30 g/m²/day, which the EVOH layer reduces to near-zero. Physics: steel is ~8x denser than HDPE while HDPE walls are only 3-4x thicker, so mass falls by ~40-50% (e.g. 16 kg → 9 kg); blow moulding produces the complex saddle in one shot instead of stamped halves + seam weld.

title: Move 48V inverter onto 8HP mechatronics: deletes separate underbody inverter box and cables
description: [MHEV] Deletes the separate inverter housing, the phase cable and connectors, the cooling hose pair and the inverter bracket; shares the transmission TCU board substrate and CAN interface. Baseline: a 48 V P0/P2 machine with a separate inverter mounted on the body or engine needs a three-phase 48 V cable (3 × 25 mm²), two sealed connectors, its own aluminium housing with coolant ports or fins, and a separate low-voltage connector — about 15-18 parts in the electrical path. ZF states its gen-4 8HP brings power electronics into the transmission, with power-electronics volume and weight cut by almost 50% and mechatronics by 42%. Proposal: specify the 48 V inverter as part of the 8HP mechatronic unit — MOSFET bridge on the transmission control unit carrier, cooled by ATF, with the motor phases connected by short internal busbars (<150 mm). Physics: at 48 V and ~450 A peak, every 1 m of 25 mm² three-phase cable dissipates ~2 × 450² × 0.0007 Ω ≈ 280 W in bursts; busbars of <0.15 m cut that loss by ~85% and eliminate EMC radiation from long phase cables.

title: P2 motor rotor carrier welded to torque-converter cover instead of separate hub and bearing
description: [MHEV] Deletes separate rotor hub forging, its support bearing, the spline coupling and intermediate housing; one balancing operation instead of two. Shorter driveline length saves tunnel space. Baseline: an add-on P2 module carries its rotor on its own forged hub with a dedicated support bearing (deep-groove ball bearing ~100 mm bore), a splined connection to the transmission input and an intermediate housing — adding ~40 mm length and 3-4 kg. BMW’s B58TU2 X5/X7 LCI combines the 48 V motor with the torque converter of the ZF 8HP (8HP60XMH). Proposal: laser-weld the laminated-rotor carrier (stamped and flow-formed from S420MC, 3.0-3.5 mm) directly onto the torque-converter cover so the converter’s existing pilot and hub bearing support the rotor; the stator presses into the bell-housing. Physics: the converter cover is already a balanced, pilot-located rotating part running at crank speed; adding the rotor (~4-5 kg) at ~140 mm radius raises its inertia, which improves idle smoothness, and the cover’s radial run-out (≤0.1 mm TIR) is compatible with a 0.8-1.0 mm motor air gap.

title: Connecting rod: fracture-split drop-forged 36MnVS4 replaces powder-forged rod
description: [MHEV] Bar stock steel is cheaper than pre-alloyed powder and the PF process (compaction press, sinter furnace, hot re-forge) is replaced by a conventional hammer/press forging line with controlled cooling. Baseline: high-output I6 engines often use powder-forged (PF) connecting rods (Fe-2Cu-0.6C pre-alloyed powder, compacted, sintered and hot-forged to near-full density), ~600-650 g, because PF gives tight weight tolerance (±1-2%) and fracture-splitting capability. Proposal: drop-forged 36MnVS4 micro-alloyed steel rod with controlled cooling from the forging heat (no Q&T), fracture-split at the big end, ~620-660 g. Fracture splitting eliminates sawing and joint-face machining of rod and cap (reported ~25% production-cost reduction vs sawn rods), and 36MnVS4 cracks cleanly with yield strength close to C70S6 while being tougher. Fracture-splitting was first introduced on PF rods and later extended to drop-forged micro-alloyed steel. Physics: 36MnVS4 controlled-cooled reaches Rp0.2 ~550-600 MPa and fatigue limit ~400 MPa — adequate for an I6 at ~110 bar peak cylinder pressure (petrol) with an I-beam section of ~3% larger area; weight balancing by mill-off pads keeps rod-to-rod variation ≤±4 g.

ideaData.title: Connecting rod: fracture-split drop-forged 36MnVS4 replaces powder-forged rod
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: high-output I6 engines often use powder-forged (PF) connecting rods (Fe-2Cu-0.6C pre-alloyed powder, compacted, sintered and hot-forged to near-full density), ~600-650 g, because PF gives tight weight tolerance (±1-2%) and fracture-splitting capability. Proposal: drop-forged 36MnVS4 micro-alloyed steel rod with controlled cooling from the forging heat (no Q&T), fracture-split at the big end, ~620-660 g. Fracture splitting eliminates sawing and joint-face machining of rod and cap (reported ~25% production-cost reduction vs sawn rods), and 36MnVS4 cracks cleanly with yield strength close to C70S6 while being tougher. Fracture-splitting was first introduced on PF rods and later extended to drop-forged micro-alloyed steel. Physics: 36MnVS4 controlled-cooled reaches Rp0.2 ~550-600 MPa and fatigue limit ~400 MPa — adequate for an I6 at ~110 bar peak cylinder pressure (petrol) with an I-beam section of ~3% larger area; weight balancing by mill-off pads keeps rod-to-rod variation ≤±4 g.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Bar stock steel is cheaper than pre-alloyed powder and the PF process (compaction press, sinter furnace, hot re-forge) is replaced by a conventional hammer/press forging line with controlled cooling.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Forging: 1 press line, 6-8 s per rod, controlled-cooling conveyor. Machining: weight-balance pads milled (+1 op), crack-split station unchanged. Scrap <1% at fracture-split.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Rod/cap remain matched pairs by fracture topography (no dowels); bolt count unchanged; same assembly process and tooling at engine line. Weight class marking laser-etched.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — 6 rods per engine
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Per vehicle: 6 rods × €1.7-2.7 saving (PF rod €9-11 vs forged 36MnVS4 €7.3-8.3) = €10.2-16.2; less added balancing op €1.2 = net €9-15. Net €9-€15 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €450k-€750k.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risk: big-end fracture plastic deformation (ovality), fatigue at the small-end under 48 V restart loads, weight scatter. Validate with 10⁷ cycle axial fatigue at +20% load, big-end ovality ≤10 µm after split, engine 600 h full-load durability. Mitigation: laser notch depth control.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Industry fracture-split micro-alloyed rods (C70S6/36MnVS4 practice) — Fracture splitting eliminates sawing and joint-face machining (~25% cost reduction); 36MnVS4 is splittable with yield close to C70S6. How this differs: Applied as a PF-to-forged swap on a 48 V MHEV I6 where 48 V restarts are gentle.

title: Crankshaft: controlled-cooled 38MnVS6 forging replaces quenched-and-tempered 42CrMo4
description: [MHEV] Eliminates Q&T furnace processing (energy, quench oil, straightening, cleaning) and uses a cheaper Cr-Mo-free grade; shorter lead time and less distortion reduce grinding stock. Baseline: a turbo I6 crankshaft forged in 42CrMo4, quenched and tempered (Q&T: austenitise ~850 °C, oil quench, temper ~600 °C), straightened, then journals induction-hardened or nitrided — ~20-22 kg, 7 main bearings. Proposal: 38MnVS6 micro-alloyed steel, forged and controlled-cooled on a fan conveyor directly from the forging heat so that V(C,N) precipitation and grain refinement provide strength without Q&T; fillets deep-rolled and journals induction-hardened (55-60 HRC, 1.5-2.5 mm case). 38MnVS6 and Q&T 42CrMo4 are both standard for induction-hardened crankshafts; micro-alloyed grades remove the separate heat-treatment step. Physics: controlled cooling at ~1-2 °C/s gives ferrite-pearlite at Rm ~900-950 MPa; fillet rolling introduces compressive residual stress (−600 to −900 MPa) that restores bending fatigue to ≥ the Q&T level. 48 V MHEV ISG damping reduces first-order torsional excitation at start/stop, easing durability margins.

title: Main and rod bearings: polymer-overlay AlSn shells replace sputtered bearings for 48V restarts
description: [MHEV] Spray coating and cure (~200-250 °C) is an inline continuous process far cheaper than vacuum sputtering; no cost for target materials and batch chamber time. Baseline: to survive frequent restarts (stop-start plus 48 V coasting engine-off, possibly 500,000-1,000,000 starts over life) and high firing loads, many premium engines use PVD-sputtered AlSn20Cu overlay bearings on the most loaded shells (rod upper and main lower) — a vacuum batch process with low throughput. Proposal: steel-backed AlSn bimetal shells with a ~6-12 µm sprayed polyamide-imide (PAI) polymer overlay containing solid lubricants (Fe2O3/MoS2-type), as Federal-Mogul’s IROX family does; IROX was introduced specifically for stop-start and hybrid engines and reports friction ~50% lower than plain aluminium bearings and multi-fold life in extreme applications. Physics: at each restart the journal runs in boundary lubrication for ~0.2-0.5 s until oil film forms; a polymer overlay with solid lubricants carries that boundary contact without seizure, while the AlSn layer provides conformability. The smooth 48 V ISG start at ~400-600 rpm/s reduces the boundary period vs a 12 V pinion start.
