title: Flexplate without starter ring gear: one-piece fine-blanked plate when ISG does all cranking
description: [MHEV] Removes the ring-gear forging/rolling, gear cutting, induction hardening and shrink-fit/weld operation; flexplate mass −0.8 to −1.2 kg; reduced rotating inertia. Baseline: an automatic transmission flexplate carries a starter ring gear (C45 / 1.0503 ring, ~140 teeth, induction-hardened flanks, shrunk or welded on), because the 12 V pinion starter engages it; the plate itself is a stamped DD13/S355MC disc with balancing holes, ~2.5-3.5 kg in total. When the 48 V machine sits between engine and transmission (as with the Mercedes M256 ISG) and is specified to perform all starts, the ring gear has no function. Proposal: a one-piece fine-blanked S420MC flexplate (3.0-3.5 mm) with integrated crank-angle trigger windows if required, no ring gear, and the 12 V starter deleted. Physics: the ring gear is sized for ~250-350 Nm pinion engagement at 10:1-14:1 ratio; without it the plate only transmits engine torque in shear at the bolt circles and must handle crank axial whip — a 3.0 mm S420MC disc covers that with ≥2× fatigue margin, verified by FEA.

title: Three-way catalyst washcoat: Pt-rich tri-metal formulation replaces Pd-dominant loading
description: [MHEV] Direct PGM-price arbitrage between Pd and Pt; recipe homologated in two variants so purchasing can switch when the spread inverts (dual-source on metals). Baseline: gasoline TWCs for large engines typically use Pd as the dominant oxidation metal with Rh for NOx reduction — e.g. close-coupled brick ~3-4 g Pd + ~0.3-0.4 g Rh on a 3.0 l I6. Proposal: reformulate to a Pt/Pd/Rh tri-metal washcoat in which ~40-50% of Pd mass is replaced by Pt on a 1:1 mass basis, with Pt stabilised on a high-Ce/Zr OSC support (to limit sintering) and Rh unchanged. The World Platinum Investment Council estimates 500-600 koz/yr of platinum displaced palladium in gasoline TWCs in 2023-2024, and once qualified the substitution is locked in for the platform life. Physics: Pt is more prone to sintering under lean/hot ageing than Pd, so OSC and layer architecture (Pt in the bottom layer, Pd/Rh in the top layer) maintain light-off. Cost: substituting 1.5-2 g Pd by Pt changes cost by Δprice × mass; at a long-run planning spread of €8-15/g in Pt’s favour the saving is ~€12-30 per vehicle, with hedging by dual-recipe homologation.

title: Rear silencer outer shells and baffles in nickel-free 1.4509 instead of austenitic 1.4301
description: [MHEV] Raw material price: ferritic 1.4509 typically trades well below 304 because it has no nickel; ~6-7 kg of sheet substituted per vehicle. No nickel surcharge exposure on these parts. Baseline: luxury SUV rear silencers and visible tailpipe sections are frequently made in austenitic 1.4301 (304, 8-10.5% Ni) for appearance and corrosion margin: two outer shells of 1.0-1.2 mm, end caps, internal baffles and perforated tubes, ~6-8 kg of sheet per vehicle across twin silencers. Proposal: Nb/Ti-stabilised ferritic 1.4509 (441, 18Cr-Nb-Ti, nickel-free) for shells, end caps and baffles, keeping 1.4301 only on the visible polished tailpipe trim. 1.4509 is oxidation-resistant to ~950 °C and widely used for catalysts and exhaust channels; ferritic grades are nickel-free, hence cheaper and price-stable vs 304. Physics: rear-silencer metal temperatures are typically 300-600 °C — well within 1.4509’s range — and ferritic grades have ~30% lower thermal expansion than austenitic (≈10.5 vs 16-17 µm/m·K), reducing thermal-fatigue stress at seams. Condensate corrosion (chlorides + acidic condensate) is covered by 18% Cr with Nb/Ti stabilisation preventing weld sensitisation.

title: Cast-in cylinder liners with as-cast spiny outer surface replace machined grooved liners
description: [MHEV] Deletes outer-diameter turning/grooving of six liners and grit-blast pre-treatment; thinner liner wall saves iron mass and boring time; better heat transfer may avoid additional bore-bridge cooling drillings. Baseline: aluminium crankcases with cast-iron liners (the Ingenium family uses an aluminium block with cast-iron liners) often use liners whose outer surface is machined with grooves or knurls, or grit-blasted, so the aluminium mechanically locks onto them during casting; liner wall is typically 2.5-3.0 mm after boring, six liners per I6. Proposal: centrifugally cast grey-iron liners (EN-GJL-250 class, pearlitic with type-A graphite) with an as-cast "spiny" outer surface — a mould coating containing a surfactant forms protrusions of ~0.4-0.8 mm height at ~10-20 per cm² during solidification — so the outer surface needs no machining and the aluminium forms an interlocked bond. Physics: the protrusions create a mechanical interlock and ~3× the contact area, which improves liner-to-block heat transfer (reducing bore temperature by ~5-10 K) and bore roundness under head-bolt load; the liner wall can drop by ~0.5 mm, saving iron mass and bore-finishing stock.

title: DC-DC power inductors: planar PCB-integrated magnetics enabled by 250 kHz switching
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes wound copper parts and through-hole insertion/potting; ferrite cores are commodity; winding copper comes with the PCB at heavy-copper premium below the wound-part cost. Baseline: a 48/12 V DC-DC at ~100 kHz uses wound power inductors per phase (e.g. 2.2 µH, ~120 A sat, flat-wire copper on a powder-iron or ferrite core), hand- or robot-placed through-hole and potted — the costliest passive line on the BOM after the switches. GaN 48/12 V converters at 250 kHz reach 97% efficiency at 800 W/phase. Proposal: at 250 kHz the required inductance per phase falls to ~0.8-1.0 µH, small enough for planar magnetics — a two-piece low-profile MnZn ferrite E/I core clamped around 4-6 heavy-copper (≥140 µm) PCB layers that form the winding — so the inductors become SMT-compatible and the windings are printed. The same planar inductor family serves the BEV’s 800/48 V or 48/12 V zonal converters (powertrain-shared). Physics: inductor energy ½LI² at 1 µH and 70 A is 2.45 mJ — about 40% of a 2.2 µH design — so core volume falls by ~half; planar windings give repeatable leakage (±3%) improving phase current balance.

title: Front-axle decoupler shift sleeve: sinter-hardened powder metal replaces machined 20MnCr5 forging
description: [MHEV] Net-shape PM removes broaching, hobbing, carburising and grinding; material utilisation >95% vs ~55% for forging + machining. Heat-treatment logistics also disappear. Baseline: dog-clutch shift sleeves in axle decouplers are typically forged 20MnCr5, turned, broached (internal spline), hobbed/shaped (external dog teeth), case-carburised and ground — 6-7 operations, ~0.4-0.6 kg. Audi’s quattro ultra opens a decoupler integrated in the secondary-axle differential to stop drag losses, showing the function is production-proven. Proposal: press-and-sinter Fe-1.5Mo-2Cu-0.6C (sinter-hardening grade, density ≥7.1 g/cm³ by warm compaction) with net-shape internal spline and back-tapered dogs, sinter-hardened by accelerated convective cooling in the sinter furnace (≥35 HRC apparent, martensitic), then steam-treated or tempered; only the fork groove is turned. Physics: decoupler dogs engage at low differential speed (<50 rpm) under predictive control, so impact energy is small; static torque per half-shaft ≤2,500 Nm is carried by 18-24 dogs with contact stress well inside PM fatigue limits (~300 MPa bending at 7.1 g/cm³).

title: Low-range planetary carrier: two fine-blanked steel plates replace cast-iron one-piece carrier
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Fine-blanking replaces casting + multi-setup machining; mass −0.4 to −0.6 kg; no foundry scrap or porosity rejects. Lead time also shortens. Material utilisation rises from ~60% to ~80%. Baseline: low-range planetary carriers in two-speed transfer cases are commonly one-piece EN-GJS-600-3 ductile-iron castings, machined on 4-5 setups (pin bores, splines, bearing seats), ~1.8-2.2 kg. Two-speed transfer cases with ~2.5:1 low (Ineos Grenadier, Land Cruiser 250) are the benchmark for capability. Proposal: a two-plate carrier: two fine-blanked S500MC (or 16MnCr5 normalised) plates, 6-7 mm, joined by four pressed-in bridge pillars or projection-welded spacers, with planet-pin holes fine-blanked to IT7 so no boring is required; only the spline hub is broached and the plates are carbonitrided where the pins sit. Physics: carrier torque at 2.5:1 low and 3,500 kg towing on 30% grades can reach ~5-6 kNm at the output; two 6.5 mm S500MC plates (Re ≥ 500 MPa) with 4 bridges carry the pin bending loads with FEA-predicted stress ~60% of fatigue limit, while fine-blanking holds pin-bore position to ±0.02 mm, which governs planet load share.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: a luxury off-road SUV typically carries separate control units for the transfer-case/AWD coupling, the adaptive-damper and air-suspension controller, the terrain-mode/off-road coordinator, the active anti-roll controller, rear-axle steering and a vehicle-motion supervisor that arbitrates ESC, e-motor or engine torque requests - six to seven ECUs, each with its own housing, connector, CAN-FD node, 12 V feed, fusing and bracket, and each exchanging torque/slip signals with 10-20 ms bus latency. Proposal: one ASIL-D driving-dynamics computer (lockstep multicore MCU, e.g. a 6-core 400 MHz class automotive controller) hosts the vehicle-motion supervisor, AWD torque split (transfer-case clutch on MHEV, front/rear e-motor split on 800V BEV), damper and ride-height control, roll control and terrain-mode logic as software components; the actuators keep only smart drivers in the corner/zone controllers. ESC hydraulic unit and EPS keep their own safety controllers but take set-points from the new computer. Physics: wheel-slip control on loose surfaces (sand, mud, rock crawl at 1-5 km/h) benefits from one control loop seeing all wheel speeds, motor/clutch torque and suspension travel at ~1 ms instead of stitching three loops across a gateway. Benchmark: BMW iX3 Neue Klasse runs a dedicated driving-dynamics "superbrain" (Heart of Joy) handling drivetrain, brakes and steering about 10x faster than conventional ECUs with ~1 ms latency; this idea extends the same partitioning to the off-road functions (terrain modes, transfer case, ride height) a 3,500 kg-towing SUV needs, on one board shared by MHEV and BEV.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes five ECU housings, PCBs, MCUs, power stages, connectors and brackets (each €18-€35 at volume) and their bus/feed circuits, against one larger computer (~€60-€75 more than the largest deleted ECU). Calibration is done once on one software platform for MHEV and BEV rather than per supplier box.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Removes five ECU mounting, connection and EOL-flash operations from trim/final (~25 s each, ~2 min total). Flashing collapses to one diagnostic session on one computer. Capex: one new HIL rig for the integrated software (~€1.5M) offset by retiring supplier-specific HIL benches; no body-shop change.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count -5 ECUs, -5 brackets, -5 connector pairs, roughly -40 terminals. One coded connector family on the computer with keyed headers to avoid cross-plugging. Service: one replaceable unit with variant coding by VIN instead of six supplier parts; off-road software updated by OTA.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the MHEV variant has a 48 V net limited to the belt starter-generator, e-compressor/e-booster and a 48 V/12 V DC-DC, while every body, chassis and comfort load runs at 12 V; the BEV variant has an 800 V/12 V DC-DC and a fully 12 V body net. Two different power-distribution boxes, two DC-DC converters and several load variants (12 V on BEV, 12 V on MHEV but with different fusing) are engineered and validated twice. Proposal: make 48 V the primary low-voltage bus on both powertrains. MHEV: the existing 48 V Li-ion BSG battery (~0.9 kWh) feeds the zone controllers directly. BEV: an 800 V/48 V 3.5 kW DC-DC feeds the identical zone controllers, buffered by the same 48 V battery module part number. High-power loads (EPS, active roll, seat/screen heaters, blower, pumps, rear-axle steer) are specified at 48 V once; residual 12 V legacy loads (infotainment peripherals, lamps) are supplied by small buck stages inside the zone controllers. Physics: at 4x the voltage, current is 1/4 and I²R loss 1/16 for the same power, so the 300 W blower feeder drops from ~25 A to ~6 A and its conductor from 4 mm² to 0.75-1.0 mm². Benchmark: Tesla Cybertruck combines an 800 V traction architecture with a 48 V low-voltage architecture, cutting LV current ~4x and heat ~16x versus 12 V; this idea applies that to a dual-powertrain platform so the whole body/cabin net is one design for MHEV and BEV.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Copper reduction on high-power feeders (~2.5-3.5 kg Cu at ~€9/kg in harness form), deletion of the MHEV 48/12 V DC-DC (replaced by small zone bucks), one power-distribution and load set validated once instead of twice, and one 48 V battery part number across both powertrains.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: One harness/zone-controller family on the line for both powertrains removes variant sequencing for ~60% of the LV net. 48 V connectors need arc-safe design (no hot-unplugging); EOL test adds a 48 V insulation check (~10 s). Supplier capex shift for 48 V-rated actuators is amortised over 50,000 units/yr.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Fewer power-distribution part numbers (2 → 1 front PDU, 2 → 1 DC-DC family). Colour-coded (violet) 48 V circuits and keyed connectors prevent 12 V/48 V cross-mating. Service procedures unify across powertrains; 48 V stays below the 60 V DC touch-safe limit so no HV training is needed.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High - copper, DC-DC and duplicate engineering all fall
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Copper 2.5-3.5 kg × €9/kg = €22-€32; deleted MHEV 48/12 V DC-DC on MHEV share (50%) €60-€80 → €30-€40 averaged; one PDU/load set validated once €15-€25; minus zone buck stages and 48 V connector premium €12-€12 => €55-€85. Net €55-€85 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €2.75M-€4.25M per year (estimate).

ideaData.riskNotes: Arc sustain at 48 V on connector separation and fretting; 12 V legacy suppliers may charge premiums for 48 V parts. Validate per LV 148/VDA 320 (48 V component requirements), ISO 21780 (48 V supply voltage ranges), ISO 16750-2 and EMC per CISPR 25. Mitigate arc risk with load-shedding before connector disengagement and e-fuse trip times <100 µs.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Tesla Cybertruck (2023) — 48 V low-voltage architecture alongside 800 V traction; LV current ~4x lower and heat ~16x lower than 12 V.. How this differs: Uses 48 V as the platform-common LV bus for an MHEV and a BEV derivative, with the MHEV BSG battery and the BEV DC-DC as interchangeable sources.

ideaData.title: Scalable central compute: depopulated ADAS SoC footprint for MHEV base trims
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: luxury SUVs that offer L2 and L2+ packages commonly fit two different ADAS computers (a single-SoC front-camera ECU for base L2 and a separate high-performance ADAS controller for the hands-free package), each with its own housing, cooling, harness branch and software stack, plus a camera/radar wiring variant. Proposal: one automated-driving computer PCB designed with two SoC footprints and a shared power tree, housing and liquid/air cold plate. Base MHEV trims are built with one SoC populated (SMT program variant, same bare board), delivering L2 with the full camera set; L2+/hands-free trims populate the second SoC and its LPDDR5 memory. Physics/engineering: SoC thermal design power scales roughly linearly with populated dies, so a cold plate sized for 2 × 40-60 W runs the single-SoC build with large margin; the one-board approach removes a second box rather than adding cost to the base car. Benchmark: Volvo EX90 states that its core computing with the remaining sensor set (5 radars, 8 cameras, 16 ultrasonics) delivers driver support with or without lidar, i.e. one compute platform spans sensor configurations; BMW Neue Klasse bundles automated driving into one of four superbrains. ideaData.costReductionMechanism: One computer part family instead of two (tooling, validation, EMC, software integration done once), no second ADAS ECU on base trims, no harness variant for the compute branch; the base car carries only the cost of an unpopulated footprint (~€3-€5 of PCB area).
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Supplier SMT line runs one bare board with two placement programs; EOL test fixtures are shared. Vehicle plant removes one compute variant from sequencing and one connector set. Avoids a separate housing tool (~€250-€400k) and separate HIL.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Same mounting bracket, cold-plate interface and connector positions for every trim; mis-build prevented by reading the populated-SoC ID at EOL against the build code. Upgrades after sale are a board swap in the same housing, not a re-harness.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium - saves one box on base trims and duplicate engineering on all

ideaData.riskNotes: Base trims carry wiring sized for the full sensor set (small copper penalty, included in the estimate). Software must detect populated hardware robustly. title: Gigabit Ethernet ring between zone controllers replaces central gateway star
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the central gateway ECU, 6-10 domain home-runs (CAN pairs and 100BASE-T1 links of 2-4 m each) and duplicated safety CAN lines, net of switch silicon added inside zone controllers (~€4-€6 per zone). Baseline: a domain-architecture luxury SUV routes body, chassis, powertrain and infotainment traffic through a central gateway with 8-12 CAN-FD channels plus point-to-point 100BASE-T1 links, so each domain controller has a home-run to the gateway behind the dashboard; redundancy for safety signals is achieved by duplicated CAN lines. Proposal: connect four zone controllers (front, centre-left, centre-right/rear, roof) and the central computers in a 1000BASE-T1 ring using single unshielded twisted pairs, with each zone embedding a 5-7 port automotive Ethernet switch (TSN: 802.1Qbv scheduling, 802.1CB frame replication for safety streams). The ring gives every node two paths, replacing duplicated CAN lines; CAN-FD and LIN survive only as short local branches from each zone to its actuators. Physics/engineering: a 1 Gbit/s ring carries 10x the throughput of a 100BASE-T1 star with fewer pairs; replication over both ring directions tolerates a single cable cut with <1 ms failover, which is what duplicated CAN was paying for. Benchmark: Tesla Cybertruck uses an "Etherloop" - a continuous gigabit Ethernet loop connecting multiple controllers - and reports 155 wires

title: Powertrain-agnostic harness: MHEV/BEV differences confined to the front-zone branch
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Harness module variants fall (powertrain axis removed from 3 of 4 zones), lowering KSK complexity premium at the harness supplier, buffer stock and sequencing logistics; 40-80 powertrain circuits leave the cabin harness. ideaData.title: Robot-ready harness: straight zone segments with machine-loaded connectors
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: a luxury-SUV body harness is a single 3-D tree of 1,500-2,500 circuits, 50-70 kg, built manually on formboards; harness assembly is 60-70% labour content, with terminals pushed into connector housings by hand and taping/clipping done manually, so wire harnesses remain one of the most labour-intensive vehicle components and are produced in low-wage regions with long logistics chains. Proposal: design the zonal harness so each segment is "robot-ready": mostly straight or 2-D sub-bundles of ≤60 circuits between a zone controller and its loads, wires of 0.13-2.5 mm² from a limited gauge set, connectors from a standard family with machine-insertable terminals and straight-pull cavities, no inline splices in the robot segments, and attachment by pre-placed clips rather than spot taping. Fully automated cells then cut, strip, crimp and insert terminals directly into housings (automatic module-loading), twist pairs, and apply spiral wrap. Engineering: with ≤60 circuits and one connector per end, automatic cells reach 15-25 terminal insertions per minute with 100% insertion-force monitoring, while manual insertion averages ~6-8 per minute. Benchmark: Tesla Cybertruck uses modular wiring designed around its 48 V architecture and a Low-Voltage Connector Standard, and reports 155 wires vs 490 in Model 3; fewer, standardised segments are the precondition for automation that this idea exploits.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Labour share of harness cost drops on automated segments (target 50-60% of circuits machine-built), allowing regional production nearer the plant (lower freight and buffer stock); first-pass yield rises through insertion-force monitoring, cutting repair and warranty.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Supplier capex for 2-3 automated module-loading cells (~€1.5-€2.5M each) replaces ~40% of manual formboard stations; cycle per robot segment 3-6 min; harness logistics shift from sea freight to regional truck, reducing in-transit inventory by 2-4 weeks.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Connector family reduced to machine-insertable types; uniform clip positions allow fixtureless vehicle installation with poka-yoke colour bands. Fewer inline connectors and splices improve serviceability; segments are replaceable individually.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High - labour is the largest cost element of the harness

title: Wade-depth estimation from parking ultrasonics and cameras, deleting mirror wade sensors
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] [Off-road] Deletes two mirror-base wade sensors, their brackets, four door-harness circuits through the door grommets and the mirror-housing variant; the function is added in software on existing compute, with no new hardware. Proposal: estimate water level from sensors already fitted: (1) the front and rear bumper ultrasonic transducers detect immersion by the step change in ringing/decay time when the membrane is wetted, giving discrete level points at known heights (front ~450-550 mm, corner ~500-600 mm); (2) the mirror surround-view cameras detect the waterline on the body side by edge/specular segmentation against the known door geometry; (3) air-suspension ride height and pitch correct the reference. title: Single wide-FoV RGB-IR cabin camera replaces separate driver and occupant cameras
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes one camera module, one illuminator board, one SerDes link/cable and one bracket; the remaining camera is ~€6-€9 dearer (5 MP RGB-IR, wider lens). Baseline: premium vehicles increasingly fit two interior cameras - a near-IR driver-monitoring camera on the steering column or cluster for drowsiness/distraction (EU ADDW requirement) and a second occupant/cabin camera in the roof console for occupant classification, child presence or video calls - each with its own 940 nm illuminator, SerDes link and processing. Proposal: one 5 MP RGB-IR global-shutter camera with a 110-130° lens in the rear-view-mirror base or overhead console, two 940 nm VCSEL illuminators pulsed in sync with exposure, processed on the central computer. Driver eye/gaze tracking uses a 1-2 MP region-of-interest crop; the full frame serves occupant classification, belt-use detection and seat occupancy. Engineering: at ~0.7 m to the driver eyes, a 5 MP sensor with 120° FoV gives ~10-12 pixels across the iris, above the ~8 px commonly needed for gaze estimation; RGB-IR pixels allow colour video when ambient light allows. Benchmark: Volvo EX90 is fitted with two interior cameras alongside its exterior set; this idea consolidates the interior pair into one sensor while meeting the same monitoring functions.

title: Digital audio bus daisy-chains cabin microphones and speakers, deleting analogue runs
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces 40-60 m of shielded analogue/speaker pairs with ~15-20 m of a single UTP chain, deletes shielding and large connectors, and lets amplifier channels sit at the doors (shorter, thinner speaker leads). Baseline: a luxury SUV with road-noise cancellation, in-car communication and hands-free telephony routes 6-12 microphones and 4-6 accelerometers as individual shielded analogue pairs back to the amplifier, and 14-20 speaker channels as point-to-point twisted pairs (0.5-1.5 mm²) from a trunk-mounted amplifier, giving 40-60 m of audio wiring and several heavy multi-way connectors. Proposal: a two-wire digital audio bus (unshielded twisted pair, phantom-powered, ~50 Mbit/s, deterministic latency <50 µs) daisy-chains microphones, accelerometers and distributed amplifier nodes; door/headliner nodes host small class-D amplifier channels driving their local speakers over <1 m, and the head unit/central compute is the bus master. Engineering: deterministic low latency is what makes ANC/RNC work (control loop needs <1 ms), and bus power over the same pair removes separate microphone supply wires. Benchmark: Tesla Cybertruck shows the wire-count effect of bus architectures, 155 wires versus 490 in Model 3 while serving more end points; this idea applies that bus principle to the audio domain, which zonal architectures often leave as point-to-point analogue.

title: Base and mid audio amplifiers integrated onto the infotainment computer board
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the standalone amplifier housing, die-cast heat sink, connector, bracket, power feed and separate DSP on standard/mid tiers; amplifier ICs on the main board cost less than the full external box. Baseline: luxury SUVs commonly fit a stand-alone external amplifier (8-16 channels, 400-900 W class-D) with its own housing, heat sink, DSP and power feed even on the standard audio tier, while premium branded audio uses a second, larger amplifier. Proposal: for the standard and mid tiers, integrate 8-10 channels of 40-50 W class-D (multi-channel amplifier ICs at 48 V supply where available, or 14.4 V boosted) and the audio DSP onto the infotainment computer board, cooled by the computer's existing cold plate; only the premium branded tier keeps an external amplifier, connected via the digital audio bus. Engineering: class-D efficiency of ~85-90% means 8 × 45 W at typical program levels (1/8 power) dissipates only ~10-15 W, well within a cold plate already sized for an SoC; running amplifier stages from a 48 V rail allows higher output per channel without boost converters. Benchmark: Rivian Gen 2 keeps infotainment on its own ECU while consolidating other functions to cut ECUs from 17 to 7; this idea folds the base amplifier into that infotainment computer, removing a box that consolidated architectures commonly still keep.

title: Steering-wheel node on CAN-FD cuts clock-spring circuits from 16 to 6
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Narrower single-flex clock spring (fewer tracks, no second heater flex), fewer connector cavities at wheel and column, simplified column switch module, offset by a ~€4-€6 wheel node. Baseline: a luxury steering wheel carries switch packs (LIN), haptic or capacitive hands-on detection, heated rim (8-10 A), paddles, a mode/terrain button cluster and the airbag squibs; the clock spring (rotary connector) consequently carries 14-18 flat-cable tracks plus a separate heater flat cable, and the column switch module duplicates some decoding. Proposal: one steering-wheel node (small MCU with CAN-FD transceiver, capacitive hands-on sensing, LIN master for switch packs, heater PWM switch) inside the wheel, so the clock spring carries only: 2 CAN-FD lines, 2 power lines sized for the heater, and 2 squib pairs routed on the same flex (airbag circuits stay hard-wired, 4 tracks), totalling 8 tracks or 6 + squibs depending on airbag stages. title: OTA for zone MCUs: single-bank flash with central A/B staging
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Smaller MCU flash variant or deletion of external QSPI NOR on each zone (4-6 zones), against modest central storage already present; fewer field rework events thanks to central rollback lowers warranty. Baseline: to support full-vehicle OTA, each ECU or zone controller is often specified with dual-bank (A/B) embedded flash so it can receive an image while running and roll back if needed - doubling on-chip flash (e.g. 8 MB instead of 4 MB) or adding an external 16-32 MB QSPI NOR per zone. Proposal: only the central computers (with UFS/eMMC storage) keep A/B partitions and act as the OTA staging server. title: Telematics baseband moved onto central computer; roof module becomes RF-only
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes TCU housing, application processor, RAM/flash, power supply, connectors and bracket; modem module cost remains. Fewer coax runs and connectors. Baseline: luxury SUVs fit a stand-alone telematics control unit (TCU) with a 4G/5G modem, application processor, its own RAM/flash, CAN/Ethernet interfaces, eCall audio path, GNSS receiver and backup battery, typically in the roof or IP area, plus 3-5 coaxial cables to the roof antenna. Proposal: the cellular modem module (5G RedCap/LTE Cat-4 class M.2/LGA) and GNSS receiver are populated on the infotainment computer board, using its application processor, memory and Ethernet; the roof shark-fin keeps only antennas and low-noise amplifiers, connected by two coax/high-speed links. eCall keeps a minimal independent supervisor and backup supply as required. Engineering: a separate application processor and RAM in the TCU duplicate resources that the infotainment SoC already has in abundance; modem modules expose PCIe/USB interfaces designed for host processors. title: Trailer reverse assist using existing rear camera, no hitch-angle sensor
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] [Off-road] Deletes the hitch-angle sensor (or dedicated high-mount tow camera), its harness branch to the towbar and the towing-pack sensor variant; adds software only. Baseline: luxury SUVs rated for 3,500 kg towing offer trailer reverse-steer assistance with either a hitch-angle sensor on the towbar, a trailer-mounted target sticker plus a dedicated high-mount tailgate camera, or both, with extra wiring to the towbar area and a towing-pack variant of the rear harness. Proposal: estimate hitch angle from the existing rear-view camera alone, using the drawbar and trailer front edges segmented by a neural network running on the central computer, fused with steering angle, wheel speeds and yaw rate in a kinematic trailer model (wheelbase and drawbar length learned during the first 200-500 m of forward driving). Rear corner radars (retained in the sensor set) confirm trailer width and length for blind-spot extension. Engineering: at reversing speeds of ≤5 km/h, a ±1° hitch-angle accuracy suffices for jack-knife prevention; the rear camera at ~1 m from the ball sees the drawbar at a resolution of ~3-4 px/degree. Benchmark: Volvo EX90 carries eight exterior cameras and five radars as standard; this idea uses the standard rear camera and rear radars for trailer functions instead of towing-specific sensors.

title: BEV front harness insulation: T3 cross-linked to T2 PVC without engine heat
description: [800V BEV] Cheaper PVC insulation compound and no e-beam or silane cross-linking step on ~120-180 m of BEV front-zone cable; slightly thinner wall and higher-runner cable types reduce material and price further. Baseline: front-end harnesses of platforms that share an engine bay with ICE/MHEV derivatives are specified with temperature class T3 (125 °C) cable - typically FLR...X cross-linked polyolefin (e.g. FLR2X-B/FLRYK) - throughout the front compartment because exhaust manifolds and turbochargers create 110-130 °C local ambients. Proposal: on the 800V BEV front-zone harness, where the front compartment contains no combustion heat sources and peak ambients are set by the e-motor, inverter and frunk (typically <85-95 °C locally), specify T2 (105 °C) cable - FLRY-B (PVC, ISO 6722-1 class B) or thin-wall T2 PE - except near brake discs, compressor and heat-pump hot-gas lines, which keep T3 locally. Engineering: PVC insulation retains elongation >50% after 3,000 h at 105 °C per ISO 6722 class B; measured BEV front-compartment temperatures in hot-climate soak are below that limit. Cross-linked insulation costs ~20-35% more per metre in small gauges and requires e-beam or silane cross-linking. title: Cabin harness corrugated conduit: PA6 to impact-modified PP
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Lower resin price (PP ~40-55% below PA6) and ~20% lower mass per metre on 25-40 m of cabin, roof, door and boot conduit; matching PP clips and fittings are also cheaper. Baseline: harness suppliers commonly use one corrugated conduit material across the vehicle - PA6 or PA12 slotted convoluted tube rated to 125-150 °C with fuel/oil resistance - including in the cabin, roof, door and boot zones where peak temperatures are 85 °C and no fuel or oil exposure occurs. A luxury SUV carries 25-40 m of conduit in these zones. Proposal: specify impact-modified polypropylene (PP copolymer, flame-retardant grade meeting FMVSS 302/ISO 3795 burn rate <100 mm/min, temperature class 105 °C) slotted conduit for cabin, roof, door and boot zones, keeping PA6/PA12 in the engine bay, underbody and wheel arches. Engineering: PP density ~0.90-0.91 g/cm³ versus PA6 ~1.13 g/cm³ gives ~20% lighter tube for the same wall; PP raw-material cost is ~40-55% below PA6; abrasion resistance is lower but adequate inside trim where relative motion is limited, and PP does not take up moisture. Benchmark: BMW Neue Klasse zonal harness uses shorter, thinner and lighter cables per zone, ~30% lighter overall; zone-specific harnesses make zone-specific protection specifications practical, which this idea applies to conduit.

title: Harness splices: crimp sleeve plus heat-shrink to ultrasonic weld with gel cap
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes crimp sleeves (~€0.03-€0.06 each) and adhesive heat-shrink (~€0.08-€0.15 each in wet zones), and shortens cycle per splice by ~30-50 s in wet zones; first-pass quality improves. Baseline: a luxury-SUV harness contains 250-400 splices; many suppliers still use crimped splice sleeves (tinned Cu) for mixed-gauge and ground splices, sealed in wet zones with adhesive-lined heat-shrink tube (3:1, ~45-60 s oven/hot-air cycle), and tape-wrapped in dry zones. Proposal: ultrasonic welding of splices (20-40 kHz, 1-3 kJ per weld, cycle 1-2 s, typical cross-sections 0.35-25 mm²) with automatic compaction-height monitoring for every weld, sealed in wet zones by a pre-filled silicone/TPE gel cap snapped over the weld (cycle ~5 s) instead of heat-shrink. Engineering: an ultrasonic weld creates a solid-state metallurgical bond with resistance typically below a crimp sleeve and no added sleeve metal; elimination of the shrink step removes a thermal process and its 45-60 s bottleneck. Weld monitoring (energy, time, height) gives 100% in-process quality data. Benchmark: Rivian Gen 2 reduced wiring by 2.6 km and eliminated about 80 connectors, improving manufacturing efficiency and quality - with fewer connectors, remaining joints such as splices carry a larger share of harness reliability, which favours monitored ultrasonic splicing.

title: Signal terminals: full-surface gold to selective spot gold on contact zone
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Gold consumption falls 50-70% on 400-800 terminals (gold at ~€90-€110/g; typical full-area deposits 0.3-0.6 mg/terminal), and moving non-dry-circuit terminals to tin removes gold entirely there. Baseline: low-current and safety-relevant signal terminals (0.5/0.64 mm tab systems for airbag squibs, sensors, Ethernet and SerDes contacts) are often supplied with gold plating of 0.4-0.8 µm over nickel across the whole contact spring area or by reel-to-reel stripe plating wider than the actual contact zone. A luxury SUV uses 400-800 gold-plated terminals across harness and ECU headers. Proposal: specify selective spot/brush plating confined to the contact point (spot ~0.8-1.2 mm wide on the spring, ≥0.4 µm Au over 1.3-2.5 µm Ni), and tin or tin-silver on the crimp barrel and carrier; for 48 V/12 V power and non-critical signals above dry-circuit thresholds (>10 mA, >1 V), use tin plating with higher normal force designs. Engineering: gold is needed only where the contact interface must stay film-free under dry-circuit conditions; confining it to the wipe track reduces gold use by 50-70% while keeping contact resistance <10 mΩ after fretting tests. Benchmark: Tesla Cybertruck introduced a Low-Voltage Connector Standard (LVCS) to optimise wiring; connector specification is a primary cost lever, and this idea applies it to plating specification.

title: Body ground points consolidated to zone-local stud clusters
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Fewer weld studs, stud-weld cycles, paint masks and nut tightenings (each stud point costs ~€0.8-€1.2 all-in), and shorter ground leads routed to zones. Baseline: a luxury SUV harness typically uses 25-40 body ground points: arc-welded M6 studs with stacked ring terminals scattered wherever a load is located, each needing a stud welding operation in the body shop, a mask during e-coat/paint, a nut tightening with torque check (8-10 Nm) in final assembly, and a separate harness branch. Proposal: with a zonal harness, loads return to their zone controller, so grounds are consolidated into 6-10 clusters (one double-stud cluster per zone controller plus engine/motor, battery and EMC-critical points), each with a multi-way ground bar or ground eyelet strip receiving 4-8 ring terminals in one tightening. Engineering: ground current per cluster stays <80-100 A peak at 12/48 V; a M8 stud on 1.5-2.0 mm steel with ≥3 threads engagement carries this with contact resistance <0.5 mΩ; EMC grounds for cameras/radars remain local. Benchmark: Rivian Gen 2 zonal architecture cut 2.6 km of wiring and about 80 connectors; zonal partitioning is what allows the ground network to be collapsed to the zones.

title: Centre display touch: out-cell PCAP film stack to in-cell touch LCD
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the separate touch sensor (~€8-€14 at 12-15"), one OCA lamination (~€3-€5 incl. yield) and the separate touch controller IC/FPC (~€2-€3), net of a small TDDI panel premium. Baseline: automotive centre and passenger displays (12-15") typically use an out-cell projected-capacitive touch sensor - a separate glass or film sensor with ITO or metal-mesh electrodes - laminated with optically clear adhesive (OCA) between cover glass and the LCD, i.e. two optical bonding steps, one touch controller FPC and one extra layer that costs transmission and yield. Proposal: in-cell (or hybrid in-cell/TDDI) LTPS/a-Si LCD panels in which touch electrodes are formed by the segmented common electrode and driven by a combined touch-and-display driver IC; the stack becomes cover glass + one optical bond + LCD. Engineering: removing one sensor layer and one OCA layer improves transmission by ~3-5%, lowers thickness by 0.5-0.8 mm and removes a lamination yield loss (typically 1-3% per bond on large formats); TDDI removes the separate touch controller. Automotive TDDI panels with glove and water rejection exist at 12-15" sizes. Benchmark: Rivian Gen 2 and BMW Neue Klasse consolidate infotainment into dedicated computers driving the displays; this part-level idea reduces cost inside the display module that those computers drive.

title: Zone controller PCB: 10-layer HDI to 6-layer 1+4+1 by partitioning switch silicon
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Lower PCB cost per cm² (fewer lamination cycles and microvia layers), heavy copper only on the power board, and higher panel utilisation, net of a board-to-board connector. Baseline: first-generation zone controllers often combine a large multi-core MCU (BGA 0.8 mm pitch, 300-500 balls), an Ethernet switch, DDR or large flash, and 30-60 smart power channels on one board, ending up as 8-10-layer HDI (2+N+2 microvia stack-up) of 150-250 cm², with heavy copper for power stages on the same laminate. Proposal: partition into (a) a 6-layer 1+4+1 HDI logic board carrying MCU and Ethernet PHY/switch with an MCU in a 1.0 mm pitch or LQFP-exposed-pad package where available, and (b) the power stages on a 2-4 layer FR-4 board with 70-105 µm copper, connected board-to-board; or a single 6-layer board when the MCU fan-out allows. Engineering: stacked microvias (2+N+2) cost roughly 1.5-2x per area versus 1+N+1, and heavy copper on the whole HDI panel is wasted on logic areas; partitioning lets each laminate do one job. Signal integrity for 100BASE-T1/1000BASE-T1 is maintained with controlled impedance on the 6-layer stack. Benchmark: Rivian Gen 2 raised the computational capability of each ECU while cutting ECU count from 17 to 7, and BMW Neue Klasse relies on smaller zone controllers - board technology choice drives a large share of such controllers' cost.

ideaData.title: One HVAC case: MHEV heater-core pocket accepts 800 V PTC air-heater cartridge
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: a luxury SUV built as MHEV and BEV on one platform typically carries two HVAC module variants — the MHEV case with a brazed aluminium heater core fed by engine coolant (plus 48 V-era auxiliary electric heat), and a BEV case re-tooled around a high-voltage coolant PTC heater loop, extra coolant connections and a different heater pocket. Two PP-T20 case families means roughly 9-11 extra injection tools, two sets of blend-door kinematics and two climatic-wind-tunnel validation programmes. Proposal: design ONE HVAC case whose heater pocket is dimensioned to accept either (a) the MHEV brazed EN AW-3003/4343-clad heater core, 2-row, 38 mm core depth, or (b) an 800 V PTC air-heater cartridge of identical envelope (ceramic PTC stones bonded to louvred aluminium fins, 6-7 kW), slid into the same rails and sealed with the same TPV lip. Coolant ports are blanked on the BEV with a moulded PP plug; HV connector exit uses a knock-out window on the MHEV case that stays closed. Air-side heating directly in the HVAC module avoids the water-loop losses at low ambient. Benchmark: Audi developed an 800 V PTC air heater for the Q6 e-tron (PPE) precisely to heat cabin air directly and cut water-circuit losses, and Mercedes uses a multi-source heat pump on the GLC with EQ Technology for primary heat; our cartridge strategy keeps the heat pump as primary and makes the air-side PTC the BEV top-up.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Money comes from (1) ~€3.0-3.6M of avoided duplicate HVAC case/door tools amortised over 6 years × 50,000 = €10-12 per vehicle, (2) a single validation programme and one supplier part-number family, and (3) on BEV, deletion of the cabin HV coolant-PTC loop branch (pipes, valve, small pump) worth €14-20 net of the PTC-air cartridge premium.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: One HVAC module assembly line at the Tier-1 instead of two sub-variants; heater pocket station gets a 2-position nest (core or cartridge). Cartridge insertion adds no cycle time (same 18 s slide-and-clip). Case tooling capex drops by roughly €3M; scrap unchanged. HV end-of-line insulation test (1,500 V DC hipot) added to the module EOL for BEV units only.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Single case part numbers for all powertrains; heater element variant is the only difference and is mechanically keyed (cartridge rail width 3 mm wider than core rail) so a core cannot be fitted where the HV harness exits. Service: cartridge removable from the footwell side without IP removal, same as heater core today.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — tooling and validation duplication eliminated, BEV coolant branch removed
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Tooling amortisation €10-12 + BEV coolant-branch deletion net €14-20 × 50% BEV mix (€7-10) + validation/part-number overhead €1-4 = €18-26 per vehicle (blended across the mix). Range €18-€26 × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €900k-€1.3M/yr.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: PTC air heater surface temperature near the case (PP-T20 HDT ~115 °C) — mitigated by a PA66-GF30 heater-frame insert and PTC self-limiting at ~160 °C stone temperature; HV safety in the cabin — IP2XB touch protection, ISO 6469-3 and LV 123 compliance; noise from air-side heater ticking. Validate with climatic-tunnel warm-up (-20 °C soak, ECE R122 defrost), ISO 16750-4 thermal cycling and LV 124/LV 123 electrical tests.

How this differs: We use the air-side PTC as a drop-in cartridge in the SAME HVAC case that carries the MHEV heater core, so both powertrains share one module family.

ideaData.title: Radiant knee and footwell panels delete rear auxiliary heater unit on 3-row BEV
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: a 3-row luxury BEV usually carries a roof- or C-pillar-mounted rear auxiliary HVAC unit (blower, evaporator, heater element, 2 actuators) plus 3-5 m of rear ducting and refrigerant/coolant lines to give row 2/3 occupants heat in winter — typically 9-12 kg and 30-40 parts. Proposal: for the BEV derivative, delete the heating function of the rear auxiliary unit and replace it with radiant panels: printed carbon-ink PTC film heaters (110 °C max element temperature, 24 W per panel at 12 V, far-infrared emitting fabric face) laminated behind the front seat-back lower panels (row-2 knees), the row-2 door map-pocket trims and the row-3 side-trim panels, 8 panels in total (~200 W). The rear unit becomes a cooling-only unit with one fewer actuator, no heater element, no coolant lines. Physics: radiant heat warms skin directly, so occupants report comfort at lower cabin air temperature; Hyundai Motor Group measured that its Radiant Heating System, used alongside the air-conditioning, reduces heating energy by 17%, and Genesis tested the system for EVs; the GV90 flagship applies radiant under-floor heating in the rear. Panels sit behind trim surfaces the customer already touches, so luxury perception is preserved or improved.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Removed: rear heater element and frame €22-28, two coolant/refrigerant branch lines and clips €18-24, one actuator €6, labour 4 min €3. ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Film heaters are laminated to trim substrates at the trim supplier (hot-melt PO web, 150 °C, 25 s), so no new GA station; GA loses the rear coolant-line routing station (~4 min). ideaData.dfmDfa: Each radiant panel uses the existing trim connector and is pre-tested at the trim supplier (resistance check). No new fixings. Serviceable by replacing the trim panel. Removing coolant lines from the rear removes leak paths and a GA fluid-fill step for the rear loop.

title: Common floating console upper: BEV rail mount, MHEV tunnel adapter bracket
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Avoids a second full console tool set (~€2.5-3.0M) → €8-10 per vehicle over 6 years; one decor/colour variant matrix instead of two halves JIS complexity; shared armrest/hinge/charger hardware buys at 2× volume (2-4%). MHEV adds bracket and closing panel (€5-6). Baseline: luxury SUVs sharing MHEV and BEV variants commonly carry two consoles — the MHEV a full-length tunnel-mounted console (substrate PP-T20, 18-24 parts, 7-9 screws into tunnel brackets) and the BEV a floating console whose lower is open for storage. Each is fully tooled (substrate, side panels, bin, armrest structure): 2 × €2.5-3.5M of tools. Proposal: design one console upper module — armrest, cup-holder/wireless-charge deck, bin, switch bezel and side-panel uppers — as a floating bridge carried on a stamped steel spine (HC420LA, 1.5 mm). On BEV the spine bolts to two floor-mounted M8 studs and an IP lower bracket, leaving an open storage pass-through underneath. On MHEV, the same spine bolts to a tunnel adapter bracket (HC340LA, 1.2 mm, 4 M6 welds nuts) and a simple PP-T20 lower closing panel hides the tunnel. Only the lower closing panel and bracket differ. Benchmark: Hyundai Ioniq 9 uses a universal island console that slides, and the Lucid Gravity offers a configurable centre console with movable "bento box" storage — i.e. the console is decoupled from a tunnel and conceived as a module.

title: Factory hose-out floor pack: TPV floor skin with drain plugs for off-road trims
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] [Off-road] TPV skin + felt (€38-46) costs less than tufted carpet + felt + 4 premium mats (€55-65); carpet-wet warranty claims on off-road trims reduced; accessory-liner cannibalisation recovers margin (not counted). Option take rate assumed 30% of volume. Baseline: off-road-branded luxury SUV trims still ship with tufted PA6 carpet (600 g/m²), PET felt and loose carpet mats, then dealers sell accessory TPE liners; wading and mud use generates carpet-wet warranty claims (odour, mould, corroded floor connectors) and carpet replacement at €350-600 per claim. Proposal: an off-road "utility" floor pack, factory option on adventure trims: a vacuum-formed TPV floor skin (Shore A 75, 2.0 mm, grained, PP-based TPV recyclable with PP trim) bonded to a 15 mm PET felt decoupler, with moulded raised-edge footwell trays and 4 sealed drain plugs (EPDM bungs in existing BIW drain holes, 25 mm) so the cabin can be hosed out. Floor-level electrical connectors in the footwell are relocated or upgraded to IP67 sealed. Benchmark: the Ineos Grenadier offers rubber flooring with drain plugs and wipe-down upholstery so the interior can be hosed out, and the Land Rover Defender 130 offers a choice of carpet or hard-wearing rubber mat flooring. Our pack keeps luxury aesthetics by grain and colour-matching the TPV to the IP lower skin.

ideaData.title: Eleven-level adaptive belt load limiter enables passenger knee-airbag deletion
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: many luxury SUVs fit knee airbags on both driver and passenger sides (passenger KAB module €28-35, plus glovebox-door reinforcement, a deployment door and a squib channel) to control femur loads and submarining for 5th-95th percentile occupants. Proposal: on the passenger side, delete the knee airbag and recover lower-body control with (a) a multi-level adaptive load-limiting retractor (pyro-switchable or motor-controlled torsion bar stages) driven by the occupant-sensing and crash-severity inputs, and (b) a stiffened energy-absorbing knee bolster: glovebox door inner in PP-LGF30 with crush ribs tuned to 4-6 kN knee force over 80-100 mm travel, plus a stamped HC420LA knee-bolster bracket on the cross-car beam. Driver knee airbag retained because of the steering column geometry. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 support documentation lists a driver upper airbag plus a knee airbag on the driver side, but a single front airbag on the passenger side; Volvo has also introduced a multi-adaptive safety belt (debuting on EX60) that expands load-limiting profiles from three to eleven using interior/exterior sensor data. Combining those two benchmarks gives a restraint architecture that controls passenger loads with the belt rather than a second knee bag.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deleted: passenger KAB module €28-35, deployment door/hinge €4, squib channel and connector on the ACU €3, harness €2. Added: adaptive load-limiter premium on passenger retractor €12-16 and knee-bolster bracket €3. Net €22-25 per vehicle.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: IP sub-assembly loses one module install (~45 s) and one airbag connector check; glovebox-door tool modified for crush ribs (€0.15M). ACU loses a firing loop. No new capex at GA.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Removes one pyrotechnic device (hazardous-goods handling, logistics, end-of-life). The adaptive retractor is the same footprint as the baseline pretensioning retractor; poka-yoke by connector coding. Glovebox serviceability improves without the KAB behind it.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — removes a pyro module per vehicle
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Removed €28-35 + €4 + €3 + €2 = €37-44; added €12-16 + €3 = €15-19; net €22-25; × 0.8 realisation (if a US-market variant keeps the KAB) ≈ €18-20, upper bound €25 when global. Range €18-25. Range €18-€25 × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €900k-€1.25M/yr.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: femur load / KTH (knee-thigh-hip) criteria and submarining in Euro NCAP MPDB and FW, US NCAP and FMVSS 208 unbelted tests — FMVSS 208 unbelted 50th male requires the knee bolster to carry load; must be confirmed by sled and full-vehicle tests. Validate with FMVSS 208, Euro NCAP 2026 protocols, IIHS small overlap passenger side; keep KAB as a regional option if US unbelted results are marginal.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Volvo EX90 (2024, SPA2) and Volvo multi-adaptive belt (EX60, 2026) — EX90 has a driver knee airbag but a single front airbag on the passenger side; Volvo’s multi-adaptive belt expands load-limiting profiles from 3 to 11 using sensor data.. How this differs: We pair an adaptive load limiter with a crush-ribbed glovebox knee bolster to delete the passenger knee airbag on our SUV, rather than adding the belt as a pure safety upgrade.

title: BEV-tuned base dash insulator with clip-in MHEV engine-order barrier cassette
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] BEV: insulator mass 9-11 kg → ~4.5 kg; material saving €16-22 per BEV. MHEV: common felt + cassette ≈ baseline cost (±€2). Mixed 50/50 → €8-11 blended; plus weight saving improves BEV range (not monetised). Baseline: shared-platform luxury SUVs commonly fit the MHEV-specification dash insulator to both powertrains — a 3.5-4.5 kg/m² EPDM/EVA heavy layer over 25 mm PU foam decoupler (total 9-11 kg) — because one part number is simpler, even though the BEV has no 6-cylinder engine orders (firing order 3 at 100-300 Hz) in the front bay. Proposal: make the base dash insulator BEV-tuned: a dual-density PET felt absorber (1,800 g/m² compressed skin over 1,200 g/m² lofted core, total ~4.5 kg) that targets e-drive whine (400-3,000 Hz) and road noise, common to both powertrains. For MHEV only, add a clip-in barrier cassette — a 3.0 kg/m² EVA heavy layer on a 10 mm PU decoupler covering just the 0.55 m² zone in line with the engine/transmission bell-housing — retained by 8 fir-tree clips on the same weld studs. Benchmark: JLR states the Range Rover Electric is 7 dB quieter than the V8 model and that NVH work concentrated on the electric drive unit (front EDU isolated in a noise-suppressing subframe), stiff HV cables and acoustic packs, i.e. the noise spectrum of a BEV is different from an ICE and the heavy dash barrier is not where BEV dB are won.

title: Shared third-row stow-in-floor module across MHEV and BEV rear floor pans

title: Two-zone HVAC plus rear seat microclimate replaces four-zone blend-door module
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deleted: 2 rear blend doors + 2 actuators (€18-22), split rear duct set (€8-10), rear climate panel (€14-18). Added: microclimate control logic in existing seat ECU and 2 extra seat-surface NTCs (€4-6). Net €36-44 on 4-zone vehicles; 60% of volume assumed 4-zone. Baseline: flagship luxury SUVs offer 4-zone climate: the front HVAC module carries 2 extra rear-zone temperature blend doors, 2 stepper actuators, split rear ducts to the B-pillars and console, and a rear climate control panel — ~25 parts, ~1.8 kg and €45-60. Proposal: standardise a 2-zone front module (driver/passenger) plus a common rear console outlet, and deliver rear-occupant individual temperature control via the seats: heated + ventilated row-2 outboard seats (already fitted on luxury trims) with a closed-loop seat-microclimate controller that biases surface temperature ±4 °C equivalent. Rear control moves to the existing rear touchscreen/switch. Benchmark: Gentherm launched its ClimateSense microclimate system on the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2024 (CELESTIQ carries 33 microclimate devices for individualised heating and cooling), and the Kia EV9 fits heated and ventilated seats as standard in rows 1 and 2 with two independent climate systems — individual comfort is increasingly delivered at the occupant rather than by additional air-blend zones.

title: Wading-mode auto-recirculation with sealed intake flap replaces raised intake plenum
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] [Off-road] Deleted: raised plenum extension and labyrinth separator (€14-18), A-pillar extension duct (€6-8), 1 of 2 drain valves (€1.5). Added: sealed shut-off flap + actuator (€7-9) and software calibration. Net €12-18. Baseline: off-road luxury SUVs rated for 850-900 mm wading protect the HVAC fresh-air path with a raised cowl intake plenum, a water-separator box with labyrinth and drain valves, and often an extended snorkel-style duct along the A-pillar — ~1.2 kg of extra mouldings (PP-T20 + EPDM seals) and €20-28 of content beyond a road SUV. Proposal: keep the standard road-car cowl intake and instead protect the cabin path by control: when the wade-sensing (ultrasonic mirror sensors or ride-height/ terrain-mode input) detects depth above 500 mm, the HVAC controller drives the recirculation door to full recirculation and closes a new sealed fresh-air shut-off flap (PP-T20 door with 2K TPV lip, IP-rated actuator) at the plenum. A single drain valve remains. Benchmark: in the Yangwang U8 emergency floating mode the air conditioning is switched to internal circulation automatically and windows close, with door seals keeping the cabin watertight for 30 minutes — showing that cabin water protection can be managed by mode logic plus sealing rather than raising hardware.

title: One pneumatic comfort block per seat drives lumbar, bolster and massage
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] One pump, one ECU and one manifold instead of two of each: €22-30 per seat saved on electronics/pumps, €4-6 on tubing and connectors. title: Moulded-in foam air channels replace spacer-fabric plenum in ventilated seats
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deleted per pad: spacer fabric + bag + adhesive + labour (€7-9 cushion, €6-8 back). Added: tooling inserts and TPU film (€2-3 per pad). Four pads (2 seats × cushion+back) on 80% of volume ventilated. Baseline: luxury ventilated seats typically use a fan under the cushion and back pushing/pulling air through a die-cut 3D polyester spacer-fabric layer (8-10 mm) encapsulated in a PU or TPU air-distribution "bag", glued on top of a foam pad that has a punched-through hole pattern, then perforated leather — 4-5 extra components per pad, hand-placed and bonded. Proposal: mould the air distribution directly into the PU foam pad: a branched channel network (6 × 10 mm channels, draft 3°) formed by tool inserts on the B-surface, sealed by a 0.2 mm TPU film skin applied in-mould (film placed in the cavity, foam bonds to it at 55-60 °C mould temperature, 4-5 min demould). Outlets align with the perforation zones of the trim. The spacer fabric and bag are deleted; the fan mounts to a moulded-in socket. Benchmark: Tesla introduced ventilated seats in the 2025 Model Y with a new patented design that combines structural airflow channels and specialised moulding techniques to improve ventilation and simplify manufacturing, and the Kia EV9 offers ventilated seats as standard in rows 1 and 2, showing ventilation moving to volume cost levels.

title: One legrest and recline actuator kit across passenger ottoman and row-2 lounge seats
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] One tool set for linkages/drives instead of two (€1.2-1.6M avoided → €4-5 per vehicle); tripled volume on drives and linkages cuts piece price 6-8% (€10-14 per 3-seat set). Applied to 50% of volume fitted with lounge seats. Baseline: luxury SUVs adding "zero-gravity" lounge functions typically engineer a front-passenger ottoman/legrest and the row-2 captain-seat legrest as separate mechanisms — different spindle motors, gear heads, four-bar linkages and stamped arms — ~38 parts per legrest and ~€85-110 each, plus a separate cushion-tilt actuator per seat. Proposal: define one legrest module — a 4-bar linkage in HC420LA 2.0 mm with one 12 V brushed DC spindle drive (1,500 N, Hall-sensed), PA66-GF30 bushings, and a hinged PP-LGF30 legrest carrier — plus one cushion-tilt drive, used on front passenger and both row-2 seats; only the mounting brackets and trim covers differ. Benchmark: the NIO ES8 third generation provides three zero-gravity seats (front passenger and both second-row) each able to lay back, tilt the cushion and extend a legrest; the AITO M9 second row has a 4-way electric legrest adjustable up to 75° with backrest recline to 43° and its front passenger seat converts into an ottoman; Li L9 row 2 has electric legrests — so a 3-seat set of lounge kinematics is now common in the segment, and building it from one module captures volume.

title: Gas-spring third-row fold with single solenoid release replaces twin-motor power fold
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deleted per side: 2 motors €30-38, LIN node/ECU share €10-12, sensors and harness €6-8. Added: locking gas spring €7-9, solenoid release €5-6, torsion bar €3-4. Net €31-39 per side, 2 sides on 3-row vehicles (assumed 60% of volume). Baseline: luxury 3-row SUVs often fit power-fold third-row 50:50 seats: per side a 12 V gear motor with cable/sector drive for the backrest, a second motor or actuator for headrest/cushion, a seat ECU or LIN node, Hall sensors and pinch-detection — ~€70-90 per side and ~2.2 kg. Proposal: replace the motors with a counterbalanced manual-assist mechanism: a locking gas spring (150-250 N, progressive) plus a torsion-bar counterbalance on the backrest pivot, so the back folds by gravity at a single solenoid release (12 V, 15 W pulse) triggered from the cargo-area switch or rear screen; raising is a one-hand pull with ≤50 N handle force at the strap. The headrest auto-folds through a Bowden cable from the backrest pivot. Benchmark: the Lucid Gravity — a ~$95k luxury SUV — uses manual third-row seats operated by the usual strap-and-handle system with power folding reserved for row 2, and the Defender 130 folds the third row with pull ropes; the Tesla Model Y 2025 offers power fold-flat from buttons in the trunk with motorised return for row 2 — so a convenient, button-triggered fold does not require motors for the return stroke.

title: TPV-overmoulded isolating clips on BEV high-voltage cable runs cut tonal transfer
description: [800V BEV] Deleted: 4-6 damping pads and their application (€10-14). Added: decoupling clips premium over hard clips €0.35-0.5 × 12 = €4-6. Net €5-9 per BEV; also −2 kg. Baseline: 800 V BEV underbody HV cables (50-95 mm², screened, stiff) are clipped hard to the floor and rear subframe with PA66 edge clips; inverter/e-motor tonal content (switching and order whine at 1-8 kHz) travels along the cable into the floor panel, and the fix is usually added damping: 4-6 extra LASD/bitumen pads or barrier patches in rear floor and cargo well (2-3 kg, €10-14). Proposal: replace the hard clips at the 10-14 body attachment points nearest the EDUs with decoupling clips — PA66-GF30 clip body with a 2K TPV (Shore A 45-55) cradle tuned to give a mount natural frequency below 80 Hz with the cable mass — and add one elastomeric hanger at each EDU exit. This lifts the isolation above the e-drive whine band and lets the extra floor damping pads be deleted. Benchmark: JLR states that on the Range Rover Electric stiff high-voltage cables could transmit sound and were fixed to reduce "machine noise" in the cabin, alongside the front EDU in a noise-suppressing subframe; the Model Y 2025 reports road noise −22% and wind noise −20% via sealing, insulation and glass, i.e. targeted path work rather than general mass.

title: Light through translucent knit: rear-mounted LED boards replace PMMA light-guide strips
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Per deleted light-guide module: guide + lip + LED driver + retainer €6-9; 12-18 modules deleted (€72-162 range, central €90-120). Added: 6-8 backlight boards with reflectors €40-55. Net €30-45 per vehicle. Baseline: luxury SUVs carry 25-40 m of ambient lighting built from PMMA side-emitting light guides (Ø3-5 mm) in chrome or satin-finish lip profiles, each fed by an RGB LED module with LIN driver at its end, plus diffusers and clip-on retainers — typically 30-40 light-guide modules, €120-180 per vehicle. Proposal: in zones where textile or knit surfaces are used (IP upper, door inserts, console sides), light passes through the material itself: 0.8 mm PC window in the substrate behind a 240 g/m² translucent knit, lit by short rear-mounted FR4 boards with 5-8 smart RGB LEDs (integrated driver, daisy-chained), with 15-20 mm air gap and a white PP reflector cavity for homogeneity (target uniformity ≥70%). Ambient strips are kept only in hard-trim zones. Expected reduction: 12-18 light-guide modules and their chrome lips. Benchmark: the BMW iX3 Neue Klasse uses textile surfaces in the cockpit that can be illuminated in places — its instrument panel fabric is backlit from below — rather than separate light lines.

title: One-shot laminated PET microfibre headliner replaces hand-wrapped Alcantara roof
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Material: ~4.3 m² × (€25-35 − €9-12) ≈ €60-100 saved on suede-equipped vehicles; labour: hand wrap 25-35 min → automated edge fold (~€12-18 saved). Applied to 35% of volume carrying suede headliner, net of €1.2M tool (€4 per equipped vehicle). Baseline: top-trim luxury SUVs specify Alcantara-type suede headliners: the suede (PET/PU microfibre, ~€25-35/m²) is cut and hand-wrapped onto a pre-formed PU/glass-fibre substrate with spray adhesive and edge-folding around sunroof and grab-handle openings — 25-35 min of manual labour per headliner and €140-190 of content for ~4 m² of cover. Proposal: use a non-woven, needle-punched and split PET microfibre suede-look cover (0.8 mm, 160-180 g/m², recyclable PET, ~€9-12/m²) pre-laminated with a PO hot-melt web, and form it in one shot with the substrate in a cold-form/back-compression tool (substrate pre-heated to 200 °C, 40-60 s) with integrated edge-folding slides at openings. Benchmark: the NIO ES8 third generation (2025) uses a microfibre rooflining as part of 52 m² of soft-touch materials, the Zeekr 9X has a suede roofliner and AITO M9 an Alcantara/suede headliner — Chinese luxury SUVs give a suede-feel roof broadly; our proposal achieves that look by process rather than by hand-wrapping a premium branded material.

title: Front-centre airbag shares inflator and cushion fabric family with seat side airbag
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Common inflator family at higher volume (−8-12% on inflator), shared fabric and coating spec (−5-8% cushion), one LHD/RHD part number (avoids one tool and halves inventory). €6-10 per vehicle. Baseline: as Euro NCAP far-side rating pushed front-centre airbags into luxury SUVs, they are often sourced as a bespoke module: a dedicated hybrid inflator (stored gas + pyro), a silicone-coated PA66 cushion with internal tethers, a separate housing and a driver-seat-specific mounting bracket, with LHD and RHD mirror-image parts — €40-55 per vehicle. Proposal: build the front-centre airbag from the seat side airbag family: same tubular hybrid inflator body (different gas charge only), same 470 dtex PA66 cut-and-sewn fabric spec and silicone coating weight (25-30 g/m²), same sewn soft-pack with a PA6-GF30 deployment chute, mounted on a symmetric inboard seat-frame bracket so one module fits driver seat LHD and RHD (rotated 180° about the vertical axis with a symmetric fold). Benchmark: the Kia EV9 (2024) is standard with 10 airbags including a front-row centre airbag alongside seat-mounted side airbags, and the Hyundai Ioniq 9 has 10 airbags across three rows — the centre airbag is now a volume part in E-GMP 800 V SUVs and can share the side-airbag supply chain.

title: Headrest armature common to speaker-ANC and plain variants via snap-in acoustic pod
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Avoids a second foam/cover/armature tool set per headrest position (€0.9-1.2M → €3-4 per vehicle); common hollow rod/shell at doubled volume (−€1-2 per headrest × 4); plain variant pays ~€0.75 per headrest for the two PP blanks. Baseline: luxury SUVs now offer headrest speakers (for audio, phone privacy and active noise cancellation) on top trims; these are engineered as a separate headrest: different steel armature (Ø10 mm rods with wider bow), dedicated PU foam mould with speaker cavities, different trim cover and harness through the rod — so each seat carries two headrest families (plain + speaker), with 2× foam and cover tools. Proposal: one headrest armature (hollow steel rod + PA6-GF30 core shell) with two lateral sockets; plain variant fills the sockets with foam-backed PP blanks, speaker variant snaps in two acoustic pods (40 mm neodymium full-range driver in PC/ABS enclosure + mesh). The rod is hollow (Ø10 × 1.2 mm tube, E355) on all variants so the harness path is free. One foam pour and one cover pattern with knit mesh zones serve both. Benchmark: the Range Rover L460 introduced noise-cancelling headrest speakers creating individual quiet zones, with a pair of speakers in each of the four main headrests, and the Cadillac Escalade IQ has speakers in the front-row head restraints as part of its AKG system with next-generation active noise cancellation

title: Nappa on contact zones only, bio-attributed PVC on seat sides and backs
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] ~2.0-2.5 m² of hide replaced by bio-attributed PVC: (€55 − €14) × 2.2 m² ≈ €80-95 per leather vehicle; improved hide yield €8-12. Applied to 45% of volume with full Nappa. Per vehicle blended €40-48. Baseline: many luxury SUVs with "full leather" trim specify Nappa on A-, B- and much of the C-surface of the seat (inserts, bolsters, side panels, back panels): ~5-6 m² of hide per vehicle at €45-70/m² cut-yield-adjusted, with 25-35% cutting loss from hide defects. Proposal: keep Nappa (1.0-1.2 mm, semi-aniline) on all body-contact surfaces — cushion and back inserts, bolster faces, headrest front, armrest tops — and switch the seat sides, back panels, lower skirt and headrest rear to a bio-attributed PVC-coated fabric (tall-oil-based plasticiser/polymer, on recycled PET knit carrier, 1.0 mm, grain and colour matched to the hide, €12-16/m²). Cut nesting on hide improves because only smaller panels remain (yield +5-8 points). Benchmark: the Zeekr 9X uses genuine Nappa leather on all areas of the seats that touch the body, the centre armrest and parts of the door panels while other areas use leatherette, and the Polestar 3 standard upholstery "MicroTech" is a bio-attributed vinyl with a recycled polyester carrier whose bio-attributed component is derived from tall oil.

title: Regenerated nylon-6 BCF yarn replaces virgin PA6 in tufted carpet face
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Zoned tufting: ~0.9 m² hidden under seats/console reduced 650 → 400 g/m² saves ~0.23 kg yarn at €6-7/kg ≈ €1.4-1.6 per vehicle plus back-coat €0.4; regenerated yarn assumed price-neutral ±€0.5. Recycled-content credit/compliance value not counted. Baseline: luxury SUV floor and load-floor carpets use virgin PA6 or PA6.6 bulk-continuous-filament (BCF) yarn tufted at 550-750 g/m² pile weight on a PET non-woven primary backing, with PE or latex back-coat. Proposal: specify chemically regenerated PA6 BCF (depolymerised from post-consumer nets/carpet back to caprolactam and re-polymerised, giving virgin-equivalent properties) for the face yarn at the same pile weight, and simultaneously drop pile weight on hidden zones (under seats and under console) to 400 g/m² by zoned tufting. Regenerated PA6 trades close to virgin PA6 price but tends to carry a CO₂/regulatory premium value; the cost lever here is mainly the zoned pile-weight reduction enabled by re-qualifying the yarn spec, plus avoiding future recycled-content penalties. Benchmark: Volvo states the EX90 carpets partly consist of regenerated polyamide and the car contains almost 50 kg of recycled plastics and bio-based materials; BMW states around one third of the new iX3 is made from secondary raw materials.

title: Fixed-vane slot vent with crossing jets replaces four discrete dash registers
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deleted: 2 centre registers (€36-50 including bezels and motor on top trims). Added: slot louver moulding €5-7, one duct flap + actuator €9-12, duct split €3. Net €18-28 per vehicle. Baseline: luxury SUV dashboards carry 4 front face-level registers (2 centre, 2 outboard), each with 8-12 vanes, a thumb-wheel, a shut-off damper, a chrome bezel, linkage pins and often an electric motor on top trims — 25-35 parts and €18-30 per register. Proposal: replace the two centre registers with one slot vent (full width of the centre stack, 12 mm high) with fixed vanes, where air direction is set by two crossing jets from upper and lower channels whose relative flow is controlled by a single motorised flap in the duct behind — the Coanda-effect principle used in recent EV slot vents. Outboard registers retained (side-window demist). The visible part is a single PP-T20 louver moulding with a satin PVD-film inlay. Benchmark: Tesla’s 2025 Model Y extends its "Air Wave" vent system to the first and second row with rear passengers able to control ventilation from the rear screen — i.e. the slot-vent concept is carried into a second application at volume cost.

title: Key-switch passenger airbag deactivation outside US deletes occupant-classification mat
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deleted on non-US vehicles: OCS mat + ECU €18-26, harness €2; added: deactivation switch €3-4 (or software menu €0-1), belt-reminder mat €3-4. Net €12-20 per non-US vehicle; assumed 60% non-US volume. Baseline: global luxury SUVs often fit the US-required occupant classification system (OCS) — a capacitive or pressure-sensing mat in the passenger cushion with its own ECU or a weight-sensing seat rail — to all markets, plus an indicator lamp, even where regulation allows a manual deactivation switch. Proposal: for EU, UK, China and RoW builds, delete the OCS mat/ECU and fit a mechanical key-operated (or menu-based with key-equivalent) passenger airbag deactivation switch that also controls the passenger seat side airbag and the related pretensioner stage; keep OCS for US/Canada (FMVSS 208 advanced airbag). The seat-cushion foam/pan carries an OCS-ready pocket so one cushion part remains. Belt-reminder sensing stays (thin seat-belt reminder mat or radar). Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 passenger airbag can be disabled to accommodate rear-facing child restraints, with the switch also controlling the passenger seat side airbags and parts of the seatbelt pretensioner.

title: Roll-formed CP1000 long-slide seat rail replaces stamped HSLA rail pair
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Per seat (2 rails pairs): steel mass −0.7-0.9 kg (€0.9-1.2), weld reinforcement deleted (€2-3), roll-forming vs progressive die conversion €1.5-2.5; ~€4.5-6.5 per seat; 2 seats row 2 + 2 front (if adopted) → €9-13 per vehicle (row 2 and front, conservatively). Baseline: row-2 captain or lounge seats with 200+ mm slide use stamped HSLA (HC420LA, 2.0-2.5 mm) upper and lower rails produced on progressive dies, often with a welded reinforcement for seat-belt anchorage loads; with long-slide floors (flat BEV floor or MHEV row-2) rails reach 500-650 mm length and 2.8-3.4 kg per seat. Proposal: roll-form both rail profiles from CP1000 (complex-phase, 1.6 mm) — a continuous roll-form line with in-line piercing and cut-off, 15-25 m/min — with the latch window pierced post-forming; delete the welded reinforcement by using a closed-hook interlocking profile for belt load path. Mass falls ~22-28% and press tonnage/ die cost drop. Same rail family serves row-2 on MHEV and BEV because rail length is set by cut-off, not by a die. Benchmark: the AITO M9 second-row seats slide over 200 mm on rails and recline to 43°, and the Zeekr 9X third row has 140 mm of fore/aft adjustment — long seat slide is now standard in China-frontier luxury SUVs, making rail mass and cost a growing item.

title: TPV wash-out cargo floor liner with moulded drain channel replaces carpeted load floor
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] [Off-road] Deleted: tufted/needle-punch carpet wrap + adhesive + edge-fold labour €14-18 on the board. Added: TPV skin and lip €9-12. Net €4-7 per equipped vehicle; load-floor replacement claims cut (€2-4 per equipped vehicle). Take rate 30%. Baseline: luxury SUV boot floors are a paper-honeycomb or PP-sandwich board (8-12 mm) wrapped in needle-punch or tufted textile (wrap, edge fold, spray adhesive, ~1.6 m²); owners who carry wet wetsuits, muddy boots, tow straps or recovery boards buy a separate accessory tray, and the textile wrap soaks, stains and delaminates at the folded edges, leading to dealer replacement of the whole board (€250-400). Proposal: for adventure trims, laminate a compression-moulded TPV skin (PP/EPDM, Shore A 80, 1.8 mm, tread grain) to the PP sandwich board in the same press stroke that forms the board, with an integral 6 mm upstand around the perimeter and a fall of 1° toward a rear gutter that exits through a tethered EPDM plug at the tailgate sill; the upstand retains ~1.5 l. The skin is grained and colour-matched to the boot side trims so the space still reads as premium. Benchmark: Ineos built the Grenadier cabin to be hosed out, and Land Rover offers the Defender 130 with a hard-wearing rubber mat alternative to carpet - both treat washable surfaces as factory content rather than accessories.

title: Wipe-clean PU-coated technical textile seat inserts for off-road trims instead of perforated leather
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] [Off-road] Insert/bolster area ~2.8 m² per vehicle: leather €45-70/m² vs PU technical textile €18-25/m² → €70-120 saved per equipped vehicle; seat-cover warranty claims on off-road trims reduced (€3-6). Take rate 30% → €22-38 per vehicle averaged. Baseline: off-road-branded luxury trims still default to perforated semi-aniline leather inserts, which absorb mud, sand and water, stain and crack at perforations; seat-cover warranty and goodwill replacements cluster on outboard bolsters and inserts. Proposal: on off-road trims, specify a PU-coated technical textile for inserts and bolsters: water-based PU (solvent-free) on a recycled PET knit carrier, 1.1 mm, laser-perforated with small (0.8 mm) holes for ventilation, with a fluorine-free hydrophobic/oleophobic topcoat, rated Martindale ≥ 100,000 rubs. Contact-zone haptics are tuned to leather softness (grain embossing, matte topcoat). Benchmark: JLR offers Ultrafabrics, a PU material with the tactile qualities of leather but about 30% lighter and generating about a quarter of the CO₂, on the Range Rover’s leather-free interior, and the Ineos Grenadier uses wipe-down, stain-resistant seat upholstery for hose-out use — combining luxury haptics with washability.
